notes: LSAT Swipe question bank. All questions are original (written for this app), not LSAC material. Labels match the Taxonomy tab exactly.

questions.stimulus: A café owner surveyed 200 customers, and 70 percent said they would buy a new oat-milk latte if it were offered. The owner concludes that adding the latte will raise monthly revenue, since most customers will buy it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to consider that customers who buy the latte might stop buying other drinks
choices.B: takes for granted that customers who say they would buy a product will actually buy it
choices.C: relies on a sample too small to represent the café's customers
choices.D: assumes that oat milk is more popular than other milk alternatives
choices.E: ignores the possibility that the café's competitors offer a similar drink

questions.explanation:
The premise is about what customers said they'd do; the conclusion treats it as what they will do. B names that gap, and it's the gap the 'since' clause rests on.
A — A real weakness, but the argument's stated reasoning goes from 'said they would' to 'will'; B is the flaw it actually commits.
C — Nothing shows 200 customers is unrepresentative. Survey size isn't the problem; survey content is.
D — The argument never compares oat milk with other milks.
E — Competitors don't change whether this café's customers follow through.

traps.C: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: Riverton's city council plans to convert two downtown traffic lanes into protected bike lanes. Council members argue that the conversion will reduce downtown traffic congestion, because residents who now drive downtown for short errands will bicycle instead once they have a safe route.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the council members' argument depends?

choices.A: Every resident who drives downtown for short errands would prefer to bicycle if a safe route existed.
choices.B: The reduction in driving by residents who switch to bicycling will not be outweighed by the effect of losing two traffic lanes.
choices.C: Protected bike lanes provide cyclists with a safe route.
choices.D: Other cities that installed protected bike lanes saw downtown congestion fall afterward.
choices.E: Bicycling downtown is faster than driving downtown for short errands.

questions.explanation:
The plan takes road space away from cars. Fewer drivers only means less congestion if losing two lanes doesn't cancel that out. Negate B — the lost lanes more than offset the drop in drivers — and the conclusion collapses.
A — 'Every' is far more than needed; the argument works if enough drivers switch.
C — The argument already treats the lanes as a safe route. Repeating that adds nothing.
D — Other cities' results could support the plan, but the argument doesn't depend on them.
E — Plausible in real life, but the argument's mechanism is safety, not speed.

questions.stimulus: A nutrition researcher found that office workers who kept a filled water bottle on their desks drank, on average, 40 percent more water during the workday than office workers who did not. The researcher concludes that keeping a filled water bottle in view causes people to drink more water.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?

choices.A: Workers who keep water bottles on their desks are more likely than other workers to exercise regularly.
choices.B: Many office workers report that they forget to drink water when they are busy.
choices.C: When workers who had not kept water bottles on their desks were given filled bottles, their water intake rose to match that of workers who already kept bottles.
choices.D: Drinking more water during the workday improves concentration.
choices.E: Some workers who keep water bottles on their desks drink less water than some workers who do not.

questions.explanation:
The evidence is a correlation; the conclusion is causal. Maybe people who already drink a lot are the ones who keep bottles. C is a mini-experiment: give bottles to non-keepers and their intake rises. That points to the bottle as the cause.
A — Exercise is an alternative cause of drinking more water. That weakens.
B — Sounds true, but it doesn't connect the bottle to the extra drinking.
D — Why drinking water is good is irrelevant to whether the bottle causes it.
E — Averages already allow some individual exceptions. This compares individuals in a way the argument doesn't need.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Harlow County began requiring all new restaurant employees to complete a food-safety course. This year, the number of reported foodborne-illness cases traced to Harlow County restaurants fell by 30 percent. County officials conclude that the course requirement was responsible for the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' conclusion?

choices.A: Employees who completed the course scored significantly higher on food-safety tests than employees who had not taken it.
choices.B: Foodborne illnesses can also be contracted from food prepared at home.
choices.C: The course requirement applied only to employees hired after the requirement took effect.
choices.D: This year, the county health department cut its staff of inspectors in half, sharply reducing the number of illness reports it could investigate and trace to a source.
choices.E: The number of restaurants operating in Harlow County increased slightly this year.

questions.explanation:
The evidence is a drop in reported and traced cases. D says the county lost much of its ability to trace cases, so fewer would be traced whether or not actual illness fell. That's an alternative explanation for the data.
A — Shows the course taught something. That supports the officials.
B — Home-cooked illness isn't counted in the restaurant figures.
C — The stimulus already says 'new' employees. Nothing new here.
E — More restaurants with fewer traced cases makes the drop look more impressive. That strengthens, if anything.

questions.stimulus: Every member of the Dalton Debate Society who competes at the state tournament must first win a regional round. No one who wins a regional round is eligible for the novice award. Priya and Marco are both members of the society. Priya competed at the state tournament this year, and Marco is eligible for the novice award.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Marco has never competed at the state tournament.
choices.B: Every member who wins a regional round competes at the state tournament.
choices.C: Priya is not eligible for the novice award.
choices.D: Some members who won a regional round this year did not compete at the state tournament.
choices.E: Marco will not win a regional round next year.

questions.explanation:
Chain: state tournament → won a regional round → not eligible for novice award. Priya competed at state, so she won a regional round, so she's not eligible. C.
A — The chain only tells you about this year. 'Never' goes too far.
B — Flips the first rule. Competing at state requires a regional win; a regional win doesn't guarantee competing.
D — Could be true, but nothing forces it.
E — Eligibility is about now. Nothing says what Marco does next year.

questions.stimulus: Critics of the proposed four-day school week claim that it will hurt student achievement because students will spend fewer hours in class. But districts that have adopted the schedule lengthened each remaining school day, so total instructional time barely changed. The critics' prediction, then, rests on a misunderstanding of how the schedule works. That said, the four-day week may still create real difficulties for working parents who must arrange childcare on the fifth day.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: The critics' claim that the four-day week will hurt achievement is based on a mistaken view of how the schedule affects class time.
choices.B: The four-day school week will not hurt student achievement.
choices.C: Districts that adopted the four-day week lengthened their remaining school days.
choices.D: The four-day school week may create difficulties for working parents.
choices.E: Total instructional time is the most important factor in student achievement.

questions.explanation:
'Then' flags the conclusion: the critics' prediction rests on a misunderstanding. The longer-days fact supports it. The last sentence is a concession, not the point. A.
B — The author only attacks the critics' reasoning. Showing their reason is bad doesn't prove achievement won't drop.
C — A premise.
D — A concession tacked on after the conclusion.
E — The author never ranks factors in achievement.

questions.stimulus: At Lakeside Hospital, patients operated on by Dr. Okafor have a higher rate of post-surgical complications than patients operated on by any other surgeon at the hospital. Yet Dr. Okafor is widely regarded by her colleagues as the most skilled surgeon on staff.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?

choices.A: Surgeons with more years of experience generally have lower complication rates than less experienced surgeons.
choices.B: Post-surgical complication rates at Lakeside Hospital are lower than the national average.
choices.C: Patients often judge a surgeon's skill by his or her bedside manner.
choices.D: Dr. Okafor's complication rate has risen over the past two years.
choices.E: Because of her skill, Dr. Okafor is assigned the hospital's most complex and highest-risk cases.

questions.explanation:
You need both facts to be true together. If the best surgeon gets the hardest cases, a higher complication rate is expected. E.
A — Sounds true in general, but it doesn't explain anything about Dr. Okafor.
B — Comparing the hospital to the nation doesn't touch the gap between Okafor and her colleagues.
C — The stimulus is about colleagues' judgment, not patients'.
D — Makes the puzzle worse, not better.

questions.stimulus: Any policy that raises the cost of entering a profession reduces the number of people from low-income backgrounds who enter it. The state's new rule requiring all prospective electricians to complete a two-year apprenticeship raises the cost of entering the profession. Therefore, the rule will reduce the diversity of the state's electricians.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: A profession's diversity is reduced only if fewer people from low-income backgrounds enter it.
choices.B: Two-year apprenticeships cost more than the training electricians previously needed.
choices.C: Most electricians in the state come from low-income backgrounds.
choices.D: Any reduction in the number of people from low-income backgrounds entering a profession reduces that profession's diversity.
choices.E: Some professions with long training requirements are less diverse than professions with short ones.

questions.explanation:
Premises get you to: the rule → fewer low-income entrants. The conclusion jumps to: reduced diversity. The new term is diversity. D bridges exactly: fewer low-income entrants → reduced diversity. Add it and the conclusion is guaranteed.
A — 'Only if' makes fewer low-income entrants a requirement for reduced diversity, not a guarantee of it. Backwards.
B — The stimulus already says the rule raises costs.
C — Even if most electricians are low-income, nothing links fewer of them to less diversity.
E — 'Some' professions tells you nothing certain about this one.

questions.stimulus: Some economists predict that raising Fenwick's minimum wage will lead small businesses there to cut jobs. However, when the neighboring city of Alder raised its minimum wage three years ago, employment at its small businesses actually grew. Admittedly, Alder's economy was expanding rapidly at the time, which may have masked job losses. Still, Alder's experience gives reason to doubt that a higher minimum wage would cause Fenwick's small businesses to cut jobs.
questions.stem: The claim that Alder's economy was expanding rapidly at the time plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It acknowledges a consideration that weakens the force of the evidence the argument offers against the economists' prediction.
choices.B: It establishes that the economists' prediction is correct.
choices.C: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
choices.D: It is a premise that directly supports the argument's main conclusion.
choices.E: It explains why employment at Alder's small businesses grew despite the minimum-wage increase.

questions.explanation:
'Admittedly' flags a concession. The author's evidence is Alder's job growth; the booming economy is a reason that evidence might be less telling. The author grants it, then says 'Still'. A.
B — It weakens the counterevidence a bit. It doesn't prove the economists right.
C — The conclusion is the last sentence.
D — It cuts against the conclusion, not for it.
E — It offers a possible reason the losses were hidden, but the author doesn't present it as the explanation of the growth, and that misses its job in the argument.

questions.stimulus: Mayor Ruiz claims that the city's new recycling program has failed because the volume of material collected for recycling dropped last year. But last year the city also launched a campaign urging residents to buy fewer packaged goods, and household trash volume fell by an even larger percentage. A drop in recycling volume is exactly what we would expect if residents were simply using less packaging.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by

choices.A: showing that the mayor's conclusion contradicts one of the mayor's own premises
choices.B: arguing that reducing consumption is more important than recycling
choices.C: questioning the accuracy of the data on recycling volume
choices.D: attacking the mayor's motives for criticizing the program
choices.E: offering an alternative explanation for the evidence the mayor cites as showing that the program failed

questions.explanation:
The author accepts that recycling volume fell, then gives another reason it fell: people used less packaging. That's an alternative explanation for the mayor's evidence. E.
A — The mayor's premises never contradict each other.
B — Matches the topic, but the author never ranks recycling against reduced consumption.
C — The author accepts the data and reinterprets it. Challenging its meaning isn't challenging its accuracy.
D — No attack on motives.

traps.B: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus:
Nadia: The town should ban gas-powered leaf blowers. Their noise disrupts residents who work from home, and electric models are now a practical alternative, widely available at comparable prices.
Owen: Electric leaf blowers are not yet a practical substitute. Commercial landscapers need equipment that runs all day, and current electric models' batteries last under an hour.
questions.stem: Nadia's and Owen's statements provide the most support for the claim that they disagree over whether

choices.A: gas-powered leaf blowers are noisy enough to disrupt residents
choices.B: the town should ban gas-powered leaf blowers
choices.C: electric leaf blowers are currently a practical replacement for gas-powered ones
choices.D: commercial landscapers should be exempt from noise regulations
choices.E: residents who work from home deserve more consideration than landscapers

questions.explanation:
Nadia says electric models are a practical alternative. Owen says they're not a practical substitute. Both speak to it, and they're opposite. C.
A — Only Nadia talks about noise.
B — The obvious fight, but Owen never states a view on the ban. He only attacks one of Nadia's reasons.
D — Neither discusses exemptions.
E — Neither weighs these groups against each other.

questions.stimulus: Every restaurant in this district that has earned a Michelin star sources its produce locally. Bistro Lumen, a restaurant in this district, sources its produce locally. So Bistro Lumen must have earned a Michelin star.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?

choices.A: Every marathon runner on the team trains at dawn. Lena does not train at dawn, so Lena is not a marathon runner on the team.
choices.B: Bistro Lumen's chef claims that locally sourced produce tastes better. But the chef profits from selling local produce, so the claim must be false.
choices.C: No one who skipped the prep course passed the bar exam. Jamal did not skip the prep course, so Jamal must have passed the bar exam.
choices.D: Every award-winning novel on this shelf was published by Harrow Press. The novel at the far left of this shelf was published by Harrow Press, so it must be an award-winning novel.
choices.E: Some violinists in the orchestra studied in Vienna. Ana is a violinist in the orchestra, so Ana must have studied in Vienna.

questions.explanation:
Structure: All X are Y. This one is Y. So it must be X. That reverses the conditional (star → local, not local → star). D does the same: award-winner → Harrow; this one is Harrow; so it's an award-winner.
A — Valid contrapositive. The stem asks for a flawed argument.
B — Same restaurant topic, completely different flaw (attacking the source).
C — A conditional error, but a different one: it negates both sides (skipped → failed, so didn't skip → passed) instead of reversing.
E — Same 'must' about an individual, but it starts from 'some', not 'every'. Different flaw.

traps.B: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: Marisol borrowed her roommate's car without asking because she needed to drive an injured neighbor to the emergency room, and no other transportation was available. Although Marisol would normally need her roommate's permission, her action was justified.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.A: People should always ask permission before using property that belongs to someone else.
choices.B: It is permissible to use another person's property without permission when doing so is necessary to address a medical emergency and no reasonable alternative exists.
choices.C: A person who uses another's property without permission should compensate the owner for any resulting costs.
choices.D: Using another person's property without permission is justified only if the owner would have consented had he or she been asked.
choices.E: A person who is injured should seek medical care as quickly as possible.

questions.explanation:
Facts: medical emergency, no alternative. Conclusion: justified. B says emergency + no alternative → permissible. The facts trigger it, and it delivers the conclusion.
A — Says she was wrong. Opposite direction.
C — About compensation, not whether the act was justified.
D — 'Only if' gives a requirement, not a guarantee, and we don't know whether the roommate would have consented.
E — Supports the neighbor going to the ER, not Marisol taking the car without asking.

questions.stimulus: Students at Greenfield High who joined the school's chess club this year raised their math grades by an average of half a letter grade. The principal concludes that playing chess improves students' math performance and plans to require all ninth graders to take a chess class.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the principal's argument?

choices.A: whether chess is more popular than other extracurricular activities at Greenfield High
choices.B: whether the chess club meets during school hours
choices.C: whether some ninth graders would object to being required to take a chess class
choices.D: whether every student who joined the chess club raised his or her math grades
choices.E: whether students who joined the chess club also began receiving additional math tutoring this year

questions.explanation:
The principal infers cause from a before-and-after change. Tutoring is a competing cause. If yes, the argument weakens; if no, a key alternative is ruled out. Either answer matters. E.
A — Popularity doesn't bear on whether chess improves math.
B — When the club meets doesn't affect the causal claim.
C — Matters for the policy's popularity, not for whether chess causes better grades.
D — An average can rise without every student improving. 'Every' isn't needed.

questions.stimulus: In a study of 500 adults, those who reported reading printed books for at least 30 minutes before bed fell asleep, on average, 12 minutes faster than those who reported using a phone or tablet during that time. The difference persisted even among participants whose phones and tablets used a filter that reduced blue light.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Blue light alone does not fully account for the difference in how quickly the two groups fell asleep.
choices.B: Reading printed books before bed causes people to fall asleep faster.
choices.C: Blue-light filters do not reduce blue light.
choices.D: People who use phones before bed sleep fewer total hours than people who read printed books.
choices.E: Most adults prefer reading printed books to using phones before bed.

questions.explanation:
Filtered devices still showed the gap, so something besides blue light is involved. A is modest and follows directly.
B — The study is a correlation. It doesn't establish cause.
C — The stimulus says the filters reduced blue light. C contradicts it.
D — Total sleep time is never measured.
E — Preferences aren't in the data.

questions.stimulus: Each of the five musicians in the Halvorsen Quintet has won a major international solo competition. Therefore, the Halvorsen Quintet is certain to be one of the finest chamber ensembles performing today.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

choices.A: relies on the judgments of competition panels whose members may have been biased
choices.B: draws a conclusion about all chamber ensembles from a single example
choices.C: presumes that a group must have a certain quality because each of its members has that quality
choices.D: takes for granted that musicians who win solo competitions enjoy performing in groups
choices.E: treats the fact that each musician won a competition as evidence that each musician is skilled

questions.explanation:
Excellent individuals don't guarantee an excellent ensemble. That's the part-to-whole flaw. C.
A — A generic worry about judges, and the argument's problem isn't the judges.
B — The conclusion is about one ensemble, not all of them.
D — Enjoyment is beside the point. The gap is about the group's quality.
E — Accurately describes a step in the argument, but that step is reasonable. It isn't the flaw.

questions.stimulus: Calloway, a software firm, switched its employees to a four-day workweek. Over the following six months, the number of projects completed per employee rose 15 percent compared with the previous six months. Calloway's CEO concludes that the shorter workweek made employees more productive.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the CEO's argument?

choices.A: Employees reported higher job satisfaction after the switch.
choices.B: Several other firms that adopted a four-day workweek reported no change in productivity.
choices.C: The four-day workweek was especially popular among employees with long commutes.
choices.D: Projects completed after the switch were, on average, about as complex as those completed before it.
choices.E: At the start of the six-month period, Calloway laid off a fifth of its employees, mostly those who had completed the fewest projects.

questions.explanation:
'Per employee' is an average. Cut the least productive people and the average rises even if no one works better. E explains the 15 percent without the schedule.
A — Happier employees fit the CEO's story. Supports, if anything.
B — Other firms' results don't show what caused Calloway's change.
C — Popularity isn't productivity.
D — Rules out 'they just did easier projects'. That strengthens.

questions.stimulus: At the Tel Harun excavation, archaeologists found charred seeds of cultivated barley in soil layers dated to 9,000 years ago, about 500 years earlier than any previously known evidence of barley cultivation in the region. The archaeologists conclude that barley cultivation in the region began at least 500 years earlier than had been believed.
questions.stem: The archaeologists' conclusion depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: The seeds did not work their way down into the 9,000-year-old layers from more recent layers.
choices.B: Tel Harun was the first site in the region where barley was cultivated.
choices.C: The method used to date the Tel Harun layers is more accurate than the methods used at other sites in the region.
choices.D: Barley was the most important crop grown at Tel Harun.
choices.E: The charred seeds came from cultivated barley rather than wild barley.

questions.explanation:
The seeds' age is inferred from the layer they sit in. If they migrated down from younger soil, the layer's date says nothing about them. Negate A and the conclusion falls apart.
B — Being first in the region is far more than the argument needs.
C — The dating only has to be accurate enough, not better than everyone else's.
D — The crop's importance is irrelevant to when cultivation began.
E — The stimulus already says the seeds are cultivated barley. This repeats a premise.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the population of red foxes on Bram Island declined sharply, while the population of the island's ground-nesting seabirds tripled. Ecologists hypothesize that the seabird increase resulted from reduced predation by foxes on seabird eggs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologists' hypothesis?

choices.A: Ground-nesting seabirds tend to lay more eggs per year than cliff-nesting seabirds.
choices.B: The seabirds on Bram Island also benefited from a decade-long increase in the fish stocks they feed on.
choices.C: The decline in the fox population was caused by a disease that does not affect birds.
choices.D: On a nearby island where the fox population remained stable over the same decade, ground-nesting seabird populations did not increase.
choices.E: Seabird populations on Bram Island were already rising before the fox population began to decline.

questions.explanation:
D is a control group: same decade, similar island, foxes unchanged, no seabird boom. That makes the fox decline a better explanation for Bram Island's boom.
A — Ground vs. cliff nesters is a comparison the argument doesn't need.
B — More food is a competing cause. Weakens.
C — Why the foxes declined doesn't matter to whether their decline helped the seabirds.
E — If the rise started before the fox decline, something else was driving it. Weakens.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A journalist should not publish information obtained from a confidential source unless the information is of significant public interest and the journalist has made a reasonable effort to verify it independently.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.A: Lena should publish her confidential source's account of the zoning vote, since the account is of significant public interest and she verified it against two independent records.
choices.B: Ravi should not publish the memo his confidential source gave him because, although it concerns a matter of significant public interest, he has not been able to verify any of it.
choices.C: Tom should not publish a story based on public court records, because the records are not of significant public interest.
choices.D: Mia should publish her confidential source's tip about a city contract because she trusts the source completely.
choices.E: Jae should not publish any information from confidential sources, because such sources are usually unreliable.

questions.explanation:
Publish → public interest AND verified. Contrapositive: missing either → don't publish. Ravi's memo isn't verified, so he shouldn't publish. B.
A — Meeting both conditions doesn't mean she should publish. The principle only says when not to. Backwards.
C — Court records aren't from a confidential source. The principle doesn't apply.
D — Trusting the source isn't independent verification, so the principle says don't publish.
E — Goes far beyond the principle, which allows publishing when both conditions are met.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant critic: Of the diners who posted reviews of Tamsin's Kitchen on a popular review site last year, 85 percent gave it the site's lowest rating. Clearly, most people who ate at Tamsin's Kitchen last year were dissatisfied with their meals.
questions.stem: The critic's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: overlooks the possibility that some diners who gave the lowest rating ate at the restaurant more than once
choices.B: concludes that the restaurant's food is poor on the basis of evidence about service
choices.C: presumes that the review site's rating scale accurately reflects diners' opinions
choices.D: fails to consider that diners who post reviews may not be representative of diners in general
choices.E: treats the opinion of a majority of reviewers as though it were the opinion of every reviewer

questions.explanation:
The evidence covers only diners who chose to post reviews; the conclusion covers everyone who ate there. People with bad experiences may be far more motivated to post. That unrepresentative sample is the flaw.
A — Repeat visits don't change whether reviewers represent all diners.
B — The argument never separates food from service; it just says diners were dissatisfied with their meals.
C — The argument does take ratings at face value, but even perfectly accurate ratings would still come from a skewed group. The scale isn't the gap.
E — The conclusion says "most," not "all," so it doesn't overgeneralize in this way.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: Any theory that cannot be proven is merely a guess. But scientists themselves acknowledge that no scientific theory can be proven with absolute certainty. So every scientific theory is merely a guess, no better supported than any other speculation.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: relies on a term that is used in one sense in a premise and in a different sense in the conclusion
choices.B: takes for granted that scientists are reliable judges of whether their theories can be proven
choices.C: draws a conclusion about all scientific theories on the basis of evidence about only some of them
choices.D: assumes that what is true of science as a whole must be true of each scientific theory
choices.E: infers that because a theory is unproven, it must be false

questions.explanation:
"Merely a guess" in the first premise refers to anything short of absolute proof; in the conclusion it suddenly means something "no better supported than any other speculation." Lacking certainty is not the same as lacking support. The argument shifts meanings.
B — The scientists' acknowledgment is used as a premise, but the argument's problem is the shift in what "guess" means, not the scientists' reliability.
C — The premise already covers all scientific theories ("no scientific theory"), so there's no hasty generalization.
D — No part-to-whole move occurs; the premise is already about each theory.
E — The argument never concludes that theories are false, only that they are guesses.

traps.D: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: Career counselor: To be hired as a staff attorney at the Hollis Law Group, an applicant must have passed the bar exam on the first attempt. Devon passed the bar exam on his first attempt. Therefore, if Devon applies for a staff attorney position at the Hollis Law Group, he will be hired.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the counselor's reasoning?

choices.A: It fails to consider that Devon may not want to work at the Hollis Law Group.
choices.B: It presumes without justification that passing the bar exam on the first attempt reflects legal skill.
choices.C: It treats a requirement for being hired as if it were enough to guarantee being hired.
choices.D: It relies on information about one law firm to draw a conclusion about law firms generally.
choices.E: It infers that a condition is required for being hired merely because most hired applicants met it.

questions.explanation:
Passing on the first try is necessary for being hired ("must have"). The conclusion treats it as sufficient. Devon meets one requirement; nothing says it's the only one.
A — The conclusion is conditional: "if Devon applies." Whether he wants to apply doesn't matter.
B — Skill never enters the argument; the problem is the conditional logic.
D — The conclusion is only about the Hollis Law Group.
E — The premise states the requirement outright; nothing is inferred from "most."

questions.stimulus: To reduce the number of patients who miss medical appointments, Brightwell Clinic will begin sending text-message reminders the day before each appointment. Administrators predict the reminders will substantially reduce missed appointments.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the administrators' prediction depends?

choices.A: Most of the clinic's patients prefer text messages to phone calls.
choices.B: A substantial number of missed appointments at the clinic occur because patients forget about them.
choices.C: Every patient at the clinic owns a mobile phone capable of receiving text messages.
choices.D: Text-message reminders have reduced missed appointments at other clinics.
choices.E: Patients who miss appointments are less healthy than patients who keep them.

questions.explanation:
Reminders only help patients who would otherwise forget. If almost all missed appointments happen for other reasons, like transportation, cost, or illness, reminders can't substantially reduce them. Negate this and the prediction fails.
A — Preference between methods isn't required. Texts need only work, not be preferred.
C — "Every" is more than needed; a substantial reduction requires only that many patients receive the texts.
D — Evidence from other clinics could support the plan, but the prediction doesn't depend on it.
E — Patients' health has nothing to do with whether reminders reduce missed appointments.

questions.stimulus: Marine biologist: Over the past fifteen years, the average size of adult cod caught off the Kellen coast has declined steadily. During that period, commercial fishing fleets have targeted the largest cod, since those fetch the highest prices. Because size in cod is partly inherited, this selective fishing has likely caused the population to evolve toward smaller adult size.
questions.stem: The biologist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.A: cod populations elsewhere have not declined in average size
choices.B: fishing fleets will continue to target the largest cod in the future
choices.C: size in cod is determined more by inheritance than by environment
choices.D: commercial fishing is the only human activity that affects cod off the Kellen coast
choices.E: the decline in average size is not entirely due to cod being caught before they have had time to reach their full adult size

questions.explanation:
An alternative explanation: fish are smaller because they're caught younger, not because the population evolved. If the decline were entirely due to catching younger fish, the evolutionary conclusion would lose its support. The argument must rule that out.
A — Other populations' trends aren't needed. They could decline for their own reasons.
B — The argument explains a past change; future fishing practices are irrelevant.
C — The premise says size is "partly" inherited; the argument doesn't need inheritance to be the dominant factor.
D — "Only" is far stronger than needed. Other activities can exist as long as they don't explain the size decline.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: A promise made under duress creates no obligation to keep it. Moreover, any promise extracted by an explicit threat of harm is made under duress. Therefore, Lena has no obligation to repay the loan she promised to repay to Corbin.
questions.stem: The ethicist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Lena's promise to repay Corbin was extracted by an explicit threat of harm.
choices.B: Only promises made under duress fail to create an obligation.
choices.C: Lena would not have promised to repay Corbin if she had not been under duress.
choices.D: Corbin has extracted promises from others by explicit threats of harm.
choices.E: Lena is unable to repay the loan.

questions.explanation:
Chain: explicit threat → duress → no obligation. The premises never connect Lena's promise to the chain. Adding that her promise was extracted by an explicit threat guarantees the conclusion.
B — This says no obligation → duress, which is the reverse of what's needed, and still doesn't connect Lena.
C — Close, but it doesn't say she actually was under duress. "Wouldn't have promised unless" is a counterfactual and doesn't establish the fact.
D — Corbin's dealings with others say nothing certain about Lena's promise.
E — Inability to pay is a different issue from whether an obligation exists.

questions.stimulus: Over the five years since the town of Pell Harbor lowered its downtown speed limit from 30 to 20 miles per hour, the number of pedestrian injuries downtown has fallen by half. Town officials credit the lower speed limit with the reduction.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the officials' position?

choices.A: Most pedestrian injuries in Pell Harbor occur in the evening.
choices.B: The number of people walking downtown has not decreased over the past five years.
choices.C: Several downtown crosswalks were repainted shortly after the speed limit was lowered.
choices.D: Pedestrian injuries in neighboring towns also fell by half during the same period.
choices.E: Most residents of Pell Harbor supported lowering the speed limit.

questions.explanation:
A drop in injuries could simply reflect fewer pedestrians. Ruling out that alternative makes the speed limit a stronger candidate for the cause.
A — When injuries happen says nothing about whether the speed limit reduced them.
C — An alternative cause of fewer injuries. That weakens.
D — If injuries fell just as much where limits didn't change, something other than the speed limit is likely responsible. This weakens.
E — Popularity doesn't show the policy caused the drop.

questions.stimulus: Researchers found that elderly adults who regularly played a musical instrument scored significantly higher on memory tests than elderly adults who did not. The researchers hypothesize that playing an instrument helps preserve memory in old age.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.A: Many elderly adults who play an instrument report that playing improves their mood.
choices.B: Elderly adults who play an instrument are more likely than others to have attended college.
choices.C: Learning to play an instrument is more difficult for elderly adults than for children.
choices.D: Some elderly adults who do not play an instrument score higher on memory tests than some who do.
choices.E: Among elderly adults who had taken up an instrument only after retiring, those who practiced more hours per week showed less memory decline over the following decade.

questions.explanation:
This points to playing as the cause. Starting after retirement rules out "people with good memories became musicians in youth," and more practice going with less decline is a dose–response pattern.
A — Mood isn't memory, and self-reports of mood don't support the causal claim.
B — Education is a plausible alternative cause of better memory. That weakens.
C — Difficulty of learning doesn't bear on whether playing preserves memory.
D — Group averages allow individual exceptions; this neither helps nor hurts.

questions.stimulus: Since the Rowan Public Library extended its hours to stay open until 10 p.m., the number of books checked out each month has increased by 25 percent. The library's director concludes that the extended hours have made the library more accessible to residents who work during the day.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the director's conclusion?

choices.A: Some residents who work during the day still find it difficult to visit the library.
choices.B: Other libraries in the region have also considered extending their hours.
choices.C: Nearly all of the increase in checkouts has occurred during the library's original daytime hours.
choices.D: Residents who visit the library in the evening tend to check out more books per visit than daytime visitors.
choices.E: The library's evening staff are paid more per hour than its daytime staff.

questions.explanation:
If the new evening hours account for almost none of the increase, the extended hours can't be what made the library more accessible. The data points elsewhere.
A — The director doesn't claim every daytime worker now visits. Some exceptions are compatible with more accessibility.
B — What other libraries consider doesn't affect this conclusion.
D — This makes evening hours look responsible for more checkouts, which supports the director.
E — Staff costs are irrelevant to whether access improved.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Hospitals that adopted the new electronic records system report finding 40 percent more medication errors than they found before adopting it. This shows that the new system actually makes medication errors more likely, and hospitals should abandon it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the columnist's argument?

choices.A: Hospitals that adopted the system were larger, on average, than those that did not.
choices.B: Medication errors can have serious consequences for patients.
choices.C: Some hospitals that adopted the new system found fewer medication errors than before.
choices.D: The new system automatically flags discrepancies between prescriptions and dispensed medications, many of which previously went unnoticed.
choices.E: Training staff to use the new system took several months at most hospitals.

questions.explanation:
The data is about errors found, not errors made. If the system catches errors that used to go undetected, the increase reflects better detection, possibly even fewer real errors.
A — Size differences don't explain a before-and-after increase within the same hospitals.
B — This shows why errors matter, not whether the system causes them.
C — A few exceptions don't overturn the overall 40 percent increase.
E — Training time doesn't explain why more errors are being found.

questions.stimulus: Every applicant to the Fairmont Fellowship who submitted a writing sample was interviewed. No applicant who was interviewed was rejected without written feedback. Some applicants who received written feedback were nevertheless awarded the fellowship.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Every applicant who was awarded the fellowship submitted a writing sample.
choices.B: Some applicants who were interviewed were rejected.
choices.C: Every applicant who received written feedback was interviewed.
choices.D: No applicant who submitted a writing sample was rejected without written feedback.
choices.E: Some applicants who submitted a writing sample were awarded the fellowship.

questions.explanation:
Writing sample → interviewed → not (rejected without feedback). Chaining the first two statements gives this directly.
A — Nothing says winning requires a writing sample.
B — Possible, but nothing in the statements forces anyone interviewed to be rejected.
C — Interview → no rejection without feedback. That doesn't mean feedback → interviewed. This reverses the chain.
E — Some feedback recipients won, but nothing ties those winners to writing samples.

questions.stimulus: Last year, the Corrigan Museum's total attendance rose by 10 percent over the previous year, while the number of visitors who bought annual memberships fell. Annual members do not pay per-visit admission; all other visitors do.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: The museum raised the price of annual memberships last year.
choices.B: Either the number of visits by nonmembers rose last year, or annual members visited more often on average than the year before.
choices.C: The museum's revenue from per-visit admissions rose last year.
choices.D: The number of nonmember visits rose by more than 10 percent last year.
choices.E: Some former annual members visited the museum last year as nonmembers.

questions.explanation:
Total attendance rose. It's made up of member visits and nonmember visits. Fewer members means member visits could only grow if each member visited more. So either nonmember visits rose, or members visited more often, or both.
A — A price increase is one possible explanation for fewer members, but nothing establishes it.
C — Likely, but ticket prices or discounts could have changed. Revenue isn't guaranteed.
D — Possible, but the exact percentage depends on how member visits changed.
E — Possible, but nothing requires it.

questions.stimulus: A study of 2,000 software engineers found that those who worked fully remotely reported higher job satisfaction than those who worked fully in an office. However, remote engineers were promoted at a lower rate than office-based engineers with similar performance reviews.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Factors other than performance reviews influence promotion decisions for software engineers.
choices.B: Most software engineers would prefer to work remotely.
choices.C: Job satisfaction is more important to software engineers than promotion.
choices.D: Remote work causes lower productivity among software engineers.
choices.E: Managers deliberately discriminate against remote employees.

questions.explanation:
Same reviews, different promotion rates: something besides reviews must matter. That's all this answer claims, so it follows.
B — Higher satisfaction among remote workers doesn't show what most engineers prefer.
C — The study never compares how much engineers value these things.
D — Performance reviews were similar, so there's no sign of lower productivity, let alone that remote work causes it.
E — Deliberate discrimination is one possible explanation, but far stronger than the data supports.

questions.stimulus: Some people argue that because e-books are cheaper to produce than printed books, publishers should price them much lower. But production cost is only one factor in a book's price. Authors' royalties, editing, marketing, and design costs are the same whatever the format. So the savings from digital production are smaller than many assume, which means the case for dramatically lower e-book prices is weaker than its proponents believe.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: e-books should be priced the same as printed books
choices.B: production cost is only one factor in determining a book's price
choices.C: publishers spend the same amount on marketing for e-books as for printed books
choices.D: the savings from producing e-books are smaller than many people assume
choices.E: the argument for pricing e-books much lower than printed books is weaker than its supporters think

questions.explanation:
"Which means" introduces the final claim, which everything else supports. The point about smaller savings is an intermediate conclusion that leads to it.
A — The author says the case for dramatic cuts is weaker, not that prices should be equal.
B — A premise.
C — Part of a supporting premise.
D — An intermediate conclusion; it supports the main point rather than being it.

questions.stimulus: Historian: It is often claimed that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Certainly, printed pamphlets spread reformist ideas with unprecedented speed. But religious reform movements had arisen repeatedly in earlier centuries without printing, and several of them gained wide followings. The press therefore accelerated a reform movement whose causes lay elsewhere.
questions.stem: The claim that printed pamphlets spread reformist ideas with unprecedented speed plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?

choices.A: It is a claim that the historian argues is false.
choices.B: It is evidence offered to show that the printing press caused the Reformation.
choices.C: It is a point the historian concedes in a way that limits, but does not undermine, the historian's conclusion.
choices.D: It is a premise used to support the claim that earlier reform movements gained wide followings.
choices.E: It is the main conclusion of the historian's argument.

questions.explanation:
"Certainly" marks a concession. The historian grants that printing spread ideas fast and folds it into the conclusion: printing accelerated reform but didn't cause it.
A — The historian accepts it.
B — It is evidence that others might use for that claim, but the historian doesn't offer it that way. The historian concedes it.
D — Earlier movements are a separate premise; this claim doesn't support that one.
E — The conclusion is the last sentence.

questions.stimulus:
Laila: Every great novelist has been an avid reader of other novelists' work.
Marcus: That isn't so. Elena Varga is widely considered one of the century's great novelists, yet she has said in interviews that she rarely read fiction while developing her craft.
questions.stem: Marcus responds to Laila's claim by

choices.A: offering a specific case that, if accurate, would show that her generalization is false
choices.B: showing that Laila's claim depends on an ambiguous definition of "great"
choices.C: suggesting that Laila has confused a cause with an effect
choices.D: arguing that reading fiction can hinder a novelist's development
choices.E: questioning whether Laila is qualified to judge which novelists are great

questions.explanation:
Laila makes a universal claim ("every"). Marcus offers one counterexample. One exception is enough to refute it.
B — Marcus accepts Laila's notion of greatness; he applies it to Varga.
C — No causal reversal is alleged.
D — Marcus doesn't claim reading hurts; he just gives an exception.
E — Marcus never challenges Laila's qualifications.

traps.C: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus:
Priya: The city's new stadium has been a financial success. Attendance at games has exceeded projections every season, and the team's revenues have tripled.
Tomas: The team is certainly profiting. But the city borrowed heavily to build the stadium, and the tax revenue it generates doesn't come close to covering the debt payments. For the city, the stadium is a financial failure.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Priya and Tomas disagree over whether

choices.A: the city should have borrowed money to build the stadium
choices.B: the stadium generates any tax revenue for the city
choices.C: attendance at the stadium has exceeded projections
choices.D: the team's revenues have increased since the stadium opened
choices.E: the stadium has been a financial success in every relevant respect

questions.explanation:
Priya calls it a financial success without qualification. Tomas agrees the team profits but says it's a failure for the city. They disagree about whether "financial success" is the right overall verdict.
A — Neither says what the city should have done.
B — Tomas says it generates some, just not enough. Priya doesn't address tax revenue.
C — Tomas never disputes the attendance figures.
D — Tomas explicitly agrees the team is profiting.

questions.stimulus: If the reservoir's water level falls below the intake pipe, the town must draw water from the river. If the town draws water from the river, it must treat that water with additional filtration. So if the reservoir's water level falls below the intake pipe, the town must use additional filtration.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?

choices.A: If the bridge is closed, commuters must take the ferry. Commuters are taking the ferry. So the bridge must be closed.
choices.B: If the bridge is closed, commuters must take the ferry. If commuters take the ferry, they must buy a ferry pass. So if the bridge is closed, commuters must buy a ferry pass.
choices.C: If commuters take the ferry, they must buy a ferry pass. If the bridge is closed, commuters must buy a ferry pass. So commuters who take the ferry do so because the bridge is closed.
choices.D: The bridge is closed only if it is under repair. If it is under repair, commuters must take the ferry. So commuters must take the ferry.
choices.E: If the bridge is closed, commuters must take the ferry. If commuters take the ferry, they must buy a ferry pass. So if commuters have not bought a ferry pass, the bridge must be open.

questions.explanation:
Same valid chain: A → B, B → C, so A → C. All three parts match, including the "must" in the conclusion.
A — Affirms the consequent. That's a different, invalid pattern.
C — Uses similar ingredients, but the conclusion is a causal claim that doesn't follow from the structure.
D — Ends with an unconditional conclusion, and nothing establishes that the bridge is closed.
E — A valid contrapositive of the chain, but the conclusion has a different form from the original's A → C.

traps.C: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: Students who eat breakfast every day earn higher grades, on average, than students who regularly skip breakfast. Therefore, if the school provided free breakfast to all students, average grades would rise.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Hospitals with more nurses per patient have lower infection rates. Therefore, some hospitals have more nurses per patient than others.
choices.B: Cities that raised their minimum wage saw unemployment rise. Therefore, minimum-wage increases may affect employment.
choices.C: Students who eat breakfast earn higher grades. Maya earns high grades. Therefore, Maya must eat breakfast.
choices.D: Employees who take all their vacation days receive better performance ratings than employees who don't. Therefore, if the company required every employee to take all their vacation days, performance ratings would improve.
choices.E: Most students surveyed said breakfast helps them concentrate. Therefore, breakfast improves concentration.

questions.explanation:
The original goes from a correlation between groups to a prediction that imposing the trait on everyone will produce the outcome. This answer does exactly the same.
A — A trivially valid inference with no flaw that matches.
B — Hedged with "may," so it's a modest, reasonable claim rather than the original's confident prediction.
C — A conditional reversal flaw. Same topic, different flaw.
E — A flaw involving self-reports, not a correlation applied as a policy fix.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A company should recall a product if the product poses a significant safety risk and that risk cannot be eliminated by providing customers with clear warnings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.A: Delmar should recall its space heater, since the heater poses a significant fire risk, even though a clear warning label would eliminate that risk.
choices.B: Esker Foods should recall any product that has ever been the subject of a safety complaint.
choices.C: Arvo Toys should recall its spinning top, since the top's small parts pose a significant choking hazard that warnings cannot prevent, because young children cannot read them.
choices.D: Corvin Tools need not recall its saw, since only a few customers have been injured using it.
choices.E: Bellcrest should recall its blender, since customers have complained that it is too loud.

questions.explanation:
Both conditions are met: significant risk, and warnings can't eliminate it. The principle says recall.
A — The first condition is met, but the risk can be eliminated by warnings, so the principle doesn't call for a recall.
B — Far broader than the principle, which requires a significant risk that warnings can't fix.
D — The principle doesn't say when a recall is unnecessary, and "few injuries" doesn't settle whether the risk is significant or fixable by warnings.
E — Noise isn't a safety risk, so the principle doesn't apply.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: The school board is wrong to cancel next year's art program to save money. Studies show that students in art programs develop problem-solving skills that improve their performance across many subjects.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?

choices.A: A school board should consult parents before making budget decisions.
choices.B: Art programs are more valuable than athletic programs.
choices.C: Any program that improves problem-solving skills should be expanded.
choices.D: A school should not eliminate a program to save money if the program improves students' performance across many subjects.
choices.E: Schools should spend money only on programs that improve students' test scores.

questions.explanation:
Facts: the program improves performance across subjects; it's being cut to save money. This principle says such a program shouldn't be cut for that reason, which delivers the columnist's conclusion.
A — Consultation isn't the columnist's complaint.
B — No athletic program is at issue.
C — Calls for expansion, more than the columnist argues. It also doesn't address the money-saving rationale.
E — This sets a requirement for spending, not a reason against cutting. It also mentions only test scores.

questions.stimulus: In the decade after the town of Merrow built a bypass highway that diverted through traffic away from its main street, sales at main-street businesses increased substantially. Yet business owners had strongly opposed the bypass, predicting that losing the through traffic would devastate their sales.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how the business owners' prediction could have been so wrong?

choices.A: The bypass took longer to build than originally planned.
choices.B: Several main-street businesses closed during the decade after the bypass was built.
choices.C: Most of the vehicles on the bypass are trucks traveling between distant cities.
choices.D: Business owners in other towns have made similar predictions about bypasses.
choices.E: Before the bypass was built, heavy through traffic made the main street so congested and noisy that many local residents avoided shopping there.

questions.explanation:
The through traffic wasn't bringing customers; it was driving local ones away. Removing it let locals return, so sales rose despite less traffic.
A — Construction delays don't explain rising sales.
B — This makes the sales increase more puzzling, not less.
C — This explains why diverted traffic wouldn't stop, but it doesn't explain why sales rose.
D — Others' predictions don't explain what happened in Merrow.

questions.stimulus: A shipping company found that after it installed new navigation software on half of its fleet, the ships with the software used 12 percent less fuel per voyage than the ships without it. The company concludes that installing the software on the rest of its fleet will reduce its fuel costs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the company's conclusion?

choices.A: whether the software was developed by the company or purchased from a vendor
choices.B: whether the software is easy for crews to learn
choices.C: whether the ships chosen for the software tend to sail different routes from the other ships
choices.D: whether fuel prices are expected to rise next year
choices.E: whether other shipping companies have installed similar software

questions.explanation:
If ships with the software sail shorter or calmer routes, the 12 percent gap could come from the routes, not the software. Either answer to this question moves the argument.
A — Who made the software has no bearing on whether it saves fuel.
B — Ease of use might matter a little, but the software is already working on half the fleet.
D — Fuel prices affect how much money is saved, not whether fuel use falls.
E — Other companies' choices don't test this causal claim.

questions.stimulus:
Nadia: Requiring cyclists to wear helmets will reduce head injuries, but it will also discourage many people from cycling at all, which harms public health overall. So the city shouldn't require helmets.
Russell: Helmet laws do reduce head injuries. And the city should require helmets anyway; the effect on how many people cycle is small.
questions.stem: Nadia and Russell are committed to agreeing with which one of the following?

choices.A: A helmet requirement would reduce head injuries among cyclists.
choices.B: The city should require cyclists to wear helmets.
choices.C: Most cyclists already wear helmets.
choices.D: Public health is harmed when fewer people cycle.
choices.E: A helmet requirement would discourage many people from cycling.

questions.explanation:
Both explicitly say helmet requirements reduce head injuries. That's the shared commitment.
B — They disagree on exactly this.
C — Neither addresses this.
D — Only Nadia commits to this.
E — Russell says the effect on cycling is small.

questions.stimulus: Certain species of desert ants navigate by counting their steps. In experiments, researchers lengthened some ants' legs with tiny stilts after the ants had walked to a food source. On the return trip, those ants overshot their nest. Ants whose legs were shortened undershot it.
questions.stem: The findings described above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Most ant species navigate by counting steps.
choices.B: The ants' navigation depends at least partly on the length of their strides.
choices.C: Ants with longer legs are better navigators than ants with shorter legs.
choices.D: Desert ants navigate solely by counting their steps.
choices.E: Ants that overshoot their nest eventually find it by smell.

questions.explanation:
Longer legs (longer strides) made ants overshoot; shorter legs made them undershoot. Stride length plainly affects their estimate of distance. "At least partly" keeps it modest.
A — The findings concern certain desert species only.
C — Both modified groups erred. Neither navigated better.
D — The results show stride counting matters, not that it's the only method.
E — Nothing about recovery or smell is reported.

questions.stimulus: Councilmember Ortiz argues that the proposed rezoning of the Eastfield neighborhood will raise property values for current homeowners. But Ortiz owns three rental properties in Eastfield and stands to gain substantially if the rezoning passes. We should therefore reject her claim that the rezoning will raise property values.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

choices.A: rejects a claim solely because of the personal interests of the person who makes it
choices.B: takes for granted that rising property values benefit all residents of a neighborhood
choices.C: presumes that a rezoning cannot raise property values unless homeowners support it
choices.D: fails to consider that Ortiz's rental properties might lose value under the rezoning
choices.E: concludes that the rezoning will lower property values merely because Ortiz's evidence is weak

questions.explanation:
Ortiz's financial interest might be a reason to scrutinize her claim, but it says nothing about whether the claim is true. The argument attacks the source rather than the reasoning.
B — The argument never says who benefits; it only dismisses Ortiz's prediction.
C — Homeowner support isn't mentioned.
D — If anything, this would make Ortiz's interest point the other way. It doesn't describe the flaw.
E — The argument doesn't predict lower values, and it never assesses Ortiz's evidence; it ignores it.

questions.stimulus: Analyst: Last year, the proportion of Harlan County's jobs that were in manufacturing fell from 22 percent to 18 percent. Clearly, then, fewer people in Harlan County held manufacturing jobs last year than the year before.
questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: assumes that the decline in manufacturing's share was caused by layoffs
choices.B: presumes that manufacturing jobs are more valuable to the county than other jobs
choices.C: fails to consider that some people may hold more than one manufacturing job
choices.D: relies on data from only one year to support a claim about a long-term trend
choices.E: overlooks the possibility that the total number of jobs in the county grew enough that the number of manufacturing jobs did not decline

questions.explanation:
A smaller share doesn't mean a smaller number. If total jobs grew fast enough, 18 percent of the new total could exceed 22 percent of the old one. The argument confuses a proportion with an absolute count.
A — The argument draws no causal conclusion about layoffs.
B — The argument makes no judgment about the value of jobs.
C — Technically jobs and job holders differ, but the core error is share versus count. Multiple jobs is a minor wrinkle that doesn't describe the main flaw.
D — The conclusion is only about a one-year change, not a long-term trend.

questions.stimulus: Investigators examined every financial record of the Alder Foundation from the past decade and found no evidence that any foundation official misused funds. Therefore, no foundation official misused funds during that period.
questions.stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: draws a conclusion about a decade on the basis of evidence about a single year
choices.B: treats a lack of evidence that something occurred as conclusive proof that it did not occur
choices.C: assumes that the investigators examined the records thoroughly
choices.D: presumes that officials who misuse funds always attempt to conceal it
choices.E: fails to establish that the investigators were independent of the foundation

questions.explanation:
Finding no evidence of misuse in the records doesn't prove there was none. Misuse could leave no trace in financial records, or records could be falsified. The argument jumps from "no evidence" to "it didn't happen."
A — The records covered the whole decade.
C — The premise already says they examined every record; the flaw isn't about thoroughness but about what the records can show.
D — The argument assumes the opposite, that misuse would show up in the records.
E — A reasonable worry in real life, but even independent investigators finding nothing wouldn't prove no misuse occurred.

questions.stimulus: A proposed ordinance would require all new commercial buildings in Lowell City to include rooftop solar panels. Supporters claim this will reduce the city's reliance on electricity from coal-fired plants, since the panels will supply much of the power these buildings would otherwise draw from the regional grid.
questions.stem: The supporters' reasoning requires the assumption that

choices.A: the ordinance will be supported by most commercial property owners
choices.B: new commercial buildings use more electricity than existing ones
choices.C: all of the regional grid's electricity comes from coal-fired plants
choices.D: at least some of the electricity the regional grid would otherwise supply to these buildings comes from coal-fired plants
choices.E: solar panels are more cost-effective than other renewable energy sources

questions.explanation:
If none of the grid power these buildings would use came from coal, replacing it with solar couldn't reduce reliance on coal. Negate this and the argument collapses.
A — Support isn't required. The ordinance mandates the panels.
B — The argument doesn't compare new and old buildings.
C — Far more than needed; some coal is enough.
E — Cost compared with other renewables is irrelevant to whether reliance on coal falls.

questions.stimulus: Linguist: Children raised in bilingual households tend to begin speaking somewhat later than children raised in monolingual households. Yet by age six, bilingual children's vocabularies, when words in both languages are counted, equal or exceed those of monolingual children. Thus, the delay in beginning to speak does not reflect any lasting disadvantage in language ability.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.A: The delay in beginning to speak is caused by the need to learn two languages at once.
choices.B: Most children raised in bilingual households begin speaking later than most monolingual children.
choices.C: A child's combined vocabulary across two languages is an adequate measure of that child's language ability.
choices.D: Bilingual children eventually speak each of their languages as fluently as monolingual children speak theirs.
choices.E: Vocabulary size at age six predicts academic success later in life.

questions.explanation:
The evidence is about combined vocabulary; the conclusion is about language ability. If combined vocabulary didn't reflect ability (if, say, ability in each language lagged badly), the evidence wouldn't support the conclusion.
A — The cause of the delay doesn't matter. The argument only claims the delay isn't lasting.
B — The premise already says "tend to." Restating it adds nothing required.
D — Stronger than required. The argument uses combined measures and doesn't need equal fluency in each language.
E — Academic success is beyond the argument's scope.

questions.stimulus: Every member of the Hawthorne String Quartet trained at the Bellamy Conservatory. So every member of the Hawthorne String Quartet can sight-read difficult music.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The Bellamy Conservatory is the most prestigious conservatory in the country.
choices.B: Everyone who can sight-read difficult music trained at the Bellamy Conservatory.
choices.C: Everyone who trained at the Bellamy Conservatory can sight-read difficult music.
choices.D: Most musicians who trained at the Bellamy Conservatory can sight-read difficult music.
choices.E: Some members of the Hawthorne String Quartet can sight-read difficult music.

questions.explanation:
Members → Bellamy-trained (premise). Bellamy-trained → can sight-read (assumption). So members → can sight-read. It bridges exactly.
A — Prestige isn't sight-reading.
B — Reverses the needed link.
D — "Most" doesn't guarantee that every member can.
E — "Some" falls short of the "every" in the conclusion.

questions.stimulus:
Any proposal that would increase the town's debt requires approval by voters in a referendum. No proposal that requires a referendum can be implemented this fiscal year. The proposal to build a new fire station cannot be implemented this fiscal year.
Commentator: So the fire station proposal would increase the town's debt.
questions.stem: The commentator's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: No proposal that would increase the town's debt can be implemented this fiscal year.
choices.B: Any proposal that requires a referendum would increase the town's debt.
choices.C: Some proposals that would increase the town's debt can be implemented in future fiscal years.
choices.D: The fire station proposal requires approval by voters in a referendum.
choices.E: Any proposal that cannot be implemented this fiscal year would increase the town's debt.

questions.explanation:
The premises give: debt → referendum → not this year. The commentator goes from "not this year" to "debt," which reverses the chain. Only an assumption that directly states not this year → debt makes the conclusion follow.
A — This just follows from the premises (debt → not this year). It's the original direction, not the reversal the conclusion needs.
B — Gives referendum → debt, but nothing establishes that the fire station proposal requires a referendum.
C — Future years are irrelevant to the link needed.
D — Combined with the premises this gets the proposal to "not this year," which we already know. It never reaches "debt."

questions.stimulus: A survey of residents of Calder Springs found that those who live within half a mile of a public park report exercising outdoors more frequently than those who live farther away. Urban planners conclude that building new parks in underserved neighborhoods would increase outdoor exercise among residents there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the planners' argument?

choices.A: Residents who moved closer to a park reported exercising outdoors more often after the move than before it.
choices.B: Outdoor exercise has been linked to improved mental health.
choices.C: People who exercise outdoors frequently tend to seek out homes near parks.
choices.D: Parks in Calder Springs are well maintained and have walking trails.
choices.E: Residents of underserved neighborhoods report wanting more parks.

questions.explanation:
The worry is self-selection: active people may choose to live near parks. Tracking the same people before and after moving shows proximity itself increases exercise.
B — Explains a benefit of exercise, not whether parks increase it.
C — This is the self-selection alternative. It weakens.
D — It describes the existing parks but doesn't show proximity causes exercise. New parks might differ.
E — Wanting parks isn't the same as exercising more if parks are built.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Pottery shards found at the Mesa Verde site bear decorative patterns nearly identical to those on pottery from a settlement 300 miles to the south. This similarity indicates that the two communities were in regular contact through trade.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the archaeologist's argument?

choices.A: The decorative patterns at both sites are unlike those found at any other known settlement.
choices.B: Chemical analysis shows that the clay in many of the Mesa Verde shards came from deposits near the southern settlement.
choices.C: Some pottery at the Mesa Verde site bears patterns found nowhere else.
choices.D: Trade routes in the region were common during the period in question.
choices.E: Both communities made pottery primarily for storing grain.

questions.explanation:
Similar patterns could arise from independent invention or a shared ancestral tradition. Clay from the south means physical objects moved between the communities, which is direct evidence of exchange.
A — This makes coincidence less likely, but a shared ancestral tradition could still explain it. It's weaker than physical evidence of movement.
C — Local, unique patterns suggest independent development, if anything.
D — General background that makes contact plausible, but it doesn't tie these two sites together.
E — Shared function doesn't indicate contact.

questions.stimulus: Sales of sunscreen in the coastal town of Marisol increased sharply last summer. During the same period, the number of skin-cancer screenings performed at the town's clinic also rose. The clinic's director concludes that a public awareness campaign the clinic ran last spring made residents more concerned about sun exposure.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the director's conclusion?

choices.A: The awareness campaign was funded by a grant from a sunscreen manufacturer.
choices.B: Sunscreen prices in Marisol rose slightly last summer.
choices.C: Skin-cancer screenings can detect cancer at an early, treatable stage.
choices.D: Last summer, the town's tourist population was nearly double that of any previous summer.
choices.E: Residents who saw the campaign reported that it was informative.

questions.explanation:
A surge of visitors would explain higher sunscreen sales and more screenings without any change in residents' concern. It's an alternative explanation for both data points.
A — The funding source doesn't show the campaign failed to affect residents.
B — Higher prices would tend to lower sales, making the increase more notable. It doesn't weaken.
C — Explains why screenings matter, not why they rose.
E — Suggests the campaign had an effect. That supports the director.

questions.stimulus: Medical researcher: Among patients who underwent the new knee surgery at Elmwood Hospital, 92 percent reported significant pain relief one year later. Among patients who received physical therapy alone, only 61 percent reported significant relief. Clearly the surgery is more effective than physical therapy for treating chronic knee pain.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researcher's argument?

choices.A: Pain relief is difficult to measure objectively.
choices.B: Patients who underwent the surgery were required to complete several weeks of physical therapy afterward.
choices.C: Elmwood's surgeons recommended surgery only to patients whose pain had a structural cause that surgery could correct, and recommended physical therapy to patients whose pain had no clear cause.
choices.D: Some patients who received physical therapy later underwent the surgery.
choices.E: Knee surgery is considerably more expensive than physical therapy.

questions.explanation:
The two groups weren't comparable. Surgery patients were chosen because their problems were fixable; therapy patients had harder-to-treat pain. The gap may reflect who got which treatment, not which treatment works better.
A — Measurement concerns apply to both groups equally, so this doesn't explain the gap.
B — This suggests therapy contributed to surgery patients' outcomes, but surgery plus therapy beating therapy alone still supports the surgery's value. It's a weaker challenge.
D — Could matter in some way, but it doesn't directly undercut the comparison. These patients may have been counted in either group.
E — Cost doesn't bear on effectiveness.

questions.stimulus: At Tremont College, every student who majors in chemistry must complete a senior thesis. Of this year's graduating seniors, 40 completed a senior thesis, and 25 majored in chemistry. No student has more than one major.
