questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Exactly 15 of this year's graduating seniors majored in a subject other than chemistry.
choices.B: Every student who completed a senior thesis majored in either chemistry or a related science.
choices.C: Fewer than half of this year's graduating seniors majored in chemistry.
choices.D: Exactly 15 of this year's graduating seniors who completed a senior thesis did not major in chemistry.
choices.E: Some chemistry majors did not complete a senior thesis.

questions.explanation:
All 25 chemistry majors had to complete a thesis, so all 25 are among the 40 thesis writers. The other 40 − 25 = 15 thesis writers can't be chemistry majors. Exactly 15.
A — Many seniors may have written no thesis and majored in something else. The 15 counts only thesis writers.
B — Nothing is said about related sciences.
C — The total number of seniors isn't given. If there were exactly 40, 25 would be a majority.
E — Contradicts the rule that every chemistry major must complete one.

questions.stimulus: All the paintings in the Ravel Gallery's east wing were donated by private collectors. Most of the paintings donated by private collectors to the gallery were painted before 1900. None of the paintings painted before 1900 is on loan to other museums.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Some paintings in the east wing are on loan to other museums.
choices.B: Most paintings that are not on loan to other museums were donated by private collectors.
choices.C: Every painting painted before 1900 is in the east wing.
choices.D: Most paintings in the east wing were painted before 1900.
choices.E: None of the paintings in the east wing that were painted before 1900 is on loan to other museums.

questions.explanation:
Anything painted before 1900 isn't on loan, which applies to any subset, including east-wing paintings painted before 1900.
A — Nothing requires any east-wing painting to be on loan.
B — Pre-1900 → not on loan doesn't tell you where most unloaned paintings came from. The gallery could own many unloaned paintings from other sources.
C — Nothing says pre-1900 paintings must be in the east wing.
D — Most donated paintings were pre-1900, but the east wing could hold mainly the post-1900 donations.

questions.stimulus: In a long-term study, researchers tracked children who were given a daily vitamin D supplement from infancy and a comparable group who received no supplement. By age ten, the supplemented group had significantly fewer bone fractures. However, among children whose diets were already rich in vitamin D, supplementation made no measurable difference.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The benefit of vitamin D supplementation for reducing fractures depends at least partly on a child's existing vitamin D intake.
choices.B: Supplementation causes children to eat fewer vitamin D–rich foods.
choices.C: Children with vitamin D–rich diets have fewer fractures than other children.
choices.D: Vitamin D supplements are unnecessary for most children.
choices.E: Vitamin D is the most important nutrient for bone health.

questions.explanation:
Supplements helped overall but not for children who already got plenty. So the effect depends on baseline intake.
B — Nothing suggests supplements change diet.
C — Plausible, but the study reports only that supplements made no difference for them, not how their fracture rates compared.
D — The study shows a benefit overall; it's unnecessary only for children with rich diets.
E — The study compares no other nutrients.

questions.stimulus: Many critics charge that standardized tests disadvantage students from low-income families, since those students score lower on average. But lower average scores alone do not show that a test is unfair; a fair test of skills that wealthier students have had more opportunity to develop will also show a gap. The real question is whether the tests accurately measure the skills they claim to measure, and here the evidence is mixed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: Standardized tests should be abolished.
choices.B: That low-income students score lower on standardized tests does not by itself establish that the tests are unfair.
choices.C: Standardized tests are fair to students from low-income families.
choices.D: Wealthier students have more opportunity to develop the skills that standardized tests measure.
choices.E: The evidence about whether standardized tests measure what they claim to measure is mixed.

questions.explanation:
The author's core move rebuts the critics: score gaps alone don't prove unfairness. The fair-test example supports this, and the last sentence redirects what matters.
A — The author never proposes this.
C — The author doesn't conclude the tests are fair, only that the critics' evidence doesn't show unfairness.
D — Part of an illustration used as support.
E — A further remark, not the claim the argument works to establish.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Rent control is often defended as a way to keep housing affordable. But by capping the returns landlords can earn, rent control discourages the construction of new rental housing. With fewer new units being built, the supply of housing fails to keep pace with demand, and rents on uncontrolled units rise sharply. Thus, rent control ultimately makes housing less affordable for many of the people it is meant to help.
questions.stem: The claim that rent control discourages the construction of new rental housing plays which one of the following roles in the economist's argument?

choices.A: It is a view the economist attributes to defenders of rent control.
choices.B: It is the only evidence offered for the claim that rents on uncontrolled units rise sharply.
choices.C: It is the argument's main conclusion.
choices.D: It is a claim offered in support of a further claim that in turn supports the argument's main conclusion.
choices.E: It is a claim the economist concedes but argues is irrelevant.

questions.explanation:
Less construction → supply lags demand and uncontrolled rents rise → housing becomes less affordable. The claim sits at the start of the chain, supporting the next step, which supports the conclusion.
A — Defenders say rent control keeps housing affordable; this claim is the economist's own.
B — "Fewer new units" and "supply fails to keep pace" also do work. The "only" makes this too strong. The structure description in the correct answer is more accurate.
C — The main conclusion is the final "thus" sentence.
E — The economist relies on it rather than conceding it.

questions.stimulus: Some legislators propose banning a pesticide because a few studies suggest it may harm bee populations. But by that standard we would have to ban nearly every pesticide in use, along with many common fertilizers, since for almost any agricultural chemical one can find a few studies suggesting some harm. Surely the legislators don't intend that.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by

choices.A: attacking the motives of the legislators who propose the ban
choices.B: questioning the scientific methods of the studies the legislators rely on
choices.C: showing that the standard implicit in a proposal would, if applied consistently, lead to a result its proponents would reject
choices.D: arguing that the benefits of the pesticide outweigh its harms
choices.E: citing evidence that the pesticide in question does not harm bee populations

questions.explanation:
The author extends the legislators' standard ("a few studies suggest harm → ban") to show it would require banning almost everything, an outcome the legislators wouldn't accept. That's a reductio.
A — The author says nothing about motives. "Surely they don't intend that" is about the consequences of their standard.
B — The author doesn't challenge the studies' methods, only the standard for acting on them.
D — No cost–benefit comparison is made.
E — The author offers no evidence about this pesticide's effects.

questions.stimulus:
Kenji: Public libraries should eliminate late fees. Studies show that fees deter low-income patrons from borrowing books, and fees bring in very little revenue.
Olivia: Fees do deter some patrons. But without them, many books would never be returned, and replacing lost books costs far more than the fees bring in.
questions.stem: Kenji and Olivia most clearly disagree over whether

choices.A: late fees bring in substantial revenue
choices.B: public libraries should eliminate late fees
choices.C: low-income patrons return books later than other patrons
choices.D: late fees deter some patrons from borrowing books
choices.E: replacing lost books is expensive

questions.explanation:
Kenji says eliminate them. Olivia's rebuttal (books wouldn't come back, and replacing them costs more) implies they should be kept. That's their disagreement.
A — Olivia says replacement costs exceed fee revenue, which is consistent with fees being small. She doesn't dispute Kenji here.
C — Neither addresses this.
D — Olivia concedes this.
E — Only Olivia speaks to this.

questions.stimulus: Most of the volunteers at the food bank are retirees. Most retirees in this town are members of the Civic League. So at least some of the volunteers at the food bank must be members of the Civic League.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above, including in any flaw it may contain?

choices.A: All the players on the soccer team are sophomores. Most sophomores take Spanish. So most players on the soccer team take Spanish.
choices.B: Most of the players on the soccer team are sophomores. All sophomores at this school take Spanish. So most players on the soccer team take Spanish.
choices.C: Most players on the soccer team take Spanish. Some sophomores take Spanish. So some players on the soccer team are sophomores.
choices.D: Most sophomores at this school take Spanish. The soccer team is mostly sophomores. So the soccer team should offer Spanish lessons.
choices.E: Most of the players on the soccer team are sophomores. Most sophomores at this school take Spanish. So at least some players on the soccer team must take Spanish.

questions.explanation:
Same structure: most A are B; most B are C; so some A are C. That inference is actually invalid (the volunteers who are retirees might all be among the retirees who aren't in the League), and this answer shares the same flaw.
A — The premises use "all" and "most," and the conclusion is "most." The shape differs.
B — Uses "all" in the second premise and concludes "most." That's a valid argument, so it doesn't match the original's flawed structure.
C — Different quantifier structure and a different flaw.
D — The conclusion is a recommendation, not a "some" claim.

traps.D: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: Ravi must be the best candidate for the scholarship. After all, the selection committee chose him, and the committee always chooses the best candidate. We can be sure the committee always chooses the best candidate because the candidates it has chosen, such as Ravi, have been the best.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: This restaurant must serve the best food in town, since the town's food critic recommends it, and the critic recommends only the best restaurants. We know the critic recommends only the best restaurants because the restaurants the critic recommends, like this one, serve the best food.
choices.B: Ravi will win the scholarship because he has the highest grades, and the scholarship always goes to the student with the highest grades.
choices.C: The town's food critic must be unreliable, because the critic once recommended a restaurant that later closed.
choices.D: This restaurant must serve the best food in town, since it has won more awards than any other restaurant in town.
choices.E: The committee should choose Ravi, because choosing anyone else would be unfair to him.

questions.explanation:
Both are circular. The reliability of the selector is supported by the very conclusion it's used to prove.
B — Same scholarship topic, but this is a valid argument with no circularity.
C — A hasty generalization from one case, a different flaw.
D — An appeal to awards, but not circular.
E — Question-begging in a loose sense, but it isn't the structured circle of the original.

traps.B: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: Principle: Employees should not use company resources for personal purposes, except when the use is minimal and causes no measurable cost to the company, or when a supervisor has explicitly approved it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following actions most clearly violates the principle above?

choices.A: Arjun printed a one-page boarding pass on the office printer, with his supervisor's approval.
choices.B: Luis briefly used his work computer to check the weather forecast before his commute.
choices.C: Mei used the company's conference room after hours to hold a meeting for a client project.
choices.D: With her manager's explicit permission, Hana used a company van to help a friend move on a Saturday.
choices.E: Without asking anyone, Tobias used the company's high-volume printer to print 300 flyers for his band's concert.

questions.explanation:
Personal use, not approved, and 300 flyers on a commercial printer is neither minimal nor cost-free. Neither exception applies.
A — Both exceptions could apply. Not a violation.
B — Minimal use with no measurable cost fits the first exception.
C — A client project is a business purpose, not personal use.
D — Personal use, but explicitly approved by a supervisor, so the second exception covers it.

questions.stimulus: Judge: The defendant violated the city's sign ordinance by posting his political banner without a permit. But the city has routinely ignored unpermitted commercial banners for years and has enforced the ordinance only against political ones. The charges against the defendant should therefore be dismissed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the judge's reasoning?

choices.A: A city should enforce each of its ordinances against every violator.
choices.B: Anyone charged with violating an ordinance should be given an opportunity to obtain a permit afterward.
choices.C: A law that is enforced selectively against a particular category of speech should not be the basis for penalizing someone engaged in that category of speech.
choices.D: Political speech deserves greater protection than commercial speech.
choices.E: Sign ordinances are an inappropriate use of government authority.

questions.explanation:
Facts: the ordinance is enforced only against political banners; the defendant posted one. The principle says such selective enforcement can't be the basis for a penalty, so the charges should be dismissed.
A — Criticizes the city's practice but doesn't say the defendant's charges should be dropped.
B — The judge's reasoning is about selective enforcement, not after-the-fact permits.
D — Supports the general direction, but it doesn't say anything about dismissing charges for selective enforcement.
E — Condemns all sign ordinances, which goes well beyond the judge's narrow, enforcement-based reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Parent: My daughter's school should not require students to buy a specific brand of graphing calculator. Several other brands perform all the functions needed for the courses and cost much less.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the parent's position?

choices.A: Schools should provide all required supplies free of charge.
choices.B: A school should not require students to buy a particular product when less expensive alternatives would serve the same educational purpose.
choices.C: A school may require a specific product only if every student can afford it.
choices.D: Students learn best when they can choose their own tools.
choices.E: Calculator manufacturers should not be allowed to market products in schools.

questions.explanation:
Facts: other brands do everything needed and cost less. This principle says don't require the specific product in that case, which is exactly the parent's conclusion.
A — Goes much further than the parent's narrow point about brands.
C — Gives a requirement for mandates, but even affordable mandates might still be unjustified under the parent's reasoning. It doesn't capture the "cheaper alternatives" point.
D — The parent's argument is about cost and function, not learning benefits of choice.
E — Marketing restrictions aren't at issue.

questions.stimulus: In the early 1900s, the introduction of steel helmets for soldiers in the trenches was followed by a significant increase in the number of soldiers treated for head injuries, even though the helmets were demonstrably effective at protecting against shrapnel.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.A: Before helmets were introduced, many head wounds from shrapnel were fatal, so the soldiers never reached treatment.
choices.B: The helmets were heavy and uncomfortable to wear for long periods.
choices.C: Shrapnel was the leading cause of head injuries in trench warfare.
choices.D: The number of soldiers in the trenches increased over the same period.
choices.E: Some soldiers refused to wear the helmets.

questions.explanation:
Helmets turned many deaths into survivable injuries. More treated head injuries is what you'd expect if the helmets were working.
B — Discomfort doesn't explain the increase in treated head injuries.
C — Restates why helmets mattered without explaining the rise.
D — Possibly a partial explanation, but an increase in soldiers doesn't account for helmets' effect. The correct answer resolves the paradox directly.
E — Non-use would limit the helmets' benefit but wouldn't explain an increase in injuries.

questions.stimulus: The museum will not open its new wing in March unless the climate-control system passes inspection. The climate-control system will pass inspection only if the contractor replaces the faulty humidity sensors. The contractor will not replace the sensors before April.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: If the contractor replaces the sensors, the museum will open the new wing.
choices.B: The contractor is responsible for the delay in opening the new wing.
choices.C: The museum will open its new wing in April.
choices.D: The museum will not open its new wing in March.
choices.E: The climate-control system will pass inspection in April.

questions.explanation:
Open in March → passes inspection → sensors replaced. Sensors won't be replaced before April, so inspection fails (for March), so the wing doesn't open in March.
A — Treats a necessary condition as sufficient.
B — Responsibility isn't addressed.
C — Replacing sensors is necessary for opening, not sufficient. Opening in April isn't guaranteed.
E — Again necessary versus sufficient. Replacing sensors doesn't guarantee passing.

questions.stimulus: Over two million people have downloaded the FocusPro study app this year. With so many users, the app must be effective at improving students' concentration.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: fails to specify how many of the users are students
choices.B: confuses the cause of a phenomenon with its effect
choices.C: treats the popularity of a product as evidence that it achieves its intended effect
choices.D: assumes that concentration can be improved at all
choices.E: relies on a sample that is too small to support its conclusion

questions.explanation:
Downloads show the app is popular, not that it works. Many people may download it and never benefit.
A — Even if every user were a student, popularity still wouldn't show effectiveness.
B — No cause and effect are reversed here.
D — Not the flaw. The argument's gap is between popularity and effectiveness.
E — Two million is hardly a small sample. The problem is what's being measured.

questions.stimulus: Editorial: Either the state legislature raises the gasoline tax to fund highway repairs, or the state's highways will continue to deteriorate. Since the legislature has refused to raise the gasoline tax, the state's highways will continue to deteriorate.
questions.stem: The editorial's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that the legislature's refusal is permanent
choices.B: presumes that raising the gasoline tax would provide enough money for repairs
choices.C: confuses a condition that is sufficient for repairs with one that is necessary
choices.D: fails to consider that highway repairs might be funded by means other than a gasoline tax increase
choices.E: takes for granted that highway deterioration is undesirable

questions.explanation:
The argument presents only two options: raise the gas tax or let highways decay. Other funding sources, like bonds, tolls, federal funds, or reallocation, are ignored. It's a false dichotomy.
A — A possible gap, but even if the refusal were permanent, other funding could still exist. The false choice is the main flaw.
B — The argument doesn't depend on the tax being sufficient; it concludes that highways will deteriorate.
C — Close, but the core problem is the limited set of options presented, not a necessary/sufficient reversal in a conditional statement.
E — The argument doesn't evaluate deterioration.

questions.stimulus: Each of the three proposals before the city council would, if adopted on its own, reduce the city's budget deficit. Therefore, adopting all three proposals together would reduce the deficit by an amount equal to the sum of the reductions each would produce on its own.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on predictions about the proposals that might be inaccurate
choices.B: takes for granted that reducing the deficit is the council's most important goal
choices.C: presumes that any proposal that reduces the deficit must also reduce government spending
choices.D: fails to consider whether the proposals would be popular with voters
choices.E: overlooks the possibility that the proposals' effects on the deficit might overlap or interfere with one another

questions.explanation:
Each proposal works on its own, but together they may target the same savings or interact so the combined effect is less (or more) than the sum. Assuming effects simply add up is the flaw.
A — Every forecast might be inaccurate. The argument's distinctive flaw is how it combines the predictions.
B — The argument makes no claim about priorities.
C — The argument says nothing about how the proposals reduce the deficit, whether through cuts or new revenue.
D — Popularity has nothing to do with the deficit math.

questions.stimulus: To attract younger visitors, the Halvorsen Art Museum plans to offer free admission on Thursday evenings to visitors under thirty. The museum's director expects this will increase the number of visitors under thirty over the coming year.
questions.stem: The director's expectation depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Free admission will not reduce the museum's overall revenue.
choices.B: The cost of admission is one of the factors that currently keeps some people under thirty from visiting the museum.
choices.C: Visitors under thirty prefer evening visits to daytime visits.
choices.D: Most of the museum's current visitors are over thirty.
choices.E: People under thirty are more interested in contemporary art than in older works.

questions.explanation:
Free admission helps only if price is part of what's keeping young people away. If cost plays no role, removing it changes nothing.
A — Revenue isn't part of the director's expectation.
C — They needn't prefer evenings, only be willing to come on Thursday evenings.
D — The plan's goal implies this, but whether the plan works doesn't depend on it.
E — Art preferences don't affect whether free admission draws visitors.

questions.stimulus: Sociologist: In regions where broadband internet became available in the 2010s, the number of residents participating in local civic organizations declined over the following years. Regions without broadband saw no such decline. So the arrival of broadband likely reduced civic participation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the sociologist's argument depends?

choices.A: The regions that gained broadband did not differ from the other regions in some other way that would independently explain the decline in civic participation.
choices.B: Regions without broadband will eventually gain it.
choices.C: People who use broadband spend all their leisure time online.
choices.D: Civic organizations are less active today than they were before the 2010s.
choices.E: Civic participation is beneficial to local communities.

questions.explanation:
The comparison works only if the two groups of regions are otherwise similar. If, say, broadband regions were also urbanizing quickly and that drove the decline, the conclusion falls.
B — The future is irrelevant to the causal claim.
C — "All" is far stronger than needed for broadband to reduce participation somewhat.
D — General decline isn't required. The argument relies on a difference between regions.
E — The argument makes no value claim.

questions.stimulus: Every film that receives an R rating is barred from the youth film festival. Several films directed by Ana Cruz contain scenes of graphic violence. So several films directed by Ana Cruz are barred from the youth film festival.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Ana Cruz has never directed a film intended for young audiences.
choices.B: Every film barred from the youth film festival contains scenes of graphic violence.
choices.C: The youth film festival bars films that are unsuitable for children.
choices.D: Some films that receive an R rating contain scenes of graphic violence.
choices.E: Every film that contains scenes of graphic violence receives an R rating.

questions.explanation:
Graphic violence → R rating (assumed) → barred (premise). Cruz's violent films are therefore barred.
A — Her intentions don't bridge violence to being barred.
B — Gives barred → violence, the reverse of what's needed.
C — Vague. It doesn't establish that Cruz's films count as unsuitable or R-rated.
D — "Some" doesn't guarantee that Cruz's violent films are R-rated.

questions.stimulus: A study found that office workers whose desks were near windows took fewer sick days than workers whose desks were in interior spaces. The study's authors conclude that exposure to natural light improves workers' health.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the authors' conclusion?

choices.A: Workers with window desks reported higher job satisfaction.
choices.B: Sick days are an imperfect measure of health.
choices.C: Interior office spaces had poorer ventilation than spaces near windows.
choices.D: Desk locations in the offices studied were assigned randomly rather than by seniority or job title.
choices.E: Most office workers prefer desks near windows.

questions.explanation:
Random assignment rules out the possibility that window seats went to, say, senior employees who differ in health or flexibility. That makes light a more plausible cause.
A — Satisfaction could be an alternative pathway, or simply a correlate. It doesn't strengthen the light–health link.
B — Undermines the evidence, so it weakens.
C — An alternative cause of better health near windows. That weakens.
E — Preference isn't health.

questions.stimulus: Economist: The national government's plan to cut income taxes will increase consumer spending, because households that keep more of their income will spend much of the additional money rather than save it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?

choices.A: Consumer spending accounts for a large share of the national economy.
choices.B: In the past, when households in this country received unexpected increases in after-tax income, they spent most of the additional money within a year.
choices.C: Households currently carry high levels of debt and have indicated they plan to use any extra income to pay it down.
choices.D: The tax cut will be largest for the wealthiest households.
choices.E: Many economists have predicted that the tax cut will increase the national debt.

questions.explanation:
Direct evidence that households spend, rather than save, extra income supports the key assumption.
A — Explains why spending matters, not whether the tax cut increases it.
C — Paying down debt is a form of saving here. That weakens.
D — Wealthy households tend to save more of extra income, if anything. This mildly weakens.
E — The debt doesn't bear on consumer spending.

questions.stimulus: Tara: Our company's new four-week paid parental leave policy has been a success. Since it began, the number of employees who leave the company within a year of having a child has dropped by 30 percent.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens Tara's argument?

choices.A: In the same period, the company also opened an on-site childcare center that most new parents have used.
choices.B: Employees who took parental leave returned to work at the same rate as before.
choices.C: Some employees who took parental leave reported that four weeks was not long enough.
choices.D: Many other companies offer longer parental leave.
choices.E: The parental leave policy is more expensive than the company anticipated.

questions.explanation:
On-site childcare could explain why new parents stay. That's an alternative cause of the 30 percent drop.
B — The relevant figure is departures within a year, and this doesn't explain the drop.
C — Complaints about length don't show the policy failed to reduce departures.
D — Others' policies don't affect whether this one worked.
E — Cost doesn't speak to success in retaining parents.

questions.stimulus: Political scientist: When the island nation of Verda adopted ranked-choice voting, voter turnout in national elections rose by 15 percent. Therefore, if our country adopts ranked-choice voting, our voter turnout will also rise substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the political scientist's argument?

choices.A: Some voters in Verda opposed adopting ranked-choice voting.
choices.B: Voter turnout in our country has been declining for a decade.
choices.C: Verda adopted ranked-choice voting at the same time it made election day a national holiday, a change our country is not considering.
choices.D: Ranked-choice voting is more complicated for voters to understand than traditional voting.
choices.E: Verda has a smaller population than our country.

questions.explanation:
If Verda's turnout rose because of the holiday, the analogy gives no reason to expect our turnout to rise from ranked-choice voting alone.
A — Opposition doesn't affect turnout data.
B — A declining trend doesn't show ranked-choice voting wouldn't reverse it.
D — Possibly weakens a little, but Verda's turnout rose despite any complexity. It doesn't break the analogy.
E — Size alone doesn't explain why the voting system's effect would differ.

questions.stimulus: No vegetable variety that requires full sun can be grown successfully in the community garden's north plot. Some of the tomato varieties the garden club wants to grow require full sun. All of the pepper varieties the club wants to grow can be grown successfully in the north plot.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: None of the tomato varieties the club wants to grow can be grown in the north plot.
choices.B: The garden's other plots receive full sun.
choices.C: None of the pepper varieties the club wants to grow requires full sun.
choices.D: Some pepper varieties the club wants to grow are tomato varieties.
choices.E: Some tomato varieties the club wants to grow can be grown successfully in the north plot.

questions.explanation:
Full sun → can't grow in north plot. Contrapositive: grows in north plot → doesn't require full sun. All the club's peppers grow in the north plot, so none requires full sun.
A — Only some tomatoes require full sun. Others might grow in the north plot.
B — Other plots aren't described.
D — Nonsensical. Nothing links the two.
E — Possible, but not required. All the tomatoes might fail there.

questions.stimulus: Before 2015, every graduate of the Ellery School of Nursing passed the national licensing exam on the first attempt. In 2015, the school revised its curriculum. Since then, the school's first-attempt pass rate has been 94 percent.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Graduates since 2015 are less well prepared than earlier graduates.
choices.B: The licensing exam has become more difficult since 2015.
choices.C: The school will return to its original curriculum.
choices.D: Since 2015, some graduates of the Ellery School of Nursing have not passed the licensing exam on their first attempt.
choices.E: The revised curriculum caused the decline in the school's pass rate.

questions.explanation:
A 94 percent pass rate means 6 percent didn't pass on the first try, so some graduates since 2015 failed their first attempt.
A — Again, possible but not established.
B — A possible explanation, but not guaranteed.
C — The future isn't addressed.
E — The timing is suggestive, but causation isn't established.

questions.stimulus: Wildlife officials released 40 radio-collared wolves into a large national park. After five years, deer populations in the park had fallen by a third, and stands of young aspen trees, which deer feed on heavily, had expanded in many valleys where they had been nearly absent for decades.
questions.stem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.A: The wolves killed most of the deer that disappeared from the park.
choices.B: Aspen trees cannot grow in areas with large deer populations.
choices.C: The radio collars allowed officials to prevent wolves from leaving the park.
choices.D: Reintroducing wolves is the best way to restore aspen in any national park.
choices.E: The reduction in the deer population likely contributed to the recovery of young aspen stands.

questions.explanation:
Deer eat young aspen heavily. Fewer deer, and then aspen spread. That supports a probable contribution, which is all this claims.
A — Wolves may have caused much of the decline, but "most of the deer that disappeared" goes beyond the data.
B — Far too strong. Aspen was nearly absent, not impossible.
C — Collars track; nothing says they keep wolves in.
D — Generalizes to all parks and calls it the best method.

questions.stimulus: Researchers measured how long infants looked at various images. Infants consistently looked longer at images showing physically impossible events, such as a ball passing through a solid wall, than at images of possible events. Infants looked equally long at familiar and unfamiliar faces.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the researchers' findings?

choices.A: Infants prefer images of objects to images of faces.
choices.B: Infants' looking time is not determined solely by how unfamiliar an image is.
choices.C: Infants cannot tell the difference between familiar and unfamiliar faces.
choices.D: Infants understand the laws of physics as well as adults do.
choices.E: Infants look longer at any image that surprises them.

questions.explanation:
If looking time were purely about unfamiliarity, unfamiliar faces would draw longer looks than familiar ones. They didn't, while impossible events did. So something besides unfamiliarity affects looking time.
A — The study didn't compare object images with face images in that way.
C — Equal looking time doesn't show they can't distinguish faces, only that they didn't look longer at either.
D — Longer looking at impossible events suggests some expectation, not adult-level understanding.
E — "Any" image goes beyond the evidence, which concerns impossible physical events.

questions.stimulus: Many homeowners use leaf blowers to clear their yards each autumn. But raking is a better choice. Leaf blowers are loud enough to disturb neighbors, and gas-powered models emit significant air pollution. Raking, by contrast, is quiet, emits nothing, and provides useful exercise.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: raking is a better way to clear yards than using a leaf blower
choices.B: gas-powered leaf blowers emit significant air pollution
choices.C: many homeowners use leaf blowers each autumn
choices.D: leaf blowers should be banned
choices.E: leaf blowers are loud enough to disturb neighbors

questions.explanation:
Everything after "But raking is a better choice" gives reasons for that claim.
B — A supporting premise.
C — Background.
D — The author recommends raking but never calls for a ban.
E — A supporting premise.

questions.stimulus: Some nutritionists claim that eating late at night causes weight gain. But calories consumed at night are metabolized the same way as calories consumed during the day. What matters for weight is total calories consumed, not when they are eaten. Late-night eating may correlate with weight gain only because people who snack late tend to eat more overall.
questions.stem: The claim that eating late at night causes weight gain functions in the argument as

choices.A: an explanation of why people who snack late eat more
choices.B: evidence that calories are metabolized differently at night
choices.C: a position that the argument seeks to undermine
choices.D: a premise supporting the claim that total calories determine weight
choices.E: the main conclusion of the argument

questions.explanation:
The author introduces the nutritionists' claim and then argues against it.
A — The author offers that explanation separately.
B — The author says the opposite.
D — It's the target, not support.
E — The author rejects this claim.

questions.stimulus: Commissioner: My opponent claims that the new transit line has failed because ridership is 20 percent below the projections made before it opened. But those projections assumed the line would connect to the airport, a connection that was later canceled for budget reasons. Measured against the revised projections made after the airport link was dropped, ridership is actually 5 percent above expectations.
questions.stem: The commissioner responds to the opponent by

choices.A: suggesting that the opponent has a political motive for criticizing the transit line
choices.B: arguing that the standard the opponent uses to measure the transit line's success is inappropriate
choices.C: providing evidence that the airport connection would have increased ridership
choices.D: conceding that the transit line has failed but blaming budget cuts
choices.E: disputing the accuracy of the opponent's ridership figures

questions.explanation:
The commissioner doesn't dispute that ridership is 20 percent below the original projections. Instead, she argues those projections were the wrong benchmark and offers a better one.
A — No motives are mentioned.
C — This is implicit, but it isn't how the commissioner responds. The move is replacing the benchmark.
D — The commissioner argues the line is exceeding expectations.
E — The commissioner accepts the figures and disputes what they're compared against.

questions.stimulus:
Amara: The city's ban on short-term rentals has helped long-term renters. Since the ban took effect, more apartments have been listed for long-term lease, and average rents have stopped rising.
Felix: Rents stopped rising citywide, including in neighborhoods that had very few short-term rentals to begin with. So the halt in rent increases probably has some other cause.
questions.stem: Amara and Felix disagree over whether

choices.A: short-term rentals were common in every neighborhood
choices.B: more apartments have been listed for long-term lease since the ban took effect
choices.C: average rents have stopped rising
choices.D: the ban on short-term rentals is responsible for the halt in rent increases
choices.E: the ban should be repealed

questions.explanation:
Amara credits the ban for the halt in rising rents. Felix argues some other cause is likely. They disagree about the cause of the rent halt.
A — Felix says some had few; Amara doesn't address it.
B — Felix doesn't address listings.
C — Both accept this.
E — Neither discusses repeal.

questions.stimulus: All of the paintings in this exhibit were created before 1850. Nothing created before 1850 uses acrylic paint, since acrylics weren't invented until the twentieth century. So none of the paintings in this exhibit uses acrylic paint.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.A: Every student in this class is a freshman. No freshman has taken organic chemistry, since it is restricted to upperclassmen. So no student in this class has taken organic chemistry.
choices.B: No student in this class has taken organic chemistry. Organic chemistry is restricted to upperclassmen. So every student in this class is a freshman.
choices.C: Every student who has taken organic chemistry is an upperclassman. Maria is an upperclassman. So Maria has taken organic chemistry.
choices.D: Most students in this class are freshmen. Freshmen cannot take organic chemistry. So most students in this class have not taken organic chemistry.
choices.E: Every student in this class is a freshman. Some freshmen have taken organic chemistry. So some students in this class have taken organic chemistry.

questions.explanation:
All A are B; no B is C (with a reason); so no A is C. Same structure and same valid form.
B — Reverses direction and adds an unsupported step.
C — Affirms the consequent. Different and invalid.
D — A valid argument, but "most" makes the form different from the all/no structure of the original.
E — "Some" breaks the structure, and the conclusion doesn't follow.

questions.stimulus: I've met three people from the town of Linden, and all three were extremely friendly. So people from Linden are generally friendly.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Everyone who eats at the Golden Wok enjoys it, so I will enjoy it.
choices.B: The Golden Wok won a citywide award, so its food must be delicious.
choices.C: The Golden Wok is always crowded, so it must serve good food.
choices.D: The Golden Wok's chef trained in Paris, so its food must be expensive.
choices.E: The two dishes I've tried at the Golden Wok were both delicious, so most of the food at the Golden Wok must be delicious.

questions.explanation:
Both generalize about a whole group from a tiny sample (three people, two dishes).
A — Applies a generalization to one case rather than forming one from a few cases.
B — An appeal to authority, not a small-sample generalization.
C — Infers quality from popularity, a different flaw.
D — A non sequitur unrelated to sample size.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A teacher should give a student an extension on an assignment if the student requests one before the deadline and has a documented reason that is beyond the student's control.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: Mr. Ruiz should give Ana an extension, since she asked the day after the deadline and had a doctor's note.
choices.B: Mr. Lee should give Priya an extension, since she asked before the deadline and explained that she had procrastinated.
choices.C: Ms. Ford should not give Sam an extension, since his reason was a family emergency.
choices.D: Ms. Diaz should give every student an extension, since the assignment was difficult.
choices.E: Ms. Park should give Jalen an extension, since he asked two days before the deadline and provided a hospital record showing he had been admitted for surgery.

questions.explanation:
He requested before the deadline, and surgery is a documented reason beyond his control. Both conditions are met, so the principle says grant it.
A — Documented, but she asked after the deadline, so the principle doesn't call for an extension.
B — Procrastination isn't beyond her control.
C — A family emergency could well be beyond his control, and the principle doesn't say when to deny extensions.
D — Difficulty isn't among the principle's conditions.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: Dr. Kim discovered that a colleague had falsified data in a published study. Although reporting the colleague would damage their friendship and might harm Dr. Kim's own career, Dr. Kim was right to report the falsification to the journal.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's judgment?

choices.A: Journals should retract any study found to contain falsified data.
choices.B: One should report knowledge of scientific fraud even when doing so carries personal costs.
choices.C: Scientists should report fraud only when they are certain of it.
choices.D: One should never do anything that might harm one's own career.
choices.E: Friendships between colleagues should not interfere with professional decisions.

questions.explanation:
Facts: fraud, personal costs. The principle says report anyway, which justifies the judgment that Dr. Kim was right.
A — About journals' duties, not Dr. Kim's.
C — A requirement for reporting rather than an endorsement. It also adds a certainty condition the ethicist doesn't mention.
D — This would condemn the report.
E — Covers the friendship cost but not the career risk, and it doesn't directly call for reporting fraud.

questions.stimulus: A popular brand of running shoe was redesigned to be lighter and more cushioned. Lab tests confirmed the new version reduces impact forces on runners' knees. Yet after the redesign, the number of customers returning the shoe because of knee pain increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.A: Many runners prefer lighter shoes.
choices.B: Lab tests of running shoes are generally reliable.
choices.C: The original shoe had also been returned occasionally for knee pain.
choices.D: The redesigned shoe's extra cushioning led many runners to strike the ground harder with their heels, which places more strain on the knees.
choices.E: The redesigned shoe costs more than the original.

questions.explanation:
Lab impact forces fell, but runners changed their stride in response, increasing knee strain in real use. Both facts can be true.
A — Preference doesn't explain more returns for pain.
B — Deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it.
C — Shows returns happened before, but it doesn't explain the increase.
E — Price doesn't explain knee pain.

questions.stimulus: In the country of Tavia, the average age at which people are diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes has fallen over the past twenty years. Yet over the same period, the proportion of Tavians in every age group who have the disease has remained essentially unchanged.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?

choices.A: Type 2 diabetes is more common among older people than among younger people.
choices.B: Medical treatments for Type 2 diabetes have improved over the past twenty years.
choices.C: Over the past twenty years, routine screening has led to many cases being diagnosed years earlier in the course of the disease than they previously were.
choices.D: The total population of Tavia has grown over the past twenty years.
choices.E: Tavians today eat more processed food than they did twenty years ago.

questions.explanation:
The disease itself isn't striking younger people more often. Prevalence by age is steady, but it's being caught earlier. Earlier detection lowers the average age at diagnosis.
A — Consistent with the data, but it doesn't explain why the average diagnosis age fell.
B — Treatment quality affects outcomes, not when people are diagnosed.
D — Growth changes raw counts, not the average diagnosis age or proportions within age groups.
E — That would suggest higher prevalence, which contradicts the unchanged proportions.

questions.stimulus: Since the Ardmore School District began requiring students to put away their phones during the school day, the number of disciplinary referrals has fallen by 40 percent. The superintendent concludes that the phone policy has improved student behavior.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the superintendent's conclusion?

choices.A: whether the district also changed its criteria for what behavior warrants a disciplinary referral during the same period
choices.B: whether students' academic performance has improved
choices.C: whether the phone policy is difficult to enforce
choices.D: whether students at other districts have phones
choices.E: whether teachers support the phone policy

questions.explanation:
If referral standards were loosened, the drop could reflect counting, not behavior. If they didn't change, the conclusion is stronger. Either answer matters.
B — Interesting but separate. Better grades wouldn't confirm or refute the claim about behavior.
C — Enforcement difficulty matters only indirectly; the referral drop is already observed.
D — Other districts' phone ownership is irrelevant.
E — Support doesn't test whether behavior improved.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: People who keep a daily journal report lower levels of anxiety than people who do not. Clearly, the habit of journaling reduces anxiety.
questions.stem: The psychologist's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it fails to consider the possibility that

choices.A: journaling may have benefits other than reducing anxiety
choices.B: people may define "daily" journaling differently
choices.C: anxiety can be reduced by methods other than journaling
choices.D: people who are less anxious to begin with may be more likely to develop a daily journaling habit
choices.E: some people who keep journals still experience high levels of anxiety

questions.explanation:
The correlation could run the other way: calmer people may find it easier to journal every day. The argument assumes journaling causes calm without ruling out calm causing journaling.
A — Other benefits are irrelevant to whether it reduces anxiety.
B — A minor measurement quibble that doesn't attack the core causal leap.
C — Other methods don't challenge journaling's effect.
E — Group averages allow exceptions. This doesn't undercut a general causal claim.

questions.stimulus: Famous actor Brendan Hale has stated publicly that the new cholesterol drug Lipovant is the most effective treatment available. Given that Hale has millions of devoted fans who trust his judgment, patients with high cholesterol should ask their doctors about Lipovant.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: presumes that patients will follow their doctors' advice
choices.B: relies on the endorsement of someone who has no evident expertise on the matter in question
choices.C: concludes that a drug is effective because many people use it
choices.D: fails to consider the side effects of Lipovant
choices.E: assumes that all cholesterol drugs are equally effective

questions.explanation:
An actor's opinion on a drug's effectiveness carries no medical weight. His popularity doesn't make him an authority on cholesterol treatments.
A — The argument only recommends asking doctors.
C — The argument cites one man's endorsement and his fan count, not the number of users.
D — A real-world concern, but the argument's logical flaw is the inappropriate authority.
E — The argument claims Lipovant is the most effective, the opposite.

questions.stimulus: The average salary of employees at Kessler Corp. rose by 8 percent last year. Hence, most Kessler employees received raises of at least 8 percent last year.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

choices.A: fails to consider that salaries at other companies may have risen more
choices.B: takes for granted that salary increases reflect improved performance
choices.C: confuses the average salary with the total amount the company spent on salaries
choices.D: presumes that every employee at Kessler Corp. received a raise
choices.E: fails to recognize that an increase in an average can result from large increases for a few individuals

questions.explanation:
An average can rise 8 percent if a handful of executives got huge raises and most employees got little or nothing. It can also rise if low-paid employees left. The average says nothing about what most people received.
A — Other companies are irrelevant.
B — Performance isn't mentioned.
C — The argument doesn't discuss total spending.
D — The argument concludes "most," not "every." It does assume a distribution, but the precise flaw is ignoring how a few large changes move averages.

questions.stimulus: Shopkeeper: Since the city installed parking meters on Main Street, fewer customers have come into my store. The meters are clearly driving customers away, so the city should remove them.
questions.stem: The shopkeeper's argument relies on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Parking meters on Main Street generate little revenue for the city.
choices.B: Customers prefer free parking to paid parking.
choices.C: The decline in customers was not caused primarily by some other change that occurred around the time the meters were installed.
choices.D: Most of the shopkeeper's customers drive to the store.
choices.E: Other stores on Main Street have also lost customers.

questions.explanation:
The shopkeeper blames the meters because of timing. If another simultaneous change, like a new competitor, road work, or a recession, explains the decline, the argument fails.
A — Revenue doesn't bear on whether meters deter customers.
B — True in general, but not strictly required; customers might stay away for other reasons tied to the meters, like time limits.
D — "Most" isn't needed; some drivers being deterred could suffice.
E — This would support the argument but isn't required by it.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The new translation of the epic poem uses modern idioms and simple sentence structures, which makes it far more accessible to contemporary readers than earlier translations. Therefore, the new translation is the best version for a reader encountering the poem for the first time.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the critic's argument?

choices.A: Accessibility is not outweighed by other considerations, such as fidelity to the original, in determining which translation is best for a first-time reader.
choices.B: Modern idioms are always easier to understand than older ones.
choices.C: Most first-time readers of the poem are contemporary readers.
choices.D: Earlier translations are inaccurate.
choices.E: The new translation is faithful to every detail of the original poem.

questions.explanation:
The critic jumps from "most accessible" to "best." That works only if accessibility isn't trumped by things like accuracy. If the new translation badly distorts the poem, it may not be best despite being readable.
B — "Always" is too strong.
C — Effectively a given; first-time readers today are contemporary readers.
D — The argument doesn't need earlier translations to be inaccurate, just less suitable.
E — Perfect fidelity isn't required, just that any infidelity doesn't outweigh accessibility.

questions.stimulus: Any candidate who wins the Brennan County primary will appear on the general-election ballot. Delgado has more endorsements from local officials than any other candidate in the Brennan County primary. So Delgado will appear on the general-election ballot.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Delgado is the most qualified candidate in the Brennan County primary.
choices.B: Any candidate who appears on the general-election ballot won the Brennan County primary.
choices.C: Endorsements from local officials usually help a candidate win a primary.
choices.D: The candidate with the most endorsements from local officials always wins the Brennan County primary.
choices.E: No candidate without endorsements from local officials has ever won the Brennan County primary.

questions.explanation:
Most endorsements → wins the primary (assumed) → on the ballot (premise). Delgado has the most endorsements, so she's on the ballot.
A — Qualifications aren't linked to winning.
B — Reverses the premise and doesn't connect endorsements.
C — "Usually help" doesn't guarantee a win.
E — Makes endorsements necessary for winning, not sufficient.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: The decline of honeybee colonies in the Varden Valley over the past decade is primarily due to a new class of pesticide that farmers there began using eleven years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologist's claim?

choices.A: Some farmers in the Varden Valley have stopped using the new pesticide.
choices.B: In a neighboring valley with similar climate and crops, where farmers did not adopt the new pesticide, honeybee colonies have remained stable.
choices.C: Honeybees are important pollinators of the valley's crops.
choices.D: The new pesticide is more effective at controlling crop pests than older pesticides.
choices.E: Honeybee colonies worldwide have been threatened by a parasitic mite.

questions.explanation:
A comparable control group without the pesticide and without the decline points to the pesticide as the key difference.
A — Without data on what happened next, this doesn't support the claim.
C — Explains why bees matter, not why they declined.
D — Effectiveness against pests doesn't show harm to bees.
E — An alternative cause, so this weakens.

questions.stimulus: Teachers at Northfield High noticed that students who sat in the front rows of their classrooms earned higher grades than students who sat in the back. They concluded that sitting near the front helps students learn.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the teachers' conclusion?

choices.A: The classrooms at Northfield High are larger than average.
choices.B: Some back-row students earn high grades.
choices.C: When students were assigned seats randomly, those placed in the front rows still earned higher grades than those placed in the back.
choices.D: Front-row students participate more in class discussions.
choices.E: Students who choose front-row seats tend to be more motivated.

questions.explanation:
Random assignment removes the self-selection explanation, that motivated students choose front seats. The grade gap persisting supports a seating effect.
A — Room size doesn't bear on the conclusion directly.
B — Exceptions don't affect the averages.
D — Could be a mechanism or just another trait of motivated students. It doesn't separate cause from selection.
E — Self-selection explains the gap without any seating effect. That weakens.

questions.stimulus: A magazine asked its readers to report whether they had ever been audited by the national tax agency. Of the readers who responded, 30 percent said they had been audited. The magazine concludes that roughly 30 percent of the nation's taxpayers have been audited.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the magazine's conclusion?

choices.A: The magazine received thousands of responses.
choices.B: The national tax agency does not publish audit statistics.
choices.C: Taxpayers who have been audited generally found the experience unpleasant.
choices.D: Some respondents may not remember whether they have been audited.
choices.E: The magazine's readership consists largely of self-employed professionals, who are audited at far higher rates than other taxpayers.

questions.explanation:
The sample overrepresents a heavily audited group, so 30 percent likely overstates the national rate.
A — A large sample, if anything, supports the result, though size can't fix bias.
B — Whether official data exists doesn't affect the sample's validity.
C — Irrelevant to rates.
D — Memory errors could push the figure either way. It doesn't clearly undercut the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: The owners of Vista Cinema plan to increase ticket sales by lowering ticket prices by 20 percent. They reason that lower prices will attract more customers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the likelihood that the plan will increase ticket sales?

choices.A: Most people who do not attend Vista Cinema say they stay away because the theater's seating is uncomfortable and its screens are outdated, not because of price.
choices.B: Vista Cinema's competitors charge similar prices.
choices.C: Lowering ticket prices will reduce Vista's revenue per ticket.
choices.D: Concession sales account for much of Vista's profit.
choices.E: Some of Vista's current customers would attend even at higher prices.

questions.explanation:
If price isn't what keeps people away, a price cut won't attract many new customers.
B — If anything, cutting prices would then make Vista cheaper than rivals. That doesn't undermine the plan.
C — True, but the goal is ticket sales, not revenue.
D — Profits aren't the stated goal.
E — Current loyal customers don't affect whether new ones come.

questions.stimulus: Every attorney at Rowe & Partners who specializes in tax law has passed the CPA exam. Some attorneys at Rowe & Partners who have passed the CPA exam also hold advanced degrees in economics. No attorney at Rowe & Partners who holds an advanced degree in economics works in the litigation department.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: No attorney at Rowe & Partners who specializes in tax law works in the litigation department.
choices.B: Some attorneys in the litigation department have passed the CPA exam.
choices.C: Every attorney at Rowe & Partners who has passed the CPA exam specializes in tax law.
choices.D: Some attorneys at Rowe & Partners who have passed the CPA exam do not work in the litigation department.
choices.E: Some attorneys at Rowe & Partners who specialize in tax law hold advanced degrees in economics.

questions.explanation:
Some CPA-passers hold economics degrees, and no one with an economics degree works in litigation. So those CPA-passers aren't in litigation.
A — The tax specialists all passed the CPA, but they may not be the ones with economics degrees.
B — Possible, but nothing requires it.
C — Reverses the first statement.
E — The CPA-passers with economics degrees might not be tax specialists.

questions.stimulus: The Brightwater Ferry departs only when at least ten passengers have boarded. This morning, the ferry departed at 9:00 a.m.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Fewer passengers rode the ferry this morning than usual.
choices.B: The ferry always departs at 9:00 a.m.
choices.C: At least ten passengers had boarded the ferry by the time it departed this morning.
choices.D: Exactly ten passengers boarded the ferry this morning.
choices.E: If ten passengers board, the ferry will depart.

questions.explanation:
Departure → at least ten passengers. It departed, so at least ten had boarded.
A — No comparison is given.
B — Only this morning's time is given.
D — "At least ten" allows more.
E — Ten passengers are necessary, not sufficient.

questions.stimulus: In a survey of hospital nurses, those who worked twelve-hour shifts reported more fatigue than those who worked eight-hour shifts. However, nurses on twelve-hour shifts made no more medication errors than nurses on eight-hour shifts, and the nurses on twelve-hour shifts reported greater satisfaction with their schedules.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Fatigue has no effect on job performance.
choices.B: Most nurses work twelve-hour shifts.
choices.C: Nurses prefer longer shifts because they work fewer days per week.
choices.D: Twelve-hour shifts are safer for patients than eight-hour shifts.
choices.E: Greater reported fatigue does not necessarily translate into more medication errors among nurses.

questions.explanation:
The twelve-hour nurses were more fatigued but made no more errors. So fatigue doesn't automatically mean more errors, which is a modest claim the data supports.
A — The data concerns medication errors only, and only shows no difference.
B — Nothing about proportions is given.
C — A plausible reason for satisfaction, but the survey doesn't state it.
D — Equal error rates don't make one safer.

questions.stimulus: When the Delmont city government replaced the incandescent bulbs in its streetlights with LED bulbs, its annual electricity costs for street lighting fell by 60 percent. However, the city's total maintenance costs for street lighting rose slightly that year because of the labor required to install the new bulbs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?

choices.A: LED bulbs last longer than incandescent bulbs.
choices.B: The switch to LED bulbs moved different categories of Delmont's street-lighting costs in opposite directions that year.
choices.C: Other cities have saved money by switching to LED bulbs.
choices.D: The switch to LED bulbs reduced Delmont's total street-lighting costs that year.
choices.E: Delmont's maintenance costs for street lighting will fall in future years.

questions.explanation:
Electricity costs fell, and maintenance costs rose because of installation labor. Both are effects of the switch, going opposite ways. That follows directly without going beyond the data.
A — Commonly true, but the stimulus doesn't say so.
C — Other cities aren't mentioned.
D — Unsupported. The stimulus gives a percentage drop in electricity and a slight rise in maintenance, but no dollar amounts to compare.
E — Likely if installation was a one-time cost, but the stimulus doesn't establish it.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: City officials defend the new downtown surveillance cameras by pointing out that crime downtown fell after they were installed. But crime fell by a similar amount across the entire city during the same period, including in neighborhoods with no cameras. So the officials' evidence does not show that the cameras reduced crime, though it remains possible that they did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the columnist's argument?

choices.A: The drop in downtown crime does not demonstrate that the surveillance cameras were effective.
choices.B: City officials should remove the surveillance cameras.
choices.C: Crime fell across the entire city during the same period.
choices.D: The surveillance cameras did not reduce crime downtown.
choices.E: It is possible that the cameras reduced crime downtown.

questions.explanation:
The columnist's conclusion is that the officials' evidence doesn't show the cameras worked. The citywide drop supports it, and the final clause is a hedge, not the main point.
B — No recommendation is made.
C — A premise.
D — The columnist explicitly allows that they might have.
E — A concession tacked on, not the main conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Some argue that self-driving cars will reduce traffic fatalities. That may be true eventually. But in the near term, self-driving and human-driven cars will share the roads, and human drivers often fail to predict how automated cars will behave. Thus, at least for the next several years, the introduction of self-driving cars could increase accidents. Policymakers should therefore phase them in gradually.
questions.stem: The claim that the introduction of self-driving cars could increase accidents for the next several years plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is the argument's main conclusion.
choices.B: It is a premise that is offered without any support.
choices.C: It is a claim the argument attributes to others in order to dispute it.
choices.D: It is a concession to those who favor self-driving cars.
choices.E: It is an intermediate conclusion that is used to support the argument's main conclusion.

questions.explanation:
It's derived from the point about mixed traffic and human misprediction, and it in turn supports the final recommendation to phase them in gradually.
A — The main conclusion is the policy recommendation.
B — It is supported by the mixed-traffic point.
C — The author asserts this; the disputed claim is about reduced fatalities.
D — The concession is "That may be true eventually."

questions.stimulus:
Lin: The proposed tax on sugary drinks will hurt local businesses.
Marco: Cities that adopted similar taxes saw no drop in total business revenue. Customers simply bought other beverages from the same stores.
questions.stem: Marco responds to Lin's claim by

choices.A: citing evidence from comparable cases that conflicts with Lin's prediction
choices.B: attacking Lin's credibility
choices.C: conceding Lin's point but proposing a compromise
choices.D: showing that Lin's conclusion contradicts her own premises
choices.E: arguing that sugary drinks are unhealthy

questions.explanation:
Lin predicts harm. Marco points to cities that adopted similar taxes without that harm.
B — Marco addresses only the claim.
C — Marco disputes the point.
D — Lin gives no premises.
E — Marco makes no health claim.

questions.stimulus:
Hiroshi: The Daventry Prize should be awarded only to novels that reach a broad audience. A great book that almost no one reads has little cultural influence, and the prize is meant to recognize influential work.
Ingrid: The prize's founder did intend it to honor influential work. But influence can take decades to emerge. Many novels that sold poorly at first went on to shape generations of writers. A prize limited to bestsellers would miss them.
questions.stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that Hiroshi and Ingrid disagree over whether

choices.A: some novels that sold poorly later became influential
choices.B: the prize is meant to recognize influential work
choices.C: the prize's founder was knowledgeable about literature
choices.D: the prize should be limited to novels that have reached a broad audience
choices.E: bestselling novels are always of low quality

questions.explanation:
Hiroshi says it should be awarded only to broadly read novels. Ingrid argues such a limit would miss influential books. They disagree about the limit.
A — Only Ingrid addresses this. Hiroshi doesn't deny it.
B — Ingrid agrees with this.
C — Neither discusses the founder's knowledge.
E — Neither says this.

questions.stimulus: Whenever the Kellan River floods, the farms along its banks lose most of their crops. This year the farms along the Kellan lost most of their crops. So the Kellan River must have flooded this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits a pattern of reasoning most similar to the argument above?

choices.A: The bakery's refrigerated goods spoiled this week. So the bakery should buy a generator.
choices.B: Whenever the power goes out, the bakery's refrigerated goods spoil. The bakery's goods did not spoil this week. So the power did not go out.
choices.C: Whenever the power goes out, the bakery's refrigerated goods spoil. This week the bakery's refrigerated goods spoiled. So the power must have gone out this week.
choices.D: Whenever the power goes out, the bakery's refrigerated goods spoil. The power went out this week. So the bakery's refrigerated goods spoiled.
choices.E: The power goes out often, and the bakery loses money. So power outages cause the bakery's losses.

questions.explanation:
Both affirm the consequent: if X then Y; Y; so X. Crops could be lost to drought or pests; goods could spoil from a broken fridge.
A — A recommendation, different structure.
B — A valid contrapositive, not the original's flawed pattern.
D — Valid modus ponens, not the original's flawed pattern.
E — A correlation-to-cause pattern, not the conditional structure.

traps.A: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: To get a table at Maison Lune on a Saturday, you must make a reservation. Jordan made a reservation at Maison Lune for this Saturday. So Jordan will get a table.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: Imani has run many races. So she will win the marathon.
choices.B: To qualify for the marathon, a runner must complete a qualifying race. Imani completed a qualifying race. So Imani will qualify for the marathon.
choices.C: To qualify for the marathon, a runner must complete a qualifying race. Imani did not complete a qualifying race. So Imani will not qualify.
choices.D: Most runners who complete qualifying races qualify for the marathon. Imani completed one. So she will probably qualify.
choices.E: Imani qualified for the marathon. So she must have completed a qualifying race.

questions.explanation:
Both treat a necessary condition as sufficient: must do X to get Y; did X; so will get Y.
A — A different non sequitur.
C — A valid inference (no necessary condition, no qualification).
D — Hedged and probabilistic, so it's reasonable rather than flawed in the same way.
E — Valid. Qualifying requires the race.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A news organization should issue a public correction whenever it publishes a factual error that a reasonable reader could rely on, regardless of whether the error was brought to its attention by readers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.A: The Daily Herald should issue a correction for an opinion column that readers found offensive.
choices.B: The Daily Herald should issue a correction after its editors noticed, on their own, that an article misstated the date of a city council vote on which residents could have based their plans.
choices.C: The Daily Herald need not issue a correction for a typo in a headline that no reader could misinterpret.
choices.D: The Daily Herald should retract any article containing an error.
choices.E: The Daily Herald should issue a correction only if readers complain about an error.

questions.explanation:
A factual error readers could rely on means correct it, regardless of who noticed. The editors' own discovery doesn't matter.
A — Offense isn't a factual error.
C — Possibly correct as a judgment, but the principle says nothing about when a correction is not needed.
D — Retraction goes beyond correction.
E — The principle says corrections are due regardless of complaints.

questions.stimulus: Legal scholar: Courts should not enforce the arbitration clause in Moreno's employment contract. The clause was buried in fine print on page 30 of a 40-page document that Moreno was required to sign on her first day, with no opportunity to consult a lawyer or negotiate terms.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the legal scholar's conclusion?

choices.A: Arbitration clauses should never be included in employment contracts.
choices.B: Employees should always consult a lawyer before signing a contract.
choices.C: Courts should enforce contracts as written unless both parties agree to modify them.
choices.D: A contractual provision should not be enforced against a party who had no meaningful opportunity to notice, understand, or negotiate it.
choices.E: Contracts longer than 30 pages should be considered unenforceable.

questions.explanation:
Facts: buried in fine print, signed under pressure with no chance to consult or negotiate. This principle covers exactly that and says don't enforce.
A — Bans all arbitration clauses, which goes beyond the scholar's fact-specific reasoning.
B — Advice to employees doesn't establish non-enforcement.
C — This favors enforcement.
E — Fixates on length, which isn't the scholar's reasoning.

traps.E: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: The town of Ashford spent heavily to expand its main highway from two lanes to four, aiming to reduce rush-hour congestion. Two years after the expansion, rush-hour traffic on the highway was moving no faster than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the expansion failed to speed up rush-hour traffic?

choices.A: After the expansion, many commuters who had previously taken other routes or traveled at off-peak times began using the highway during rush hour.
choices.B: Public transit ridership in Ashford increased after the expansion.
choices.C: Before the expansion, the highway was congested only during rush hour.
choices.D: The expansion project went over budget.
choices.E: Some residents opposed the expansion.

questions.explanation:
Induced demand: the extra capacity attracted new rush-hour drivers, filling the lanes back up.
B — Fewer drivers would make congestion relief more expected, which deepens the puzzle.
C — Consistent background, but no explanation.
D — Cost doesn't explain traffic speed.
E — Opposition doesn't affect traffic flow.

questions.stimulus: If the board approves the merger, the company's stock price will rise. If the stock price rises, employees' stock options will become more valuable. The employees' stock options did not become more valuable.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: If the employees' stock options had become more valuable, the board would have approved the merger.
choices.B: The board rejected the merger because of employee concerns.
choices.C: The company's employees do not own stock options.
choices.D: The stock price fell.
choices.E: The board did not approve the merger.

questions.explanation:
Merger → price rises → options more valuable. Options didn't gain value, so the price didn't rise, so the merger wasn't approved.
A — Options gaining value is necessary for the merger chain, not sufficient. They could gain value for other reasons.
B — Reasons aren't given.
C — They do; the options just didn't gain value.
D — The price didn't rise; it may have stayed flat.

questions.stimulus: Senator Marsh has proposed modest limits on the number of hours medical residents can work per week. Apparently Senator Marsh believes that doctors should be trained without any real-world experience at all. Such a proposal would produce dangerously unprepared physicians and should be rejected.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it
