choices.A: relies on an unsupported claim about Senator Marsh's motives
choices.B: fails to consider that some residents may want to work long hours
choices.C: attacks a position that is more extreme than the one actually proposed
choices.D: concludes that a proposal will have bad effects merely because it is new
choices.E: assumes that medical residents currently work too many hours

questions.explanation:
Marsh proposed modest limits on hours; the argument treats this as eliminating real-world experience entirely. That's a straw man.
A — Close, but the argument distorts Marsh's position rather than speculating about why she holds it.
B — Residents' preferences aren't the argument's flaw.
D — Novelty isn't the basis of the objection.
E — The argument suggests the opposite and doesn't assume this.

questions.stimulus: Business columnist: I studied twenty of the most successful technology companies founded in the last thirty years and found that every one of them had a founder who dropped out of college. Clearly, dropping out of college is a smart move for aspiring technology entrepreneurs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the columnist's reasoning?

choices.A: It relies on information about too long a time period.
choices.B: It assumes that technology companies are more successful than other kinds of companies.
choices.C: It fails to define what counts as a successful company.
choices.D: It presumes that the founders dropped out of college for the same reasons.
choices.E: It ignores the many technology companies founded by college dropouts that failed.

questions.explanation:
Looking only at winners hides how many dropout-founded companies failed. Without that, the pattern among successes says nothing about whether dropping out helps. That's survivorship bias.
A — Thirty years isn't the problem.
B — No comparison with other industries is made.
C — A possible vagueness, but even a precise definition wouldn't fix the missing failures.
D — Their reasons don't affect the flaw.

questions.stimulus: A screening test for a rare disease correctly identifies 99 percent of people who have the disease and correctly clears 99 percent of people who don't. Martin tested positive. So it is 99 percent likely that Martin has the disease.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that the test's accuracy rate is the same for every age group
choices.B: fails to consider that Martin may not have followed testing instructions
choices.C: presumes that a 99 percent accurate test is reliable enough for medical decisions
choices.D: ignores how rare the disease is among the people tested
choices.E: treats a test that clears healthy people as one that detects sick people

questions.explanation:
If the disease is rare, say 1 in 10,000, then the 1 percent false positives among the huge healthy majority vastly outnumber the true positives. Most positive results would be false. The argument ignores the base rate.
A — A possible concern, but even with uniform accuracy the conclusion fails because of the base rate.
B — Testing procedure isn't the logical flaw.
C — The argument draws no conclusion about decisions.
E — The argument correctly distinguishes the two rates; its error is about base rates.

questions.stimulus: The Elmhurst Public Library wants to reduce the number of overdue books. It plans to send email reminders to patrons three days before their books are due.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the library's plan depends?

choices.A: Most overdue books are returned within a week of their due date.
choices.B: Every patron would prefer an email reminder to a phone call.
choices.C: Many of the library's patrons have email addresses on file that they check before their books are due.
choices.D: Other libraries have reduced overdue books with email reminders.
choices.E: The library charges fines for overdue books.

questions.explanation:
If patrons don't have email on file or don't check it in time, the reminders can't reduce overdue books.
A — When late books come back doesn't affect whether reminders prevent lateness.
B — Universal preference isn't needed.
D — Helpful evidence, but not required.
E — Fines aren't needed for reminders to work.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Among songbirds of the Halden Forest, males with the most elaborate songs attract mates earlier in the season than males with simpler songs. Since birds that mate earlier tend to raise more surviving offspring, elaborate song must be favored by natural selection in this population.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ornithologist's argument?

choices.A: The elaborateness of a male's song is at least partly heritable.
choices.B: Birds that mate later in the season raise no surviving offspring.
choices.C: Songbirds in other forests also prefer elaborate songs.
choices.D: Females in the Halden Forest prefer elaborate songs to all other male traits.
choices.E: Males with simple songs never succeed in attracting mates.

questions.explanation:
Natural selection favors a trait only if it can be passed on. If song elaborateness were entirely learned or random, reproductive success wouldn't shift the population toward elaborate songs.
B — Fewer surviving offspring is enough.
C — Other forests are irrelevant to this population.
D — They need only prefer song somewhat; "all other traits" is excessive.
E — The argument concerns timing, not total failure.

questions.stimulus: Only full-time employees of Garrick Industries are eligible for the company's tuition reimbursement program. Therefore, Sofia is not eligible for the program.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Sofia is a part-time employee of another company.
choices.B: Sofia is not a full-time employee of Garrick Industries.
choices.C: Some full-time employees of Garrick Industries are not eligible for the program.
choices.D: Sofia has never applied for tuition reimbursement.
choices.E: All full-time employees of Garrick Industries are eligible for the program.

questions.explanation:
Eligible → full-time. If Sofia isn't full-time, she isn't eligible.
A — She could still be full-time at Garrick too.
C — Says nothing about Sofia.
D — Applying is unrelated to eligibility.
E — Full-time → eligible doesn't tell you anything about someone who isn't shown to be not full-time.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: An action is morally praiseworthy only if it is done freely. But no action that results entirely from prior causes is done freely. Therefore, if determinism is true, no action is morally praiseworthy.
questions.stem: The philosopher's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Determinism is true.
choices.B: Any action that is not morally praiseworthy results entirely from prior causes.
choices.C: If an action is done freely, it is morally praiseworthy.
choices.D: Some actions do not result entirely from prior causes.
choices.E: If determinism is true, every action results entirely from prior causes.

questions.explanation:
Determinism → every action entirely caused (assumed) → not free (premise) → not praiseworthy (premise: praiseworthy requires free). The chain is complete.
A — Even granting it, nothing links determinism to actions being entirely caused.
B — Moves backward from the conclusion's consequent; it doesn't connect determinism.
C — Reverses the first premise and doesn't connect determinism.
D — If anything this cuts against determinism, and it doesn't create the link needed.

questions.stimulus: A survey of employees at Pinnacle Tech found that those who participated in the company's mentoring program were promoted faster than those who did not. The company concludes that the mentoring program accelerates career advancement.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the company's conclusion?

choices.A: The mentoring program costs the company very little.
choices.B: Most employees who participated in the program enjoyed it.
choices.C: Some employees promoted quickly never participated in the program.
choices.D: Participants in the mentoring program were selected by lottery from among all employees who applied.
choices.E: Employees who joined the mentoring program had higher performance ratings before joining.

questions.explanation:
A lottery means participants and non-participants (among applicants) differ only by chance. Faster promotion among participants then points to the program.
A — Cost is irrelevant.
B — Enjoyment isn't advancement.
C — Exceptions don't affect the average comparison.
E — Pre-existing differences offer an alternative explanation. That weakens.

questions.stimulus: Neuroscientist: People with damage to the brain's prefrontal cortex frequently make impulsive financial decisions. This suggests that the prefrontal cortex plays a role in restraining impulsive behavior.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the neuroscientist's argument?

choices.A: Impulsive financial decisions are common among people without brain damage.
choices.B: People who make impulsive financial decisions often regret them later.
choices.C: Patients whose prefrontal cortex was damaged in accidents had shown no tendency toward impulsive financial decisions before their injuries.
choices.D: The prefrontal cortex is also involved in planning and memory.
choices.E: Damage to other brain regions can also cause changes in behavior.

questions.explanation:
This rules out the idea that impulsive people simply tend to suffer such damage, or that impulsivity predated it. The behavior began after the damage, supporting a causal role.
A — If impulsivity is common anyway, the link to prefrontal damage is less telling.
B — Regret is irrelevant to the brain's role.
D — Showing it has other functions neither helps nor hurts the restraint hypothesis much.
E — Other regions' effects don't bear on this one.

questions.stimulus: Coaches at Riverside High noticed that players who drank a particular sports drink during practice performed better in games. The coaches concluded that the drink improves athletic performance and began requiring all players to drink it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the coaches' conclusion?

choices.A: The players who chose to drink the sports drink were mostly starters who also received extra coaching and playing time.
choices.B: Some players dislike the taste of the sports drink.
choices.C: The sports drink is more expensive than water.
choices.D: Players who drank the sports drink reported feeling more energetic.
choices.E: The sports drink contains a high amount of sugar.

questions.explanation:
Starters with extra coaching would perform better regardless. That alternative explanation undercuts attributing the improvement to the drink.
B — Taste doesn't affect the causal claim.
C — Cost is irrelevant.
D — This suggests the drink might help.
E — Sugar content doesn't show the drink doesn't help.

questions.stimulus: Demographer: For the past forty years, the average household size in the region of Vellmar has declined steadily. Therefore, over the next decade, the number of housing units needed in Vellmar will grow faster than its population.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the demographer's argument?

choices.A: Average household size has also declined in neighboring regions.
choices.B: Rising housing costs in Vellmar have recently led many young adults to remain in their parents' homes and many unrelated adults to share housing.
choices.C: Many new housing units are being built in Vellmar.
choices.D: Vellmar's population is expected to grow slowly over the next decade.
choices.E: Single-person households are more common in cities than in rural areas.

questions.explanation:
The argument extrapolates the shrinking-household trend. If new pressures are reversing it, with more people per household, housing needs may grow no faster than population.
A — Broader evidence of the trend, if anything, supports the extrapolation.
C — Supply doesn't determine how many units are needed.
D — Slow growth doesn't affect whether housing needs outpace population.
E — The urban–rural split doesn't affect the region-wide trend.

questions.stimulus: Only members of the Westfield Rowing Club may use the boathouse after 6 p.m. Every member of the Westfield Rowing Club has completed a water-safety course.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: The water-safety course is required for using the boathouse before 6 p.m.
choices.B: Anyone who uses the boathouse after 6 p.m. has completed a water-safety course.
choices.C: Some members of the Westfield Rowing Club never use the boathouse after 6 p.m.
choices.D: Anyone who has completed a water-safety course may use the boathouse after 6 p.m.
choices.E: Nonmembers may not use the boathouse at any time.

questions.explanation:
Use after 6 → member → completed the course.
A — Before-6 rules aren't stated.
C — Possible, but not required.
D — Reverses both links.
E — The restriction applies only after 6 p.m.

questions.stimulus: At the Tallis Institute, every researcher who has received a federal grant has published in a peer-reviewed journal. Most researchers at the institute have received a federal grant. No researcher who has published in a peer-reviewed journal is a first-year fellow.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Most researchers at the Tallis Institute are not first-year fellows.
choices.B: Most researchers at the Tallis Institute who have published in a peer-reviewed journal have received a federal grant.
choices.C: Some first-year fellows at the Tallis Institute have received a federal grant.
choices.D: No first-year fellow at the Tallis Institute has applied for a federal grant.
choices.E: Every researcher at the Tallis Institute who has published in a peer-reviewed journal has received a federal grant.

questions.explanation:
Most have grants → published → not first-year fellows. So most researchers aren't first-year fellows.
B — Plausible, but non-grantees could also publish, possibly in large numbers.
C — Contradicts the chain: grant → published → not first-year.
D — Applying differs from receiving; nothing is said about applications.
E — Reverses the first statement.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, enrollment in high-school computer science courses in Delford County has tripled. Yet the number of Delford County students who go on to major in computer science in college has remained roughly the same.
questions.stem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.A: High-school computer science courses in Delford County are poorly taught.
choices.B: Most Delford County students who major in computer science never took it in high school.
choices.C: Interest in computer science among high-school students has declined.
choices.D: A smaller proportion of Delford County students who take high-school computer science now go on to major in it in college than did a decade ago.
choices.E: Colleges have made it harder to major in computer science.

questions.explanation:
Three times as many take the course; the same number major in it. The proportion of course-takers who major has fallen.
A — One possible explanation, but unsupported.
B — Nothing says where majors come from.
C — Enrollment tripled, which suggests the opposite.
E — A possible explanation, not supported by the data.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Letters written by merchants in the port city of Calvane during the 1600s frequently mention delays caused by pirates. Yet surviving shipping records show that the number of ships arriving in Calvane rose steadily throughout that century.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the historian's statements?

choices.A: Shipping records from the 1600s are more reliable than merchants' letters.
choices.B: The number of pirates near Calvane declined during the 1600s.
choices.C: Merchants exaggerated the threat of piracy in their letters.
choices.D: Piracy had no economic effect on Calvane.
choices.E: Piracy, though a recurring concern for Calvane's merchants, did not prevent growth in the port's shipping traffic during the 1600s.

questions.explanation:
Pirates caused complaints and delays, yet arrivals kept rising. So piracy didn't stop growth. This stays within what's stated.
A — The two sources aren't in conflict, and no reliability comparison is supported.
B — Nothing tracks pirate numbers.
C — Possible, but the letters mention delays, which can be real alongside overall growth.
D — Delays had some effect; the data shows only that growth continued.

questions.stimulus: Although many consumers assume that "organic" produce is always grown without pesticides, organic farming standards permit certain naturally derived pesticides. Some of these, such as copper sulfate, can be harmful to soil organisms when used heavily. Consumers who choose organic produce in order to avoid all pesticides are therefore mistaken about what the label means.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: organic produce is no healthier than conventional produce
choices.B: organic farming standards should be changed
choices.C: consumers who buy organic produce to avoid all pesticides misunderstand the organic label
choices.D: organic farming standards permit some pesticides
choices.E: copper sulfate can be harmful to soil organisms

questions.explanation:
"Therefore" introduces the conclusion; the facts about permitted pesticides support it.
A — Health isn't addressed.
B — No recommendation is made.
D — A premise.
E — A supporting detail.

questions.stimulus: Economist: It is often claimed that raising the minimum wage reduces employment among young workers. Studies of several states that raised their minimum wages found small declines in teen employment. But in each case, those declines began before the wage increases took effect and continued at the same pace afterward. The studies, then, provide little evidence that minimum wage increases reduce youth employment.
questions.stem: The statement that studies of several states found small declines in teen employment plays which one of the following roles in the economist's argument?

choices.A: It is the economist's main conclusion.
choices.B: It is offered as a reason to doubt that teen employment declined in those states.
choices.C: It is a premise that directly supports the conclusion that the studies provide little evidence.
choices.D: It presents evidence that the economist then argues does not support the claim it is commonly taken to support.
choices.E: It is evidence the economist uses to support the view that minimum wage increases reduce employment.

questions.explanation:
The economist introduces the study findings and then shows (via the timing) that they don't support the claim that wage hikes reduced youth employment.
A — The conclusion is the last sentence.
B — The economist accepts the declines happened, and only disputes their cause.
C — It's the thing being evaluated, not direct support. The timing point does the supporting work.
E — The economist argues against that view.

questions.stimulus: Some people argue that because ancient humans did not eat processed grains, our bodies are not adapted to them and we should avoid them. But ancient humans also did not live long enough to develop most chronic diseases, wore no eyeglasses, and had no vaccines. That something was absent from ancient life does not make it bad for us.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by

choices.A: showing that the opposing view is based on a misunderstanding of a scientific term
choices.B: providing evidence that processed grains are healthy
choices.C: pointing out that the principle underlying the opposing view would lead to conclusions that few would accept
choices.D: questioning the accuracy of claims about ancient human diets
choices.E: arguing that modern humans are biologically different from ancient humans

questions.explanation:
The opposing view assumes that whatever was absent in ancient life is bad for us. The author shows that principle would condemn vaccines and eyeglasses.
A — No term is in dispute.
B — No evidence about grains' healthfulness is given.
D — The author accepts that ancient humans didn't eat processed grains.
E — No biological difference is claimed.

questions.stimulus:
Rosa: Our neighborhood should convert the empty lot into a community garden. It would give residents fresh produce and a place to gather.
Ben: A garden would be nice, but the lot sits next to a former gas station, and the soil is likely contaminated. Growing food there could be dangerous.
questions.stem: Rosa and Ben disagree over whether

choices.A: the empty lot is a suitable place to grow food for residents
choices.B: community gardens are generally beneficial
choices.C: the former gas station should be demolished
choices.D: a community garden would give residents a place to gather
choices.E: residents want fresh produce

questions.explanation:
Rosa proposes growing produce there. Ben thinks the soil makes it dangerous.
B — Ben calls a garden "nice."
C — Neither addresses demolition.
D — Ben doesn't dispute this.
E — Neither disputes this.

questions.stimulus: The museum's policy is that any artwork on loan must be insured. The Kessler sculpture is on loan to the museum. Therefore, the Kessler sculpture must be insured, and since all insured works are inspected annually, the Kessler sculpture must be inspected annually.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.A: Flight 220 must have a crew member trained in first aid because the airline values passenger safety.
choices.B: The airline's policy is that any international flight must carry a medical kit. Flight 220 is an international flight. Therefore, Flight 220 must carry a medical kit, and since every flight carrying a medical kit has a crew member trained in first aid, Flight 220 must have a crew member trained in first aid.
choices.C: The airline's policy is that any international flight must carry a medical kit. Flight 220 carries a medical kit. Therefore, Flight 220 is an international flight.
choices.D: Every international flight must carry a medical kit. Some domestic flights carry medical kits too. Therefore, medical kits are useful on all flights.
choices.E: The airline's policy is that any international flight must carry a medical kit. Flight 220 is a domestic flight. Therefore, Flight 220 need not carry a medical kit.

questions.explanation:
Same chain: A → B; this is A; so B; B → C; so C.
A — Lacks the chained conditional structure.
C — Affirms the consequent.
D — A generalization, not a chain.
E — Denies the antecedent.

traps.D: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: Every senator I've spoken with supports the infrastructure bill, and I've spoken with senators from both parties. So the bill will certainly pass the Senate.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Every chef recommends this knife. So it must be the best knife.
choices.B: Some chefs I've asked recommend this knife. So some chefs in the city recommend it.
choices.C: This knife is sharp and durable, so chefs will recommend it.
choices.D: Most chefs in the city prefer this knife, according to a citywide survey. So this knife is popular among chefs.
choices.E: Every chef I've asked recommends this knife, and I've asked chefs who cook many different cuisines. So every chef in the city will recommend this knife.

questions.explanation:
Both draw a certain, universal conclusion about a whole group from an unspecified, possibly small and self-selected sample, with the sample's "diversity" offered as if it guaranteed representativeness.
A — A popularity-to-quality leap, but not a sample-to-whole generalization.
B — Valid. Some asked chefs are chefs in the city.
C — Reasons from features, not a sample.
D — Reasonable. A citywide survey supports a modest claim.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A landlord may enter a tenant's apartment without advance notice only in an emergency that threatens the safety of people or the building.
questions.stem: Which one of the following actions by a landlord most clearly conforms to the principle above?

choices.A: Ms. Ito entered without notice to show the apartment to a prospective tenant.
choices.B: Ms. Bloom entered without notice because the tenant was two weeks late with rent.
choices.C: Mr. Vance entered a tenant's apartment without notice to repair a dripping faucet the tenant had reported.
choices.D: Mr. Osei entered a tenant's apartment without notice to check whether the tenant had an unauthorized pet.
choices.E: Ms. Grant entered a tenant's apartment without notice after smelling gas coming from under the door.

questions.explanation:
A gas leak threatens safety. Entering without notice is allowed in that emergency.
A — No emergency.
B — Late rent isn't an emergency.
C — A drip is a nuisance, not a safety emergency, so unannounced entry violates the principle even though the tenant wanted the repair.
D — No safety emergency, so unannounced entry violates the principle.

questions.stimulus: Coach: Kayla should not be benched for missing practice yesterday. She missed it because she was taking a required state exam that could not be rescheduled.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the coach's reasoning?

choices.A: Coaches should treat all players equally.
choices.B: Players should not be penalized for missing practice because of obligations they could not reasonably avoid.
choices.C: Academic obligations are more important than athletic ones.
choices.D: Players who miss practice should make up the time later.
choices.E: Only players who miss more than one practice should be benched.

questions.explanation:
Facts: a required, unreschedulable exam is an unavoidable obligation. This principle says no penalty.
A — Equal treatment doesn't settle this case.
C — Points in the right direction but doesn't say anything about penalties for missing practice.
D — Doesn't address benching.
E — Fits the outcome but for a reason unrelated to the coach's actual justification.

traps.E: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: The city of Harwick doubled the number of police officers patrolling its downtown district. Over the following year, the number of reported crimes downtown increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the increase in reported crimes?

choices.A: The added officers were recently hired and less experienced.
choices.B: Many downtown businesses supported the increase in patrols.
choices.C: With more officers on patrol, crimes that previously went unnoticed or unreported were more likely to be witnessed and recorded.
choices.D: Crime rose in several other districts of Harwick as well.
choices.E: The city's budget for policing increased substantially.

questions.explanation:
More officers means more detection and reporting. Reported crime can rise even if actual crime falls.
A — Inexperience might reduce effectiveness but doesn't explain an increase.
B — Support doesn't explain crime figures.
D — A citywide trend might be part of it, but it doesn't explain why more patrols downtown didn't help.
E — Obviously true with more officers, but no explanation.

questions.stimulus: A city council member argues that the city's new bike-sharing program has reduced car traffic downtown, since the program started, the number of cars entering downtown during rush hour has fallen by 8 percent.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the council member's argument?

choices.A: whether the bikes are popular with tourists
choices.B: whether cycling is good exercise
choices.C: how much the program cost the city to set up
choices.D: whether downtown parking fees or other factors affecting driving also changed after the bike-sharing program started
choices.E: whether other cities have bike-sharing programs

questions.explanation:
If parking fees rose or a big employer moved, the drop might have nothing to do with bikes. If nothing else changed, the argument is stronger.
A — Tourist use matters a little, but tourists' bike rides wouldn't explain fewer commuter cars.
B — Health benefits are irrelevant.
C — Cost doesn't bear on whether traffic fell because of it.
E — Other cities don't test this causal claim.

questions.stimulus:
Dalia: The novel's ending is unsatisfying. After three hundred pages of buildup, the central mystery is resolved in a single paragraph, and the explanation feels rushed.
Grant: I agree the explanation is rushed. But the novel was never really about the mystery. It's about the characters' relationships, which get a moving resolution.
questions.stem: Dalia and Grant are committed to agreeing with which one of the following?

choices.A: The novel's explanation of its central mystery is rushed.
choices.B: The novel's ending is unsatisfying.
choices.C: The novel is primarily about its characters' relationships.
choices.D: The novel is too long.
choices.E: The novel's mystery is the most important part of the book.

questions.explanation:
Dalia says the explanation "feels rushed," and Grant says "I agree the explanation is rushed."
B — Grant suggests the ending succeeds where it matters.
C — Only Grant says this.
D — Neither says so.
E — Grant denies this.

questions.stimulus: The Ridgeway Inn is the best hotel in the city because no other hotel in the city is as good as the Ridgeway Inn.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: confuses popularity with quality
choices.B: restates its conclusion as its only support
choices.C: fails to define what makes a hotel good
choices.D: relies on the opinion of an unnamed source
choices.E: generalizes from a single example

questions.explanation:
"Best" and "no other is as good" mean the same thing. The premise just repeats the conclusion.
A — Popularity isn't mentioned.
C — True, but the core flaw is that the support is the conclusion itself.
D — No source is cited.
E — There's no example at all.

questions.stimulus: Cities with more coffee shops per capita also tend to have higher median incomes. So opening more coffee shops in a city would raise residents' incomes.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: takes a correlation as evidence that one factor causes the other
choices.B: relies on data that may be out of date
choices.C: compares cities that are too different from one another
choices.D: assumes that all residents drink coffee
choices.E: fails to explain how incomes are measured

questions.explanation:
Coffee shops may cluster where incomes are already high, since wealthier residents spend more. The argument assumes the shops cause the income.
B — Data age isn't the issue.
C — The comparison isn't the logical problem.
D — The argument doesn't depend on universal coffee drinking.
E — A minor gap; the real problem is the causal leap.

questions.stimulus: Nutritionist: Studies show that a diet high in fiber can lower cholesterol. Ellen has recently switched to a high-fiber diet. Therefore, Ellen's cholesterol will soon be lower.
questions.stem: The nutritionist's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on studies that may have been poorly designed
choices.B: fails to consider that Ellen might switch back to her old diet
choices.C: treats something that can produce a certain effect as though it will produce that effect in a particular case
choices.D: assumes that fiber is the only factor that affects cholesterol
choices.E: presumes that Ellen's cholesterol is currently high

questions.explanation:
"Can lower" means it's possible, not guaranteed. Ellen's cholesterol might not drop, perhaps because of genetics or other diet factors. The argument moves from possibility to certainty.
A — A generic worry, not the argument's specific flaw.
B — A minor possibility; the main flaw is "can" versus "will."
D — The argument doesn't assume exclusivity.
E — Even if it's high, the problem remains; and "lower" doesn't require it to be high.

questions.stimulus: The town of Gilford plans to reduce litter in its parks by placing more trash cans along walking paths.
questions.stem: The plan's success depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Most park visitors use the walking paths.
choices.B: The new trash cans will be emptied every day.
choices.C: Littering is illegal in Gilford's parks.
choices.D: Other towns have reduced litter by adding trash cans.
choices.E: Some park visitors litter because trash cans are not conveniently located.

questions.explanation:
If no one litters for lack of a nearby can, adding cans won't reduce litter.
A — "Most" isn't needed.
B — Regular emptying matters, but "every day" is more than required.
C — Legality doesn't affect whether cans help.
D — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Electric scooters are a better solution to downtown congestion than expanding bus service. A single scooter takes up a fraction of a car's road space, and scooters can carry riders door to door, which buses cannot.
questions.stem: The columnist's argument requires assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Most downtown trips are shorter than two miles.
choices.B: Buses are less safe than electric scooters.
choices.C: Expanding bus service would be very expensive.
choices.D: Many people who ride scooters downtown would otherwise drive cars rather than take buses or walk.
choices.E: Electric scooters will eventually replace all cars downtown.

questions.explanation:
Scooters ease congestion only if they replace cars. If scooter riders would otherwise walk or take the bus, scooters add vehicles instead of removing them.
A — Helpful, but not strictly required.
B — Safety isn't part of the congestion argument.
C — Cost isn't in the argument.
E — Far more than required.

questions.stimulus: The Delacroix Foundation funds only research projects that have been approved by an independent ethics board. Dr. Huang's study on sleep deprivation has been approved by an independent ethics board. So the Delacroix Foundation will fund Dr. Huang's study, provided that the study meets the foundation's other requirements.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.A: The Delacroix Foundation funds every research project that has been approved by an independent ethics board and meets its other requirements.
choices.B: Independent ethics boards approve only scientifically sound projects.
choices.C: Dr. Huang's study is the only sleep-deprivation study approved by an ethics board.
choices.D: The Delacroix Foundation has funded sleep research in the past.
choices.E: No project that lacks ethics approval has ever been funded by the Delacroix Foundation.

questions.explanation:
The premise makes ethics approval necessary for funding. To conclude funding will happen, we need approval plus the other requirements to be sufficient, which is exactly this.
B — Soundness doesn't establish funding.
C — Uniqueness doesn't guarantee funding.
D — Past funding doesn't guarantee this grant.
E — Restates that approval is necessary.

questions.stimulus: After a bakery began displaying its pastries in a glass case near the entrance, its pastry sales rose by 30 percent. The owner believes the display caused the increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the owner's belief?

choices.A: Pastries are the bakery's most profitable item.
choices.B: The glass case was expensive to install.
choices.C: Nothing else about the bakery's prices, menu, or hours changed during the period.
choices.D: A new office building opened across the street during the same period.
choices.E: Some customers said they did not notice the display.

questions.explanation:
Ruling out other changes leaves the display as the most plausible cause.
A — Profitability doesn't bear on the cause.
B — Cost is irrelevant.
D — An alternative source of customers. That weakens.
E — Undercuts the display's influence.

questions.stimulus: Agronomist: Our trial plots show that planting clover between rows of corn increases corn yields by restoring nitrogen to the soil. Farmers throughout the region should adopt this practice.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the agronomist's argument?

choices.A: Corn requires large amounts of nitrogen.
choices.B: The soil and climate in the trial plots are typical of farmland throughout the region.
choices.C: Clover is inexpensive to plant.
choices.D: The trial plots received more rainfall than average.
choices.E: Some farmers in the region already plant clover.

questions.explanation:
The recommendation generalizes from trial plots to the whole region. If the plots are representative, the results should carry over.
A — Supports the mechanism, which the trial already demonstrated. It does less than showing the results apply regionwide.
C — Cost matters for adoption, but it doesn't strengthen the claim that yields will rise.
D — Unusual conditions undercut generalizing the results.
E — Current practice doesn't bear on effectiveness.

questions.stimulus: Since Hilltop Elementary started offering free breakfast, attendance has improved. The principal concludes that free breakfast encourages students to come to school.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the principal's conclusion?

choices.A: The breakfast program is funded by a state grant.
choices.B: Some students arrive too late to eat breakfast.
choices.C: Most students at Hilltop eat the free breakfast.
choices.D: Free breakfast programs are common in the region.
choices.E: At the same time the breakfast program began, the district started a new busing route that serves the Hilltop neighborhood.

questions.explanation:
New busing could explain better attendance on its own.
A — Funding is irrelevant.
B — A few late arrivals don't undercut the overall effect.
C — This makes the breakfast's influence more plausible.
D — Prevalence doesn't affect the cause here.

questions.stimulus: A pharmaceutical company plans to raise the price of its popular allergy medication by 25 percent, reasoning that because no competing product works as well, customers will continue to buy it and revenue will rise.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the company's reasoning?

choices.A: Allergy season is expected to be severe this year.
choices.B: Some customers have complained about the medication's side effects.
choices.C: Many customers have used the medication for years.
choices.D: A generic version of the medication, with the same active ingredient, will become available at a much lower price later this year.
choices.E: The company's other medications have also become more expensive.

questions.explanation:
A generic with the same ingredient works just as well, contradicting "no competitor works as well." Customers could switch, and revenue might fall.
A — Higher demand supports higher revenue.
B — Some complaints don't establish a large drop in sales.
C — Loyalty supports the prediction.
E — Other products don't affect this prediction.

questions.stimulus: All of the restaurants on Harbor Street serve seafood. Captain's Table is a restaurant on Harbor Street.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Every restaurant that serves seafood is on Harbor Street.
choices.B: Captain's Table serves only seafood.
choices.C: Captain's Table is the most popular restaurant on Harbor Street.
choices.D: Captain's Table serves seafood.
choices.E: Some restaurants on Harbor Street do not serve seafood.

questions.explanation:
Harbor Street restaurant → serves seafood. Captain's Table is one.
A — Reverses the statement.
B — "Only" isn't supported.
C — Popularity isn't addressed.
E — Contradicts the first statement.

questions.stimulus: In a recent election in Corwin, every registered voter who voted cast a ballot either in person or by mail, but not both. More ballots were cast by mail than in person. Fewer than half of Corwin's registered voters voted.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: More than one-quarter of Corwin's registered voters cast ballots by mail.
choices.B: Some registered voters cast ballots both in person and by mail.
choices.C: Turnout in Corwin was lower than in the previous election.
choices.D: Most of Corwin's registered voters prefer voting by mail.
choices.E: Fewer than one-quarter of Corwin's registered voters cast ballots in person.

questions.explanation:
Voters < 50 percent of registered voters, and in-person < half of voters. So in-person < half of 50 percent = 25 percent of registered voters.
A — Mail voters are more than half of those who voted, but if very few voted, mail could be well under 25 percent.
B — Contradicts "but not both."
C — No previous election data.
D — Preferences of non-voters aren't known.

questions.stimulus: A survey of college students found that those who studied in groups reported less stress before exams than those who studied alone. Students in both groups earned similar exam scores.
questions.stem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.A: Studying in groups was not associated with lower exam scores among the students surveyed.
choices.B: Stress has no effect on exam performance.
choices.C: Group study causes students to feel less stressed.
choices.D: Studying alone is ineffective.
choices.E: Most college students prefer to study in groups.

questions.explanation:
Scores were similar, so group study didn't go with lower scores. That's a safe reading of the data.
B — The data doesn't establish this generally.
C — The survey shows a correlation, not causation.
D — Scores were similar.
E — No preference data.

questions.stimulus: Physicist: In the experiment, particles were fired one at a time toward a barrier with two narrow slits. When no detector recorded which slit each particle passed through, the particles accumulated on the screen behind the barrier in a pattern of alternating bands. When a detector did record each particle's path, the bands disappeared, and the particles formed two simple clusters.
questions.stem: The physicist's statements most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: The detector damaged the particles as they passed through the slits.
choices.B: Human consciousness determines the behavior of particles.
choices.C: Whether the particles' paths are recorded affects the pattern the particles form on the screen.
choices.D: The particles travel through both slits at once when they are not observed.
choices.E: The particles were fired in pairs during the first part of the experiment.

questions.explanation:
The only difference between the two setups was the detector, and the patterns differed. Recording made a difference. Nothing further is claimed.
A — One possible mechanism, but not supported by the description.
B — Nothing suggests consciousness; the detector is a device.
D — A common interpretation, but the stated results don't establish it.
E — They were fired one at a time in both cases.

questions.stimulus: Some say that learning a second language is a waste of time for adults, since children learn languages more easily. But adults have advantages too: they can study grammar deliberately, they have larger vocabularies in their native language to draw on, and they can practice with clear goals. Adults who study a new language can become highly proficient.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: Adults can study grammar deliberately.
choices.B: Learning a second language is not a waste of time for adults.
choices.C: Children learn languages more easily than adults.
choices.D: Every adult who studies a language becomes proficient.
choices.E: Adults learn languages more easily than children.

questions.explanation:
The author rejects the opening claim. The advantages and the proficiency point support that rejection.
A — A premise.
C — Part of the opposing view, not the author's conclusion.
D — "Can become" isn't "every."
E — The author never claims adults are better.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The film's defenders praise its realism, pointing to its accurate costumes and authentic locations. Yet realism in film is not achieved by surface detail alone; a film whose characters behave in ways no real person would cannot be realistic, however accurate its sets. And the film's protagonist repeatedly makes choices that no plausible person in her situation would make. Whatever its other merits, then, the film's claim to realism is unfounded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the critic's argument?

choices.A: Accurate costumes and locations contribute nothing to a film's quality.
choices.B: The film has no artistic merit.
choices.C: The film's protagonist makes implausible choices.
choices.D: Realism in film requires that characters behave plausibly.
choices.E: The film is not realistic, despite its accurate costumes and authentic locations.

questions.explanation:
"Then" introduces the conclusion: the claim to realism is unfounded. The principle about character behavior and the protagonist's implausible choices support it.
A — The critic says they don't suffice for realism, not that they contribute nothing.
B — The critic explicitly allows "other merits."
C — A premise.
D — A general principle used as a premise.

questions.stimulus: The county fair has been held every August for over a century. This year, organizers moved it to September to avoid extreme heat. Attendance this year was the highest on record. So moving the fair to September was a good decision.
questions.stem: The statement that the county fair has been held every August for over a century plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It provides background that helps explain the significance of the change being evaluated.
choices.B: It is evidence that the move was a good decision.
choices.C: It explains why attendance was high this year.
choices.D: It is a claim the argument seeks to refute.
choices.E: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

questions.explanation:
It's context. It tells you moving to September was a departure from long tradition, but it doesn't support the conclusion.
B — It doesn't support the decision's merit.
C — Attendance isn't explained by tradition.
D — It's accepted as fact.
E — The conclusion is that the move was good.

questions.stimulus: Advocate: Opponents of the proposed bike lanes say they will hurt businesses by removing parking. But a study of comparable cities found that cyclists visit local shops more often than drivers do and spend more per month in total. So the bike lanes are likely to help, not hurt, local businesses.
questions.stem: The advocate's argument proceeds by

choices.A: drawing an analogy between bike lanes and other transportation projects
choices.B: countering a prediction with evidence suggesting the opposite outcome is more likely
choices.C: showing that the opponents' argument is circular
choices.D: conceding that the bike lanes will remove parking but arguing that parking is unnecessary
choices.E: questioning the motives of those who oppose the bike lanes

questions.explanation:
Opponents predict harm; the advocate cites evidence suggesting a benefit.
A — The comparison is between cities, not between types of project.
C — No circularity is alleged.
D — The advocate doesn't concede or address whether parking is necessary.
E — No motives are discussed.

traps.A: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus:
Mira: Homework helps elementary students develop good study habits.
Jonah: Research shows homework has little benefit for elementary students. It mostly creates stress for families.
questions.stem: Mira and Jonah disagree over whether

choices.A: elementary students should learn study habits
choices.B: research on homework is reliable
choices.C: homework is beneficial for elementary students
choices.D: homework creates stress for families
choices.E: high-school students should have homework

questions.explanation:
Mira says it helps; Jonah says it has little benefit.
A — Jonah doesn't deny the value of study habits.
B — Mira doesn't discuss research.
D — Mira doesn't address stress.
E — Neither discusses high school.

questions.stimulus: Every mammal is warm-blooded. Whales are mammals. So whales are warm-blooded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.A: Every planet orbits a star. Mars orbits a star. So Mars is a planet.
choices.B: Mars is a planet. Mars has two moons. So every planet has two moons.
choices.C: No star is a planet. The Sun is a star. So the Sun is not a planet.
choices.D: Every planet orbits a star. Mars is a planet. So Mars orbits a star.
choices.E: Some planets have rings. Saturn is a planet. So Saturn has rings.

questions.explanation:
All A are B; this is A; so it's B.
A — Affirms the consequent.
B — Overgeneralizes from one case.
C — Valid, but uses "no" rather than "every." A different form.
E — "Some" doesn't support the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: If the shipment had arrived on time, the store would have been fully stocked for the sale. The store was fully stocked for the sale. So the shipment must have arrived on time.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: If Leah had studied, she would have passed the exam. Leah passed the exam. So she must have studied.
choices.B: If Leah had studied, she would have passed. Leah studied. So she passed.
choices.C: Leah passed the exam because she studied, and everyone who studies passes.
choices.D: Leah usually passes her exams. So she will pass this one.
choices.E: If Leah had studied, she would have passed. Leah did not pass. So she did not study.

questions.explanation:
Both affirm the consequent. The store could have been stocked from other sources; Leah could have passed without studying.
B — Valid (affirming the antecedent).
C — Asserts a causal claim but isn't structured as an affirmed consequent.
D — A prediction from past patterns.
E — Valid (denying the consequent).

questions.stimulus: Principle: Students may use calculators on the exam only if the exam instructions explicitly permit them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following conforms to the principle?

choices.A: Theo used a calculator because the exam was difficult.
choices.B: Mina used a calculator because no one told her she couldn't.
choices.C: Ravi did not use a calculator because the exam instructions said nothing about calculators.
choices.D: Ana used a calculator because her teacher usually allows them.
choices.E: Leo used his phone's calculator because he forgot his own.

questions.explanation:
With no explicit permission, calculator use isn't allowed. Ravi acted consistently with the principle.
A — Difficulty isn't a condition.
B — Silence isn't explicit permission.
D — "Usually" isn't permission on this exam.
E — The device doesn't matter; there was no permission.

questions.stimulus: Environmental scientist: The city should not approve the proposed housing development on the Marsh Creek wetlands. Although the development would provide much-needed housing, the wetlands absorb floodwaters that would otherwise damage hundreds of existing homes, and the housing could be built on several vacant lots elsewhere in the city.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the scientist's reasoning?

choices.A: Wetlands should never be developed under any circumstances.
choices.B: A development that would provide a benefit should not be approved if it would cause serious harm that could be avoided by achieving the same benefit another way.
choices.C: Cities should prioritize housing over environmental concerns.
choices.D: Developments should be approved only if most residents support them.
choices.E: Vacant lots should be developed before any other land.

questions.explanation:
The benefit (housing) is achievable elsewhere, and building on the wetlands causes serious avoidable harm (flooding). The principle says don't approve.
A — The scientist's reasoning relies on alternatives existing, not an absolute ban.
C — This would favor approval.
D — Resident support isn't part of the reasoning.
E — Points in the right direction but ignores the harm, which is central to the reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Riverside Gym lowered its monthly membership fee, yet its total membership revenue went up.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: Some members canceled after the fee changed.
choices.B: Riverside Gym renovated its locker rooms last year.
choices.C: Membership fees at Riverside Gym had been unchanged for years.
choices.D: Other gyms in the area charge more.
choices.E: The lower fee attracted enough new members to more than make up for the lower price per member.

questions.explanation:
Revenue = price × members. A big enough jump in members offsets the lower price.
A — Fewer members would make the revenue rise more puzzling.
B — Renovations don't explain this unless tied to membership.
C — History doesn't explain the outcome.
D — Might help explain new members, but by itself doesn't account for higher revenue.

questions.stimulus: Hospital records in the city of Arlen show that patients transported to the emergency room by ambulance have a higher death rate than patients who arrive by private car. Yet emergency physicians in Arlen agree that ambulance transport improves patients' chances of survival.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the records with the physicians' view?

choices.A: Most patients in Arlen arrive at the emergency room by private car.
choices.B: Ambulance crews in Arlen receive extensive training.
choices.C: Some patients who arrive by car have to wait longer for treatment.
choices.D: Patients whose conditions are most severe are far more likely to be transported by ambulance than by private car.
choices.E: Arlen recently purchased several new ambulances.

questions.explanation:
Ambulance patients are sicker to begin with. A higher death rate reflects who rides in ambulances, not harm from the ride. Ambulances can help each patient while still carrying the highest-risk cases.
A — Proportions don't explain the difference in death rates.
B — Supports the physicians' view, but doesn't explain the higher death rate.
C — Would predict higher death rates for car arrivals.
E — Fleet age doesn't reconcile the data.

questions.stimulus: If it rains on Saturday, the outdoor concert will be moved indoors. If the concert is moved indoors, attendance will be limited to 300 people.
questions.stem: If it rains on Saturday, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: The concert will be rescheduled for Sunday.
choices.B: The concert would have had more than 300 attendees outdoors.
choices.C: Attendance at the concert will be limited to 300 people.
choices.D: Fewer than 300 people will attend.
choices.E: The concert will be canceled.

questions.explanation:
Rain → indoors → limited to 300.
A — Not stated.
B — Outdoor attendance isn't addressed.
D — Limited to 300 doesn't mean fewer will attend.
E — It's moved, not canceled.

questions.stimulus: Of all the cars tested, the Corsa compact had the lowest rate of mechanical failure. Thus the Corsa compact is a reliable car.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: fails to recognize that the best performer among a group may still perform poorly by a reasonable standard
choices.B: fails to consider the cost of the Corsa compact
choices.C: presumes that all compact cars are equally reliable
choices.D: relies on testing data from an unreliable source
choices.E: concludes that a car is popular because it is reliable

questions.explanation:
Lowest failure rate among those tested doesn't mean a low failure rate. If all the tested cars were unreliable, the Corsa is just the least bad.
B — Cost doesn't bear on reliability.
C — The argument singles out one model.
D — Source reliability isn't the logical flaw.
E — Popularity isn't discussed.

questions.stimulus: Since the factory closed last year, unemployment in the town of Brigham has doubled. The factory's owners must have intended to harm the town's economy.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?

choices.A: It relies on an unrepresentative sample of towns.
choices.B: It infers that an outcome was intended merely because it resulted from someone's action.
choices.C: It treats a correlation as proof of causation.
choices.D: It fails to consider that other factors may have contributed to rising unemployment.
choices.E: It assumes that unemployment in Brigham was low before the factory closed.

questions.explanation:
The closing caused unemployment, but that doesn't show the owners wanted that result. They may have closed for financial reasons.
A — No sample is involved.
C — The closing very plausibly did cause job losses; the leap is from causing to intending.
D — True, but even if the closing was the sole cause, inferring intent would still be unwarranted. The core flaw is about intent.
E — The level of prior unemployment doesn't matter to the flaw.

questions.stimulus: Admissions officer: Every student admitted to our honors program last year had a grade-point average above 3.8. So any student who has a GPA above 3.8 has a good chance of being admitted to the honors program this year.
questions.stem: The officer's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that GPA is the only factor the program considers
choices.B: relies on data about students who did not apply to the honors program
choices.C: presumes that admissions standards will be the same this year as last year
choices.D: treats a requirement for admission as something that guarantees rejection if it is not met
choices.E: infers that meeting a condition shared by all admitted students gives an applicant a good chance of admission

questions.explanation:
All admitted students had GPAs above 3.8, but that says nothing about how many applicants with such GPAs were rejected. If thousands applied and few were admitted, a high GPA alone gives little chance.
A — The argument doesn't assume this, and that's not the flaw; even so, the problem is ignoring the rejected high-GPA applicants.
B — The data concerns admitted students.
C — A potential gap, but even with identical standards the inference fails.
D — The argument doesn't discuss students below 3.8.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: Our pharmacy should begin offering vaccinations without appointments. Many customers have said that needing an appointment discourages them from getting vaccinated, so walk-in service will increase the number of vaccinations we provide.
questions.stem: The pharmacist's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.A: vaccinations are the pharmacy's most profitable service
choices.B: customers who make appointments always keep them
choices.C: other pharmacies in the area require appointments
choices.D: the pharmacy will have enough staff available to vaccinate walk-in customers without long waits that discourage them
choices.E: every customer who wants a vaccination will come in without an appointment

questions.explanation:
If walk-ins faced long waits or were turned away, the barrier would just shift, and vaccinations might not increase.
A — Profit isn't relevant.
B — Irrelevant to the walk-in plan.
C — Competitors don't matter.
E — Not every customer is needed.

questions.stimulus: Anthropologist: In the highland villages of Teravia, families traditionally build houses with very small windows. This practice must have originated as a way of conserving heat during the region's cold winters, since small windows reduce heat loss.
questions.stem: The anthropologist's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: The practice of building small windows did not originate primarily because large panes of glass were unavailable or too costly in the region.
choices.B: Winters in the Teravian highlands have always been as cold as they are today.
choices.C: Teravian families today understand why their ancestors built small windows.
choices.D: Houses in warmer regions of Teravia have larger windows.
choices.E: Small windows are the most effective way to conserve heat in a house.

questions.explanation:
The argument attributes the practice to heat conservation. If it began simply because large windows couldn't be made or afforded, the explanation would be wrong.
B — They need only have been cold enough to motivate heat conservation.
C — Current understanding doesn't matter.
D — This would strengthen, but isn't required.
E — They need only help, not be the most effective method.

questions.stimulus: Anyone who completes the advanced first-aid course is certified to serve as a camp counselor. Therefore, Nora is certified to serve as a camp counselor.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Everyone certified to be a camp counselor has completed the advanced first-aid course.
choices.B: Nora has applied to be a camp counselor.
choices.C: Nora has completed the advanced first-aid course.
choices.D: Nora has extensive experience working with children.
choices.E: Some camp counselors have completed the advanced first-aid course.

questions.explanation:
Course → certified. If Nora completed it, she's certified.
A — Reverses the premise; still doesn't mention Nora.
B — Applying doesn't establish certification.
D — Experience isn't the certification criterion.
E — Says nothing about Nora.

questions.stimulus: Politician: No bill that increases spending can pass this session unless it includes offsetting cuts. The education bill increases spending. So the education bill will not pass this session.
questions.stem: The politician's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Every bill that includes offsetting cuts passes this session.
choices.B: The education bill does not include offsetting cuts.
choices.C: Some bills that include offsetting cuts do not pass.
choices.D: The education bill increases spending by a large amount.
choices.E: The education bill is opposed by most legislators.

questions.explanation:
Increases spending and passes → includes cuts. The education bill increases spending; if it lacks cuts, it can't pass.
A — Makes cuts sufficient, which doesn't help show the bill fails.
C — Irrelevant to the education bill.
D — Size doesn't matter to the conditional.
E — Opposition makes failure likely but doesn't guarantee it.

questions.stimulus: Store manager: Since we began playing slower music in the store, customers have been spending more per visit. The slower music must encourage customers to linger and buy more.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the manager's conclusion?

choices.A: Slower music is cheaper to license.
choices.B: Other stores play fast music.
choices.C: The store held a major sale during the same period.
choices.D: Many customers say they don't notice the music.
choices.E: Customers' average time in the store increased after the music change, while prices and product selection stayed the same.

questions.explanation:
Longer visits support the "linger" mechanism, and unchanged prices and selection rule out obvious alternatives.
A — Cost is irrelevant.
B — Other stores don't matter.
C — An alternative explanation for higher spending.
D — Weakens the claim that music affects behavior.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The sudden abandonment of the city of Kesh around 1200 BCE was most likely caused by a prolonged drought. Sediment cores from a nearby lake show that rainfall in the region fell sharply in the decades before the abandonment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the historian's argument?

choices.A: Other cities in the region were abandoned for unrelated reasons around the same time.
choices.B: The lake's sediment cores also show a sharp decline in rainfall around 900 BCE.
choices.C: Evidence of a military invasion has been found in Kesh's final occupation layer.
choices.D: Excavations show that in the final decades of occupation, Kesh's residents dug progressively deeper wells and abandoned irrigated fields on the city's outskirts.
choices.E: Kesh was a major trading center with connections across the region.

questions.explanation:
This links the rainfall data to residents' actual behavior: struggling for water and giving up farmland. It shows the drought affected Kesh directly.
A — Suggests regional causes other than drought may have been at work.
B — A later drought doesn't bear on Kesh's abandonment.
C — An alternative cause.
E — Background, but trade connections don't support the drought explanation.

questions.stimulus: A survey found that people who own dogs report being happier than people who don't. Therefore, getting a dog will make a person happier.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.A: Dogs require a great deal of care and attention.
choices.B: The survey included people from many different countries.
choices.C: People who are already happier tend to be more likely to adopt a dog.
choices.D: Many dog owners say their dogs encourage them to exercise.
choices.E: Cat owners also report being happier than people without pets.

questions.explanation:
Reverse causation: happiness leads to dog ownership, not the other way around.
A — Care demands might reduce happiness for some, but they don't directly undercut the causal inference.
B — Diversity of the sample doesn't weaken the conclusion.
D — Offers a mechanism for dogs causing happiness.
E — Doesn't address whether dogs cause happiness.

questions.stimulus: Astronomer: The planet Kepler-X shows a regular dip in brightness every 14 days. This dip is best explained by a large orbiting moon passing in front of the planet, blocking some of its reflected light.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the astronomer's explanation?

choices.A: Moons large enough to cause such a dip are rare.
choices.B: Kepler-X's brightness dips by the same amount every 14 days regardless of the angle from which it is observed, including from positions from which no orbiting moon could ever appear in front of the planet.
choices.C: Most planets in Kepler-X's system have at least one moon.
choices.D: Kepler-X's dips in brightness have been observed for five years.
choices.E: Other planets show dips in brightness at irregular intervals.

questions.explanation:
A moon can only block light when it passes between the planet and the observer. A dip seen from every angle, including ones where the moon couldn't be in front, can't be explained that way.
A — Rarity reduces likelihood a little, but rare things occur.
C — Makes a moon more plausible.
D — Duration doesn't bear on the explanation.
E — Other planets' irregular dips are irrelevant to this regular one.

questions.stimulus: Every employee at Larkin Design who works remotely attends a weekly video meeting. Some employees at Larkin Design who attend the weekly video meeting are graphic designers.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Every employee who attends the weekly video meeting works remotely.
choices.B: No graphic designer at Larkin Design works remotely.
choices.C: Some employees at Larkin Design do not attend the weekly video meeting.
choices.D: Some graphic designers at Larkin Design work remotely.
choices.E: Some graphic designers at Larkin Design attend a weekly video meeting.

questions.explanation:
"Some meeting attendees are graphic designers" can be flipped: some graphic designers are meeting attendees. That's all that's guaranteed.
A — Reverses the first statement.
B — Nothing rules this out or requires it.
C — Everyone could attend.
D — The designers at the meeting might all work on site.

questions.stimulus: If the city adopts the new zoning code, developers will be permitted to build taller buildings downtown. Taller downtown buildings will be built only if construction costs fall. Construction costs will not fall this year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: No taller buildings will be built downtown this year.
choices.B: Developers will not be permitted to build taller buildings downtown.
choices.C: If construction costs fall, taller buildings will be built downtown.
choices.D: Developers oppose the new zoning code.
choices.E: The city will not adopt the new zoning code this year.

questions.explanation:
Taller buildings built → construction costs fall. Costs won't fall this year, so no taller buildings this year. The zoning code doesn't matter: it only permits building.
B — Permission depends on the code, which may be adopted.
C — Falling costs are necessary, not sufficient.
D — Opinions aren't given.
E — Adoption leads to permission; it doesn't require construction. The code could still be adopted.

questions.stimulus: Last year, a local bookstore began hosting weekly author readings. Since then, the store's sales of books by local authors have risen sharply, while sales of other books have stayed about the same.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Author readings are the most effective way to boost book sales.
choices.B: Most of the bookstore's customers are local.
choices.C: The author readings caused the increase in local-author sales.
choices.D: The rise in the bookstore's total book sales came mostly from books by local authors.
choices.E: Sales of books by nonlocal authors would have fallen without the readings.

questions.explanation:
Local-author sales rose sharply; other sales were flat. So any rise in total sales came mostly from local authors.
A — Far too strong.
B — Not stated.
C — Likely, but the information shows only a correlation.
E — No such counterfactual is supported.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: Some species of coral can survive brief periods of elevated ocean temperature by expelling the algae that live in their tissues, a process called bleaching. Bleached coral that experiences prolonged high temperatures usually dies, but bleached coral whose waters return to normal temperature within a few weeks often recovers by reacquiring algae.
questions.stem: The biologist's statements most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Algae are unnecessary for coral survival.
choices.B: All coral species can recover from bleaching.
choices.C: How long elevated temperatures last is an important factor in whether bleached coral survives.
choices.D: Ocean temperatures are rising worldwide.
choices.E: Bleaching is harmful to coral in every case.

questions.explanation:
Brief heat followed by normal temperatures often allows recovery; prolonged heat usually kills. Duration matters.
A — Recovery involves reacquiring algae, which suggests they matter.
B — Only "some species" are discussed, and recovery is only "often."
D — Not stated.
E — Bleaching helps coral survive brief heat.

questions.stimulus: Some critics argue that video games make children more aggressive. But studies that track children over many years find no lasting increase in aggression among frequent gamers. And the short-term effects found in lab studies are no larger than those produced by competitive sports. The case that video games make children aggressive is far weaker than critics suggest.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: parents should allow children to play video games freely
choices.B: long-term studies find no lasting increase in aggression among frequent gamers
choices.C: video games have no effect on children
choices.D: the evidence that video games make children aggressive is weaker than critics claim
choices.E: competitive sports make children aggressive

questions.explanation:
The last sentence states the conclusion; the long-term studies and the sports comparison support it.
A — No recommendation is made.
B — A premise.
C — The author acknowledges short-term effects.
E — Mentioned as a comparison, not the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Opponents of the new library branch say the city cannot afford it. It is true that the branch will cost $4 million. But the city spends more than that every year on overdue maintenance for its aging main library, costs that would largely disappear once the new branch takes over many of its functions. The new branch, therefore, will likely save the city money over time.
questions.stem: The claim that the branch will cost $4 million figures in the columnist's argument in which one of the following ways?

choices.A: It is acknowledged as true but argued not to support the opponents' conclusion.
choices.B: It is offered to explain why the main library needs maintenance.
choices.C: It is a claim the columnist argues is inaccurate.
choices.D: It is the conclusion the columnist sets out to establish.
choices.E: It is evidence that the columnist uses to support the claim that the city cannot afford the branch.

questions.explanation:
"It is true that" signals a concession. The columnist grants the cost and then argues the savings outweigh it.
B — It explains nothing about the main library.
C — The columnist accepts it.
D — The conclusion is that the branch will save money.
E — That's the opponents' view.

questions.stimulus:
Kofi: All birds can fly.
Elena: Penguins are birds, and they can't fly.
questions.stem: Elena responds to Kofi by

choices.A: questioning his expertise
choices.B: offering a counterexample to his general claim
choices.C: pointing out an ambiguous term
choices.D: agreeing with him but adding a qualification
choices.E: arguing that penguins are not really birds

questions.explanation:
Penguins are birds that can't fly, so Kofi's "all birds" claim is false.
A — Elena doesn't address Kofi's expertise.
C — No term is in dispute.
D — She disagrees.
E — She asserts that penguins are birds.

questions.stimulus:
Lucia: The new rule requiring restaurants to post calorie counts on menus is pointless. Studies show that most diners ignore the numbers.
Owen: Most diners may ignore them, but the rule has led many restaurants to reformulate their dishes to reduce calories, because they don't want high numbers on their menus. That benefits every diner.
questions.stem: Lucia and Owen disagree over whether

choices.A: diners should pay attention to calorie counts
choices.B: most diners ignore the calorie counts
choices.C: calorie counts are accurate
choices.D: restaurants have reformulated dishes to reduce calories
choices.E: the calorie-posting rule serves a useful purpose

questions.explanation:
Lucia calls it pointless. Owen says it benefits diners through reformulation.
A — Neither makes this recommendation.
B — Owen concedes this.
C — Neither discusses accuracy.
D — Lucia doesn't address reformulation.

questions.stimulus: The orchestra will perform the symphony only if the soloist arrives. The soloist will arrive only if her flight is not delayed. So if the orchestra performs the symphony, the soloist's flight was not delayed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.A: The team will play in the final only if it wins the semifinal. The team won the semifinal. So the team will play in the final.
choices.B: The team's captain recovered. So the team will play in the final.
choices.C: The team will play in the final only if it wins the semifinal. So if the team does not win the semifinal, it will not play in the final.
choices.D: If the captain recovers, the team will win the semifinal. The captain did not recover. So the team will not win the semifinal.
choices.E: The team will play in the final only if it wins the semifinal. The team will win the semifinal only if its captain recovers. So if the team plays in the final, its captain recovered.

questions.explanation:
Same structure: A only if B; B only if C; so if A then C.
A — Treats a necessary condition as sufficient.
B — Treats a necessary condition as sufficient.
C — Valid, but only one premise and a contrapositive. A different structure.
D — Denies the antecedent.

questions.stimulus: Most people who live in Fairview own a car. Diego lives in Fairview. So Diego must own a car.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: All students at Lakeside College live on campus. Hana is a student there. So Hana lives on campus.
choices.B: Hana lives on campus. So she must be a student at Lakeside College.
choices.C: Most students at Lakeside College live on campus. Hana is a student at Lakeside College. So Hana must live on campus.
choices.D: Most students at Lakeside College live on campus. Hana is a student there. So Hana probably lives on campus.
choices.E: Some students at Lakeside College live on campus. So most do.

questions.explanation:
Both move from "most" to a certain conclusion about one individual.
A — Valid with "all."
B — A different structure.
D — The "probably" makes it reasonable.
E — A different overgeneralization.

questions.stimulus: Principle: An expert witness should disclose any financial relationship with a party to a case if a reasonable person would view that relationship as potentially influencing the witness's testimony.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.A: Dr. Diaz need not disclose his fees from the defendant, since he is confident they do not affect his testimony.
choices.B: Dr. Chen should disclose that she once attended the same university as the plaintiff's attorney.
choices.C: Dr. Bell should disclose that she owns a single share of a mutual fund that holds a tiny fraction of the defendant's stock.
choices.D: Dr. Asante should disclose that he received consulting fees from the defendant company last year, since a reasonable juror could think those fees might color his testimony on the company's behalf.
choices.E: Dr. Evans should disclose every financial transaction he has made in the past decade.

questions.explanation:
A financial relationship with a party that a reasonable person could see as influential means disclose.
A — The standard is a reasonable person's view, not the witness's confidence.
B — Not a financial relationship.
