C — Technically financial, but a reasonable person would hardly see this as influential. The principle doesn't clearly require disclosure.
E — Far beyond the principle.

questions.stimulus: Ana should return the extra change the cashier mistakenly gave her, even though the cashier will never know the difference.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the judgment above?

choices.A: Stores should train cashiers to avoid mistakes.
choices.B: People should return money they received by mistake, whether or not anyone would discover the mistake.
choices.C: People should return money only if they will be caught otherwise.
choices.D: People should always be polite to cashiers.
choices.E: Honesty is the best policy in business.

questions.explanation:
Facts: money received by mistake, and no one would know. The principle says return it regardless of detection.
A — About stores, not Ana.
C — Would say Ana need not return it.
D — Politeness isn't at issue.
E — Vague and directed at businesses, not individuals.

questions.stimulus: In Glenmoor, a new law requires bicyclists to wear helmets. Since the law took effect, the number of bicycle-related head injuries in Glenmoor has dropped, but the total number of bicycle-related injuries treated at hospitals has risen.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.A: The number of people cycling in Glenmoor increased substantially after the law took effect, as the city also opened many new bike paths.
choices.B: Hospitals in Glenmoor have improved their record keeping.
choices.C: Some cyclists in Glenmoor do not wear helmets despite the law.
choices.D: Helmets do not protect against arm and leg injuries.
choices.E: The helmet law was opposed by many cyclists.

questions.explanation:
More cyclists means more total injuries, while helmets cut the proportion of head injuries.
B — Could affect counts, but doesn't specifically resolve the divergence.
C — Doesn't explain the rise in total injuries.
D — Explains why non-head injuries aren't prevented, but not why the total rose.
E — Opposition doesn't explain injury counts.

questions.stimulus:
Fatima: The museum's decision to charge admission was a mistake. Although it raised revenue, attendance by low-income families fell sharply, and serving the whole community is the museum's core mission.
George: Charging admission was the right decision. Yes, attendance by low-income families dropped, but the museum was on the verge of closing, and a closed museum serves no one.
questions.stem: Fatima and George are committed to agreeing that

choices.A: the museum was on the verge of closing
choices.B: charging admission was a mistake
choices.C: the museum should offer free days for low-income families
choices.D: the museum's core mission is to serve the whole community
choices.E: attendance by low-income families declined after the museum began charging admission

questions.explanation:
Fatima says it "fell sharply." George says "Yes, attendance by low-income families dropped."
A — Only George states this.
B — They disagree about this.
C — Neither proposes this.
D — Only Fatima states this.

questions.stimulus: My neighbor never wears a seat belt and has never been hurt in a car accident. So seat belts don't really make people safer.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: attacks the character of people who wear seat belts
choices.B: draws a general conclusion from a single case
choices.C: confuses a cause with an effect
choices.D: relies on an expert who is biased
choices.E: assumes that car accidents are rare

questions.explanation:
One lucky neighbor can't overturn evidence about seat belts in general.
A — No one's character is attacked.
C — No cause and effect are reversed.
D — No expert is cited.
E — Not assumed.

questions.stimulus: The law requires that every business display its permit in a conspicuous place. Since a conspicuous person is one who attracts unwanted attention, this law requires businesses to place their permits where they will attract unwanted attention.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: shifts between two different meanings of a key word
choices.B: fails to consider why the law was passed
choices.C: relies on an appeal to authority
choices.D: treats a necessary condition as sufficient
choices.E: assumes that all businesses have permits

questions.explanation:
"Conspicuous" in the law means clearly visible. The argument switches to a sense about people drawing unwanted attention.
B — Purpose might clarify meaning, but the flaw is the shift in meaning itself.
C — No authority is invoked.
D — No conditional is misused.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Bioethicist: Opponents of the new gene-editing therapy argue that it could someday be used for purposes other than treating disease, such as enhancing intelligence. But this therapy has been approved only for treating a rare blood disorder, and regulators have explicitly prohibited its use for any other purpose. Thus the opponents' concern is unfounded.
questions.stem: The bioethicist's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: confuses the approval of a therapy with evidence that the therapy is safe
choices.B: presumes that enhancing intelligence would be harmful
choices.C: relies on the authority of regulators who may lack relevant expertise
choices.D: takes for granted that a current prohibition will continue to be effective in the future
choices.E: attacks the motives of the opponents rather than their argument

questions.explanation:
Opponents worry about what could happen someday. The bioethicist answers with today's approval and prohibition, assuming the rules will hold and be obeyed. That doesn't address the future-oriented concern.
A — Safety isn't the concern being addressed.
B — The bioethicist doesn't take a position on that.
C — The issue isn't expertise but whether the prohibition will last and be enforced.
E — No motives are mentioned.

questions.stimulus: Online retailer: Our new policy of offering free returns will increase sales. Customers who know they can return items at no cost will be more willing to buy items they have not seen in person.
questions.stem: The retailer's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Free returns will not increase the company's costs.
choices.B: Most customers who buy online eventually return at least one item.
choices.C: Some potential customers currently hesitate to buy items they haven't seen in person because returning them would cost money.
choices.D: Customers prefer shopping online to shopping in stores.
choices.E: Competitors do not offer free returns.

questions.explanation:
Free returns help only if return costs are currently holding some buyers back.
A — Costs aren't part of the sales prediction.
B — Not needed.
D — Not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: To determine whether residents support building a new public pool, the town council mailed surveys to every household that had purchased a pass to the existing pool last summer. Eighty percent of respondents supported the new pool, so the council concluded that most residents support it.
questions.stem: The council's conclusion depends on the assumption that

choices.A: the existing pool is in poor condition
choices.B: residents who support the pool would be willing to pay higher taxes for it
choices.C: the views of households that bought pool passes do not differ significantly from those of other residents on this question
choices.D: a new pool would be used more than the existing pool
choices.E: every household that received a survey returned it

questions.explanation:
Pass holders are likely pool enthusiasts. The conclusion about "most residents" works only if their views are representative.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
D — Usage isn't part of the support claim.
E — Full response isn't needed.

questions.stimulus: Every bird in the aviary was banded by the staff. So the parrot in the corner cage was banded by the staff.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Parrots are the most common birds in the aviary.
choices.B: The staff band birds when they first arrive.
choices.C: Every bird banded by the staff is in the aviary.
choices.D: Some parrots in the aviary were banded by the staff.
choices.E: The parrot in the corner cage is a bird in the aviary.

questions.explanation:
Aviary bird → banded. If the parrot is an aviary bird, it was banded.
A — Doesn't place this parrot in the aviary.
B — Timing doesn't matter.
C — Reverses the premise.
D — Doesn't place this parrot in the aviary.

questions.stimulus: Politician: Any policy that would increase the cost of housing in our city is one that our constituents oppose. And we should never enact a policy that our constituents oppose. Therefore, we should not enact the proposed zoning restrictions.
questions.stem: The politician's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Any policy constituents oppose would increase the cost of housing.
choices.B: The proposed zoning restrictions would increase the cost of housing in the city.
choices.C: Constituents would support zoning restrictions that lowered the cost of housing.
choices.D: Zoning restrictions sometimes reduce the cost of housing.
choices.E: Most residents of the city rent rather than own their homes.

questions.explanation:
Increase housing costs → constituents oppose → never enact. If the restrictions raise costs, they shouldn't be enacted.
A — Reverses the first premise.
C — Says nothing about these restrictions raising costs or being opposed.
D — Would cut against the conclusion.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Researchers found that people who chew gum while studying remember more of the material than people who don't. They conclude that chewing gum improves memory.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: When the same people studied with and without gum on different days, they remembered more on the days they chewed gum.
choices.B: Gum sales have increased in recent years.
choices.C: Chewing gum can freshen breath.
choices.D: People who chew gum tend to be younger than people who don't.
choices.E: Some people find chewing gum distracting.

questions.explanation:
Comparing the same people with and without gum rules out differences between gum chewers and non-chewers.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Age is an alternative explanation.
E — Suggests gum may not help.

questions.stimulus: Urban planner: The proposed light-rail line will reduce traffic on Route 9, since many commuters who currently drive on Route 9 will switch to the train.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the planner's argument?

choices.A: Light-rail lines are expensive to build.
choices.B: Traffic on Route 9 has increased steadily for a decade.
choices.C: The light-rail line will run parallel to Route 9 for only a short distance.
choices.D: In a recent survey, a majority of Route 9 commuters said they would take the light rail if its stations were located where the proposal places them.
choices.E: Some cities with light rail still have heavy traffic.

questions.explanation:
Direct evidence that drivers would switch supports the key assumption.
A — Cost doesn't bear on traffic.
B — Shows a problem exists but not that rail will fix it.
C — Fewer drivers could switch.
E — Suggests rail may not reduce traffic.

questions.stimulus: A company found that employees who took its optional time-management course completed more projects on time than employees who didn't. The company concludes that the course improves employees' time management.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the company's conclusion?

choices.A: The course costs the company a significant amount.
choices.B: Employees who signed up for the course were already completing more projects on time than other employees before taking it.
choices.C: Employees who took the course reported feeling more organized.
choices.D: Some employees who took the course said it was too long.
choices.E: The course was taught by an outside consultant.

questions.explanation:
If they were already better before the course, the gap reflects who chose the course, not what it taught.
A — Cost is irrelevant.
C — Supports the conclusion.
D — Complaints don't show it didn't work.
E — Who taught it doesn't matter.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Medieval manuscripts from the monastery at Kelvar contain far fewer references to plague than manuscripts from neighboring monasteries during the same century. This suggests that Kelvar was largely spared from the plague that ravaged the region.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the historian's argument?

choices.A: Kelvar was located at a higher altitude than the neighboring monasteries.
choices.B: Several monks from Kelvar later moved to neighboring monasteries.
choices.C: Kelvar's monastic rule prohibited monks from recording misfortunes they believed to be divine punishments, a category that included plague.
choices.D: Plague was common throughout the region during that century.
choices.E: Many manuscripts from the period have been lost.

questions.explanation:
Fewer references could reflect a rule against writing about plague, not an absence of plague.
A — Isolation might support being spared.
B — Movement of monks doesn't explain the gap in references.
D — Background already assumed.
E — A general loss affects all monasteries. It doesn't explain Kelvar's difference.

questions.stimulus: Every film shown at the Riverside Festival this year was directed by a first-time director. None of the films directed by first-time directors this year had a budget over $2 million.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Some films shown at the festival had budgets over $1 million.
choices.B: The festival rejected all films with large budgets.
choices.C: First-time directors made only low-budget films in all years.
choices.D: Every film with a budget under $2 million was shown at the festival.
choices.E: No film shown at the Riverside Festival this year had a budget over $2 million.

questions.explanation:
Festival film → first-time director → budget not over $2 million.
A — Not established.
B — Rejections aren't described.
C — Only this year is described.
D — Reverses the chain.

questions.stimulus: In a certain chess club, every member who has won a tournament has a rating above 1800. Some members with ratings above 1800 have never played in a tournament. No member who has never played in a tournament is eligible to coach.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Some members with ratings above 1800 are not eligible to coach.
choices.B: Every member who is eligible to coach has won a tournament.
choices.C: Some members who have won a tournament have never played in one.
choices.D: Every member with a rating above 1800 has won a tournament.
choices.E: No member who has won a tournament is eligible to coach.

questions.explanation:
Some 1800-plus members never played in a tournament, and never playing makes a member ineligible to coach. So some 1800-plus members can't coach.
B — Eligibility requires having played, not winning.
C — Impossible.
D — Reverses the first statement.
E — Winners have played, so nothing rules them out.

questions.stimulus: A city's public library began lending tools such as drills and saws. In the first year, more than half of the tools were borrowed at least once a month, while the library's book circulation remained unchanged.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Tool lending caused new patrons to visit the library.
choices.B: The library should stop lending books.
choices.C: Most of the library's patrons own their own tools.
choices.D: Tool lending at the library did not come at the cost of reduced book borrowing during the first year.
choices.E: Residents prefer borrowing tools to borrowing books.

questions.explanation:
Book circulation stayed the same while tools were borrowed. No drop in books.
A — Possible, but not shown.
B — Not supported.
C — Not stated.
E — No preference data.

questions.stimulus: Some people think that because spiders are frightening, they should be eliminated from homes. But most household spiders are harmless to humans, and they eat insects like mosquitoes and flies that carry disease. Rather than killing spiders, homeowners should leave them alone.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: homeowners should not kill the spiders in their homes
choices.B: most household spiders are harmless to humans
choices.C: spiders are frightening
choices.D: homeowners should encourage more spiders to live in their homes
choices.E: spiders eat insects that carry disease

questions.explanation:
The last sentence states the recommendation, which the facts about spiders support.
B — A premise.
C — The opposing view's premise.
D — The author says leave them alone, not attract more.
E — A premise.

questions.stimulus: Many people believe that eating carrots improves night vision. This belief may have started as a deliberate rumor during wartime to hide the use of new radar technology. In fact, while vitamin A is needed for normal vision, eating extra carrots will not improve the night vision of people who already get enough vitamin A.
questions.stem: The claim that vitamin A is needed for normal vision plays which one of the following roles?

choices.A: It is the main conclusion of the passage.
choices.B: It is evidence that the belief started as a wartime rumor.
choices.C: It acknowledges a truth related to the popular belief while setting up a limit on what that truth implies.
choices.D: It explains why radar technology was kept secret.
choices.E: It is a claim the passage argues is false.

questions.explanation:
The author grants vitamin A matters for vision, then says extra carrots don't help people already getting enough. It's a qualified concession.
A — The point is that extra carrots won't improve night vision.
B — Unrelated to the rumor's origin.
D — Unrelated.
E — The passage accepts it.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The museum's new acquisition policy requires that any donated artwork be accompanied by complete documentation of its ownership history. Some argue this will deter donations. That may be so in the short term. But a museum that accepts works of uncertain provenance risks displaying stolen art, and the scandals that result drive away donors far more effectively than any documentation requirement. So the policy will ultimately help the museum attract donations.
questions.stem: The claim that the policy may deter donations in the short term plays which one of the following roles in the critic's argument?

choices.A: It is evidence for the claim that accepting undocumented works risks displaying stolen art.
choices.B: It is a premise that directly supports the critic's conclusion.
choices.C: It is a claim that the critic attempts to refute.
choices.D: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
choices.E: It is a concession that the critic accepts while maintaining that the policy's long-term effect will be the opposite.

questions.explanation:
"That may be so in the short term" grants the objection's point, then argues the long-run effect favors the policy.
A — It doesn't support that claim.
B — It cuts against the conclusion.
C — The critic concedes it rather than refuting it, and argues the long-term effect is different.
D — The conclusion is that the policy will help attract donations.

questions.stimulus:
Rae: The school should eliminate homework for first graders because it causes stress.
Sam: By that reasoning, the school should eliminate tests, recess games, and class presentations too, since all of them cause some stress. Yet these activities are valuable.
questions.stem: Sam responds to Rae's argument by

choices.A: questioning Rae's expertise in education
choices.B: providing evidence that homework does not cause stress
choices.C: arguing that stress is beneficial for children
choices.D: showing that her reasoning, applied consistently, would lead to conclusions she would likely reject
choices.E: proposing a compromise between their positions

questions.explanation:
Sam extends "causes stress → eliminate" to other valued activities.
A — No attack on expertise.
B — Sam doesn't deny homework causes stress.
C — Sam doesn't claim stress itself is good.
E — No compromise is offered.

questions.stimulus:
Kai: The city's new public art installation is a waste of money. It cost $200,000 and few people stop to look at it.
Luz: Few people stop, but thousands pass it every day, and studies show public art improves how people feel about their neighborhood even when they don't stop to examine it.
questions.stem: Kai and Luz disagree over whether

choices.A: few people stop to look at the installation
choices.B: the installation provides enough benefit to justify its cost
choices.C: thousands of people pass the installation daily
choices.D: the installation cost $200,000
choices.E: public art should be funded by private donors

questions.explanation:
Kai says it's a waste; Luz says it benefits passersby.
A — Luz concedes this.
C — Kai doesn't address this.
D — Luz doesn't dispute the cost.
E — Neither discusses funding sources.

questions.stimulus: Any student who completes all the practice problems will pass the exam. Lin did not pass the exam. So Lin did not complete all the practice problems.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.A: Most plants that receive enough sunlight bloom. This rosebush did not bloom. So it probably did not receive enough sunlight.
choices.B: This rosebush did not bloom, and it is in the shade. So shade prevents blooming.
choices.C: Any plant that receives enough sunlight will bloom. This rosebush bloomed. So it received enough sunlight.
choices.D: Any plant that receives enough sunlight will bloom. This rosebush did not bloom. So this rosebush did not receive enough sunlight.
choices.E: Any plant that receives enough sunlight will bloom. This rosebush did not receive enough sunlight. So it will not bloom.

questions.explanation:
If A then B; not B; so not A (valid contrapositive). The plant argument matches.
A — Probabilistic, so a different form.
B — A causal generalization.
C — Affirms the consequent.
E — Denies the antecedent.

questions.stimulus: The new manager has made several changes, and since then employee morale has declined. Clearly the manager's changes are responsible for the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Since the town installed new streetlights, the number of car accidents has increased. Clearly the streetlights caused the increase.
choices.B: Streetlights are bright. So they will reduce crime.
choices.C: The town installed streetlights because residents complained. So the residents caused the streetlights.
choices.D: Every time the town installs streetlights, accidents decrease. So streetlights reduce accidents.
choices.E: Some streetlights are broken. So all streetlights are unreliable.

questions.explanation:
Both infer causation from a sequence in time without ruling out other causes.
B — A prediction from a feature.
C — A trivially true causal claim.
D — Repeated correlation is somewhat stronger, and the conclusion runs the other way.
E — Overgeneralization, a different flaw.

traps.C: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.stimulus: Principle: A volunteer organization should accept a donation only if the donor's stated purpose for the gift is consistent with the organization's mission.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle?

choices.A: The Animal Rescue League should accept a donation earmarked for veterinary care only if the donor visits the shelter.
choices.B: The Literacy Alliance should accept a donation because the donor is a well-known author.
choices.C: The Food Pantry should decline a donation for buying food because the donor is a corporation.
choices.D: The Riverbank Cleanup Society should accept any donation over $1,000.
choices.E: The Riverbank Cleanup Society should decline a donation offered on condition that it be used to fund a political campaign, since its mission is cleaning local waterways.

questions.explanation:
The donor's purpose (political campaign) conflicts with the mission, so per the principle the gift shouldn't be accepted.
A — Visiting isn't a condition.
B — The donor's fame isn't the criterion.
C — Buying food fits the mission; the principle doesn't restrict corporate donors.
D — Ignores the purpose condition.

questions.stimulus: Editor: We should not publish the reader's letter accusing the mayor of taking bribes. The letter offers no evidence for its accusation, and publishing it could seriously damage the mayor's reputation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's position?

choices.A: A newspaper should verify every claim in every letter it publishes.
choices.B: Newspapers should publish all letters from readers.
choices.C: A newspaper should not publish a serious accusation against someone if the accusation is unsupported and could cause significant harm.
choices.D: Accusations of bribery should be reported to the police.
choices.E: Public officials should never be criticized in newspapers.

questions.explanation:
Facts: unsupported accusation and potential serious harm. The principle says don't publish.
A — Broader than needed, and it doesn't address harm.
B — Would require publishing.
D — Doesn't address publication.
E — Far broader than the editor's reasoning.

questions.stimulus: A small town's only grocery store extended its hours to stay open until midnight. Yet in the following months, the store's total sales did not increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: Some residents work late shifts at a nearby factory.
choices.B: Most of the store's late-night customers were people who previously shopped earlier in the evening and simply shifted their shopping later.
choices.C: The store advertised its new hours in the local newspaper.
choices.D: The store hired additional staff to cover the late shift.
choices.E: The store raised prices on some items.

questions.explanation:
Shoppers moved their visits rather than adding new purchases, so total sales stayed flat.
A — Suggests new late customers, which deepens the puzzle.
C — Advertising doesn't explain flat sales.
D — Staffing doesn't explain flat sales.
E — Could affect sales, but it doesn't explain why longer hours didn't help.

questions.stimulus: A hospital installed hand-sanitizer stations outside every patient room. Over the next year, the hospital's rate of patient infections fell by 20 percent. The hospital administrator credits the sanitizer stations.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the administrator's conclusion?

choices.A: whether the hospital also changed its cleaning procedures or staffing during the same year
choices.B: how much the sanitizer stations cost
choices.C: whether other hospitals have sanitizer stations
choices.D: whether patients liked the sanitizer stations
choices.E: what brand of sanitizer was used

questions.explanation:
Other changes could explain the drop. If none occurred, the sanitizer explanation is stronger.
B — Cost doesn't test causation.
C — Without outcome data, this doesn't test the claim.
D — Patient preferences are irrelevant.
E — Brand is a minor detail.

questions.stimulus: Our family has always celebrated holidays by cooking a large meal at home. So cooking at home is the best way to celebrate holidays.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: generalizes from a large sample
choices.B: fails to define what counts as a holiday
choices.C: treats a cause as an effect
choices.D: relies on the opinion of an expert
choices.E: assumes that a practice is best simply because it has been followed for a long time

questions.explanation:
Tradition alone doesn't establish that something is best.
A — No sample is used.
B — A vague term, but not the core flaw.
C — No causal reversal.
D — No expert.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Since the city began requiring restaurants to post health inspection grades in their windows, the number of restaurants receiving top grades has risen sharply. Clearly, posting grades has motivated restaurants to improve their cleanliness.
questions.stem: The columnist's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it fails to consider the possibility that

choices.A: other cities have adopted similar requirements
choices.B: the requirement costs restaurants money to comply with
choices.C: customers do not pay attention to posted grades
choices.D: inspectors have become more lenient in assigning grades since the requirement took effect
choices.E: some restaurants still receive low grades

questions.explanation:
More top grades could reflect easier grading rather than cleaner restaurants.
A — Other cities don't matter.
B — Cost is irrelevant.
C — If customers ignore grades, restaurants might lack motivation. But improvement could still occur for other reasons, and this doesn't explain the rise as directly as leniency.
E — A few low grades don't undercut the trend.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: For every event, there is some cause that brought it about. Therefore, there is some single cause that brought about every event.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument is flawed because it

choices.A: relies on an ambiguous use of the term "event"
choices.B: infers that because each item in a group has something related to it, there is one thing related to every item
choices.C: fails to consider that some events may have more than one cause
choices.D: confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one
choices.E: presupposes the truth of the conclusion it attempts to establish

questions.explanation:
"Every event has some cause" doesn't mean "some one cause underlies every event." The order of "every" and "some" has been swapped.
A — "Event" is used consistently. The ambiguity is in quantifier scope.
C — True, but even with single causes the inference is invalid.
D — No conditional is reversed.
E — Not circular. It's a quantifier shift.

questions.stimulus: Maria plans to save money by biking to work instead of driving. She says the savings on gas and parking will be substantial.
questions.stem: Maria's plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Most of Maria's coworkers bike to work.
choices.B: Biking is healthier than driving.
choices.C: The costs of biking to work will not be nearly as large as what she currently spends on gas and parking.
choices.D: Maria's workplace has a bike rack.
choices.E: Gas prices will rise next year.

questions.explanation:
If biking costs, such as equipment, repairs, or showers at a gym, roughly match driving costs, there's no substantial saving.
A — Not required.
B — Health isn't part of the savings claim.
D — Helpful, but parking a bike elsewhere could work.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Economist: The town of Merriton offered tax incentives to attract manufacturers, and within five years three factories had relocated there. Since those factories employ many Merriton residents, the tax incentives were clearly worth their cost to the town.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.A: The factories pay their employees more than the average wage in the region.
choices.B: Every resident employed by the factories was previously unemployed.
choices.C: No other town offered tax incentives to the same manufacturers.
choices.D: The tax incentives will be permanent.
choices.E: The factories would not have relocated to Merriton without the tax incentives.

questions.explanation:
If the factories would have come anyway, the town gave up tax revenue for nothing. The incentives' worth depends on their having made a difference.
A — Not required for the incentives to be worth it.
B — "Every" is far too strong.
C — Others' offers don't matter if Merriton's worked.
D — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Only those who attended the safety training are permitted to operate the forklift. Raj is permitted to operate the forklift. So Raj passed the safety exam.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Some people who attended the safety training passed the exam.
choices.B: Some people permitted to operate the forklift have not attended the safety training.
choices.C: Raj attended the safety training.
choices.D: Everyone who attended the safety training passed the safety exam.
choices.E: Everyone who passed the safety exam attended the safety training.

questions.explanation:
Permitted → attended training (premise). Attended → passed exam (assumption). So Raj passed.
A — "Some" doesn't guarantee Raj passed.
B — Contradicts the first premise and doesn't reach the exam.
C — Already follows from the premises; doesn't reach the exam.
E — Reverses the needed link.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: The decline of frog populations in the Merrick wetlands is likely caused by a fungal infection. Frogs collected from the wetlands in recent years show high rates of this infection.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the biologist's argument?

choices.A: The fungus also infects frogs in wetlands where populations are stable.
choices.B: Frogs are important to wetland ecosystems.
choices.C: Frogs collected from the wetlands before the decline began showed almost no signs of the infection.
choices.D: The fungus was first identified decades ago.
choices.E: Pesticide use near the wetlands has increased.

questions.explanation:
If the infection appeared only as the decline began, the timing supports it as the cause.
A — Suggests the fungus doesn't cause declines.
B — Irrelevant.
D — Irrelevant to this decline.
E — An alternative cause.

questions.stimulus: Linguist: The word "galley," meaning a ship's kitchen, probably derives from "gallery," since early ships' kitchens were often located in long, narrow passages resembling galleries.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguist's argument?

choices.A: Historical records show that sailors in the period when the word first appeared used "gallery" for narrow passages aboard ships.
choices.B: The word "gallery" is of Italian origin.
choices.C: The word "galley" also refers to a type of ship powered by oars.
choices.D: Many nautical terms derive from words for parts of buildings.
choices.E: Modern ships' kitchens are not located in narrow passages.

questions.explanation:
Evidence that sailors actually used "gallery" for such passages supports the proposed path from "gallery" to "galley."
B — Origin of "gallery" doesn't help.
C — A competing meaning suggests a different origin.
D — General support, but it doesn't specifically connect these two words.
E — Modern layouts don't bear on origin.

questions.stimulus: Since the café started offering free Wi-Fi, more customers have been visiting. The owner concludes that the Wi-Fi is attracting customers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the owner's conclusion?

choices.A: The café's coffee is popular.
choices.B: A large office building opened next to the café at the same time it began offering Wi-Fi.
choices.C: Many customers use the Wi-Fi.
choices.D: Other cafés also offer Wi-Fi.
choices.E: Wi-Fi is inexpensive to provide.

questions.explanation:
New office workers nearby could explain the rise in customers.
A — Doesn't explain the increase.
C — Supports the owner.
D — Doesn't explain the change.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Researchers found that mice given a certain dietary supplement lived 20 percent longer than mice not given it. The supplement's manufacturer claims the supplement will extend human lifespans as well.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the manufacturer's claim?

choices.A: The study used several hundred mice.
choices.B: The supplement works by blocking a metabolic process that exists in mice but is absent in humans.
choices.C: The supplement is expensive.
choices.D: Some mice given the supplement did not live longer.
choices.E: Humans live much longer than mice.

questions.explanation:
If the mechanism doesn't exist in humans, the mouse results won't carry over.
A — A larger sample supports the mouse finding.
C — Cost is irrelevant.
D — Averages allow exceptions.
E — Lifespan differences alone don't show the effect won't transfer.

questions.stimulus: No one who arrived after 9 a.m. was allowed into the exam room. Pedro was allowed into the exam room.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Pedro arrived exactly at 9 a.m.
choices.B: Some people arrived after 9 a.m.
choices.C: Pedro passed the exam.
choices.D: Pedro did not arrive after 9 a.m.
choices.E: Everyone who arrived before 9 a.m. was allowed in.

questions.explanation:
Arrived after 9 → not allowed. Pedro was allowed, so he didn't arrive after 9.
A — He could have arrived earlier.
B — Not stated.
C — Not stated.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: A bookstore sold 400 books last week. Of these, 150 were novels, and 200 were bought by customers using a store discount card. Every novel sold last week was bought with a discount card.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: More than half of the books sold last week were novels.
choices.B: Every book bought with a discount card was a novel.
choices.C: Most books bought with a discount card were not novels.
choices.D: Some novels were bought without a discount card.
choices.E: Exactly 50 of the books bought with a discount card were not novels.

questions.explanation:
All 150 novels are among the 200 card purchases, so the other 200 − 150 = 50 card purchases were not novels.
A — 150 of 400 is less than half.
B — Reverses the statement; 50 card purchases weren't novels.
C — 150 of the 200 card purchases were novels.
D — Every novel was bought with a card.

questions.stimulus: A study of 1,000 adults found that those who reported spending more than four hours a day on social media were more likely to report feeling lonely than those who spent less time.
questions.stem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.A: Among the adults studied, heavy social media use was associated with higher reported loneliness.
choices.B: People who don't use social media are never lonely.
choices.C: Lonely people should avoid social media.
choices.D: Social media causes loneliness.
choices.E: Most adults spend more than four hours a day on social media.

questions.explanation:
That's exactly what the study found: an association.
B — Far too strong.
C — No recommendation follows.
D — Causation isn't shown.
E — Proportions aren't given.

questions.stimulus: In a long-running study, children who learned a second language before age seven later scored higher on tests of mental flexibility than children who learned one after age twelve. Children who learned a second language between seven and twelve scored in between.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the study's findings?

choices.A: Parents should teach their children a second language before age seven.
choices.B: Children who never learn a second language have the lowest mental flexibility.
choices.C: The age at which children begin learning a second language is associated with differences in their later mental flexibility.
choices.D: Learning a second language after age twelve has no cognitive benefits.
choices.E: Learning a second language causes greater mental flexibility.

questions.explanation:
Scores line up with age of learning: earliest highest, middle in between, latest lowest. That's an association.
A — A recommendation beyond the data.
B — Non-learners weren't studied.
D — Too strong.
E — The study doesn't establish cause.

questions.stimulus: Although many people believe that bats are blind, most bat species can see quite well. In fact, some fruit bats rely mainly on their vision to navigate. The popular belief probably arises because many bats also use echolocation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the passage?

choices.A: Bats see better than most mammals.
choices.B: Echolocation is more useful than vision for bats.
choices.C: Some fruit bats rely mainly on vision.
choices.D: Many bats use echolocation.
choices.E: The belief that bats are blind is mistaken.

questions.explanation:
The passage refutes the popular belief. The rest supports or explains it.
A — No comparison is made.
B — Not claimed.
C — Support.
D — Explains the belief's origin.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Critics claim the new trade agreement will cost manufacturing jobs. But the agreement reduces tariffs on the raw materials our manufacturers import, lowering their costs. Lower costs will make our manufacturers more competitive abroad, increasing demand for their products. So the agreement is likely to add manufacturing jobs, not eliminate them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the economist's argument?

choices.A: The critics of the trade agreement are biased.
choices.B: Manufacturers will become more competitive abroad.
choices.C: The trade agreement is likely to increase rather than decrease the number of manufacturing jobs.
choices.D: Demand for manufactured goods will increase.
choices.E: The trade agreement will reduce tariffs on imported raw materials.

questions.explanation:
The final sentence states the conclusion the chain of reasoning leads to.
A — Not claimed.
B — An intermediate step.
D — An intermediate step.
E — A premise.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Introducing a predator to control an invasive species can backfire. When cane toads were introduced to Australia to eat crop-destroying beetles, they ignored the beetles and spread across the continent, poisoning native wildlife. Any proposal to control the invasive lionfish in the Caribbean by introducing a predator should therefore be approached with great caution.
questions.stem: The statement about cane toads plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is an example offered in support of a general claim that in turn supports the conclusion.
choices.B: It is background information that is irrelevant to the conclusion.
choices.C: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
choices.D: It is a counterexample to the ecologist's main claim.
choices.E: It is an analogy the ecologist argues is misleading.

questions.explanation:
The cane toad case illustrates "introducing a predator can backfire," which grounds the call for caution about lionfish.
B — It's central support.
C — The conclusion concerns caution about lionfish.
D — It supports the claim.
E — The ecologist relies on it.

questions.stimulus: Some say that because the novel was banned in several countries, it must be dangerous. But books have been banned for showing political dissent, for depicting ordinary romance, and even for misspellings in their titles. The mere fact of a ban tells us little about whether a book is actually dangerous.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by

choices.A: providing evidence that the novel is not dangerous
choices.B: pointing out that the claim is self-contradictory
choices.C: questioning the motives of those who banned the novel
choices.D: showing that the evidence cited for a claim is consistent with many situations in which the claim would be false
choices.E: arguing that all book bans are unjustified

questions.explanation:
Bans happen for trivial reasons too, so a ban doesn't indicate danger.
A — Nothing is said about the novel's content.
B — No contradiction is alleged.
C — Motives aren't examined.
E — Not argued.

questions.stimulus:
Yusuf: Professional athletes are paid far too much. A teacher, who shapes the future of society, earns a tiny fraction of what a star athlete makes.
Clara: Athletes' salaries reflect the revenue they generate for their teams through ticket sales and broadcasting. They're paid what the market will bear, not what their social value is.
questions.stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that Yusuf and Clara disagree over whether

choices.A: teachers should be paid more
choices.B: athletes' pay should be judged by comparison with the social value of their work
choices.C: broadcasting revenue is increasing
choices.D: teachers earn less than star athletes
choices.E: athletes generate revenue for their teams

questions.explanation:
Yusuf measures pay against social contribution. Clara says pay reflects market revenue, not social value.
A — Clara doesn't address teacher pay.
C — Neither addresses this.
D — Clara doesn't dispute this.
E — Yusuf doesn't dispute this.

questions.stimulus:
Hassan: The new park should include a dog run. Many residents own dogs, and they need a safe place for their pets to exercise off-leash.
Ingrid: Residents do need an off-leash area, but the new park is too small. A dog run there would take space from the playground.
questions.stem: Hassan and Ingrid are committed to agreeing with which one of the following?

choices.A: The playground is more important than a dog run.
choices.B: Many residents own dogs.
choices.C: The new park is too small for a dog run.
choices.D: The new park should include a dog run.
choices.E: Residents need a place where their dogs can exercise off-leash.

questions.explanation:
Hassan says they need one; Ingrid says "Residents do need an off-leash area."
A — Only Ingrid implies this.
B — Only Hassan says this explicitly.
C — Only Ingrid says this.
D — They disagree.

questions.stimulus: All the apples in this basket are ripe. This apple came from this basket. So this apple is ripe.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: Most shirts on this rack are on sale. This shirt came from this rack. So it is on sale.
choices.B: All the shirts on this rack are on sale. This shirt came from this rack. So this shirt is on sale.
choices.C: No shirts on this rack are on sale. This shirt is on sale. So it did not come from this rack.
choices.D: All the shirts on this rack are on sale. This shirt is on sale. So it came from this rack.
choices.E: This shirt is on sale. So all shirts on this rack are on sale.

questions.explanation:
Same form: all items in group X have property P; this item is from X; so it has P.
A — "Most" breaks validity.
C — Valid, but a different form (no/contrapositive).
D — Affirms the consequent.
E — Generalizes from one case.

questions.stimulus: Every successful restaurant in this city has a skilled chef. Some restaurants in this city that have a skilled chef are expensive. So some successful restaurants in this city are expensive.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: Every winning team in the league has a strong defense. Some teams in the league with a strong defense have young players. So some winning teams in the league have young players.
choices.B: Every winning team in the league has a strong defense. Some winning teams have young players. So some teams with a strong defense have young players.
choices.C: No winning team has a weak defense. Some teams have weak defenses. So some teams are not winning teams.
choices.D: Every winning team has a strong defense. This team has a strong defense. So it is a winning team.
choices.E: Some winning teams have a strong defense. So all teams with a strong defense win.

questions.explanation:
All A are B; some B are C; so some A are C. Invalid, because the B's that are C might not be A's. Same structure.
B — Valid. Some winning teams (which have defense) have young players.
C — Valid.
D — A different flaw (affirming the consequent with an individual).
E — A different overgeneralization.

questions.stimulus: Principle: An employer should give an employee a promotion only if the employee has met all performance goals for the year and has received no formal complaints.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: Mr. Odu should not be promoted, since he has been with the company only a year.
choices.B: Ms. Tan should be promoted, since she received no complaints and met most of her goals.
choices.C: Mr. Bell should be promoted, since he met all his performance goals and received no formal complaints.
choices.D: Ms. Ruiz should not be promoted this year, since although she met all her performance goals, she received a formal complaint from a colleague.
choices.E: Ms. Kim should be promoted because her supervisor recommends it.

questions.explanation:
A formal complaint means the principle's condition isn't met, so no promotion.
A — Tenure isn't a condition.
B — She didn't meet all goals.
C — The principle gives necessary conditions, not sufficient ones. It doesn't say he should be promoted.
E — Recommendation isn't a condition.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: A doctor who learns that a patient has a contagious disease that poses a serious risk to the patient's family should inform the family, even if the patient objects. Patient confidentiality is important, but it is outweighed when keeping a secret puts others in serious danger.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.A: Confidentiality is never important in medicine.
choices.B: Patients should inform their families about contagious diseases.
choices.C: The duty to protect others from serious harm can override the duty to keep a confidence.
choices.D: Doctors should report all diseases to public health authorities.
choices.E: Doctors should always obey their patients' wishes.

questions.explanation:
The ethicist's reasoning: the danger to others outweighs confidentiality. This principle states that ranking.
A — The ethicist calls it important.
B — About the patient's duty, not the doctor's.
D — Not about informing family.
E — Would forbid informing the family.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the average fuel efficiency of new cars sold in Valdonia has increased substantially. Yet the total amount of gasoline consumed by cars in Valdonia has also increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.A: Gasoline prices in Valdonia have risen over the decade.
choices.B: Fuel-efficient cars cost more than less efficient cars.
choices.C: The number of cars on Valdonia's roads and the average distance each car is driven per year have both increased considerably over the decade.
choices.D: Many Valdonians prefer larger vehicles.
choices.E: Some new cars in Valdonia are electric.

questions.explanation:
More cars driving more miles can raise total consumption even as each car becomes more efficient.
A — Higher prices would tend to reduce consumption.
B — Cost doesn't explain consumption.
D — Larger vehicles might lower efficiency, but average efficiency rose.
E — Would reduce gasoline use.

questions.stimulus: If Ana gets the internship, she will move to Chicago. If she moves to Chicago, she will sell her car. Ana will not sell her car unless she buys a bicycle.
questions.stem: If Ana gets the internship, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Ana will buy a new car in Chicago.
choices.B: Ana will stay in her current city.
choices.C: Ana will sell her car before getting the internship.
choices.D: Ana will not buy a bicycle.
choices.E: Ana will buy a bicycle.

questions.explanation:
Internship → Chicago → sell car → (sell car only if bicycle) buys bicycle.
A — Not stated.
B — She'll move to Chicago.
C — Timing isn't established.
D — The opposite.

questions.stimulus: Each ingredient in this recipe is inexpensive. So the dish this recipe produces must be inexpensive to make.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that what is true of each part must be true of the whole
choices.B: relies on an unrepresentative sample
choices.C: assumes the recipe is easy to follow
choices.D: fails to consider the cost of cooking equipment
choices.E: confuses cost with value

questions.explanation:
Many inexpensive ingredients can add up to an expensive dish, especially in large quantities.
B — No sample.
C — Difficulty isn't mentioned.
D — Equipment might matter, but the core flaw is part-to-whole.
E — Value isn't discussed.

questions.stimulus: Coach: Last season, our team's worst-performing players were assigned to an intensive training program. This season, nearly all of them performed better. The training program clearly worked.
questions.stem: The coach's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it fails to consider that

choices.A: the training program may have been expensive
choices.B: some players outside the program also improved
choices.C: players may have disliked the training program
choices.D: players who perform unusually poorly in one season tend to perform closer to their average the next season, even without intervention
choices.E: the team's overall record may not have improved

questions.explanation:
Players picked for an unusually bad season would likely improve anyway. That's regression toward the mean.
A — Cost doesn't bear on effectiveness.
B — Could matter, but the main flaw is ignoring natural rebound.
C — Enjoyment is irrelevant.
E — Team record isn't the claim.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: In every one of the 40 clinical trials of the drug Neurafen conducted so far, no participant has developed liver damage. Thus Neurafen does not cause liver damage.
questions.stem: The researcher's reasoning is flawed in that it

choices.A: presumes that a drug that causes no harm in trials must also be effective
choices.B: overlooks the possibility that a harmful effect may be too rare or slow to appear in the trials conducted
choices.C: generalizes from a sample of patients that is too large
choices.D: confuses correlation with causation
choices.E: relies on trials that may have been funded by the drug's manufacturer

questions.explanation:
Trials have limited size and duration. A rare or long-delayed effect might not show up even across 40 trials.
A — Effectiveness isn't part of the argument.
C — A large sample isn't a flaw.
D — No correlation is offered.
E — Funding bias is a real-world concern, not the logical flaw.

questions.stimulus: A school district plans to improve students' reading scores by extending the school day by thirty minutes and devoting the extra time to reading instruction.
questions.stem: The plan's success depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Other districts have extended their school days.
choices.B: Reading is more important than mathematics.
choices.C: Students will be able to learn effectively during the additional thirty minutes rather than being too tired to benefit.
choices.D: Teachers support extending the school day.
choices.E: Every student's reading score will improve.

questions.explanation:
Extra time helps only if students can actually learn during it.
A — Not required.
B — No comparison is needed.
D — Support helps but isn't strictly required.
E — Not every student needs to improve.

questions.stimulus: Pet-food company: Our new grain-free dog food is healthier than our regular food. Dogs fed the grain-free food for six months had shinier coats and more energy than dogs fed our regular food.
questions.stem: The company's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: The dogs in the study were all the same breed.
choices.B: Shinier coats and greater energy are indicators that a dog is healthier.
choices.C: All dogs prefer grain-free food.
choices.D: Dogs fed regular food never have shiny coats.
choices.E: Grain-free food is more expensive than regular food.

questions.explanation:
The evidence is about coats and energy, and the conclusion is about health. The argument needs those signs to indicate health.
A — Not required.
C — Preference isn't required.
D — Not required.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Every person who signed the petition supports the new library. Therefore, Elena supports the new library.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Every supporter of the new library signed the petition.
choices.B: Most residents signed the petition.
choices.C: Elena often visits the current library.
choices.D: Elena signed the petition.
choices.E: The petition was circulated in Elena's neighborhood.

questions.explanation:
Signed → supports. If Elena signed, she supports.
A — Reverses the premise.
B — Doesn't establish that Elena signed.
C — Irrelevant.
E — Doesn't establish she signed.

questions.stimulus: A bill cannot become law unless it passes both houses of the legislature. The transportation bill will not pass the senate unless the governor endorses it. Therefore, the transportation bill will not become law.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Most bills endorsed by the governor pass the senate.
choices.B: The transportation bill will pass the house of representatives.
choices.C: If the governor endorses the transportation bill, it will become law.
choices.D: The transportation bill is opposed by a majority of senators.
choices.E: The governor will not endorse the transportation bill.

questions.explanation:
Law → passes both houses → passes the senate → governor endorses. If the governor won't endorse, it can't pass the senate, so it can't become law.
A — Doesn't show the bill fails.
B — Passing one house doesn't block law.
C — A sufficient condition for law, the wrong direction.
D — Opposition makes failure likely but not certain.

questions.stimulus: Medical researcher: Patients who received music therapy after surgery reported less pain than patients who did not. Music therapy therefore reduces post-surgical pain.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?

choices.A: Patients were randomly assigned to receive music therapy or not, and the two groups had similar surgeries.
choices.B: Many patients enjoy music.
choices.C: Patients who received music therapy also received more visits from family.
choices.D: Patients who received music therapy had less serious surgeries.
choices.E: Music therapy is inexpensive.

questions.explanation:
Random assignment and similar surgeries make the groups comparable, so the therapy is the likely cause.
B — Irrelevant.
C — An alternative cause.
D — An alternative cause.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: The settlement at Tarn Ridge was likely abandoned because of a series of floods. Layers of river sediment cover the settlement's final occupation level.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the archaeologist's argument?

choices.A: Other settlements in the region were abandoned for economic reasons.
choices.B: Tarn Ridge was a major trading center.
choices.C: River sediment can accumulate slowly over centuries after a site is abandoned.
choices.D: Below the sediment, household goods were found in place, as though residents had left suddenly.
choices.E: The settlement's residents farmed the river valley.

questions.explanation:
A sudden departure fits a flood-driven abandonment better than a gradual one.
A — Suggests non-flood causes.
B — Irrelevant.
C — The sediment could postdate abandonment.
E — Background, not support for floods as the cause.

questions.stimulus: Sales of electric bicycles in Hartfield tripled last year. City officials attribute the increase to the bike lanes the city built.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the officials' explanation?

choices.A: Electric bicycles are popular with commuters.
choices.B: The bike lanes cost more than expected.
choices.C: Many Hartfield residents use the new bike lanes.
choices.D: Some residents oppose the bike lanes.
choices.E: Last year, the state began offering a large rebate to anyone who purchased an electric bicycle.

questions.explanation:
A big rebate could explain the sales jump without any bike lanes.
A — Doesn't explain the increase.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Supports the officials.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Countries with higher minimum wages have lower rates of poverty. So raising the minimum wage would reduce poverty.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the economist's argument?

choices.A: Some workers earn more than the minimum wage.
choices.B: Countries with higher minimum wages tend to be wealthier overall, and their wealth allows them to set higher minimum wages.
choices.C: Minimum wages differ widely between countries.
choices.D: Poverty is measured differently in different countries.
choices.E: Many economists support raising the minimum wage.

questions.explanation:
Wealth may cause both high minimum wages and low poverty. The correlation doesn't show wages reduce poverty.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Background.
D — A measurement concern that doesn't explain the correlation as well as the confound does.
E — Support isn't evidence.

questions.stimulus: Every dancer in the troupe has trained in ballet. Some dancers in the troupe have also trained in jazz. No one who has trained in jazz is allowed to perform in the classical showcase.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Some dancers in the troupe who trained in ballet are not allowed to perform in the classical showcase.
choices.B: Every dancer trained in ballet is in the troupe.
choices.C: Every dancer in the troupe has trained in jazz.
choices.D: No dancer in the troupe may perform in the classical showcase.
choices.E: Some dancers in the troupe have not trained in ballet.

questions.explanation:
Some troupe dancers trained in jazz (and all troupe dancers trained in ballet). Jazz-trained dancers can't perform in the showcase.
B — Reverses the first statement.
C — Only some have.
D — Dancers without jazz training might be allowed.
E — Contradicts the first statement.

questions.stimulus: When a factory along the Pell River closed, the concentration of a certain industrial chemical in the river dropped by 70 percent within a year. However, fish downstream continued to show elevated levels of the chemical in their tissue for several more years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The factory will reopen.
choices.B: The chemical does not harm fish.
choices.C: The chemical can persist in fish tissue for some time after exposure decreases.
choices.D: The fish in the river are unsafe to eat.
choices.E: The factory was the only source of the chemical in the river.

questions.explanation:
River levels fell fast, but fish levels stayed high for years. The chemical lingers in fish.
A — Not supported.
B — Harm isn't addressed.
D — Safety isn't addressed.
E — Only a 70 percent drop; other sources may exist.

questions.stimulus: Some argue that self-checkout machines in grocery stores benefit shoppers by shortening lines. But self-checkout often requires assistance from staff when items don't scan correctly, and many shoppers find the machines confusing. Self-checkout machines do not provide the clear benefit to shoppers that their advocates claim.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: grocery stores should remove self-checkout machines
choices.B: self-checkout machines are not as beneficial to shoppers as their advocates claim
choices.C: many shoppers find self-checkout machines confusing
choices.D: self-checkout machines often require staff assistance
choices.E: self-checkout machines shorten lines

questions.explanation:
The last sentence states the conclusion; the rest supports it.
A — Not claimed.
C — A premise.
D — A premise.
E — The advocates' claim.

questions.stimulus: Some people think tomatoes should be stored in the refrigerator to keep them fresh. However, cold temperatures break down the compounds that give tomatoes their flavor. Tomatoes are therefore best stored at room temperature.
questions.stem: The claim that cold temperatures break down the compounds that give tomatoes their flavor plays which role in the argument?

choices.A: It is the conclusion of the argument.
choices.B: It is an example of a common misconception.
choices.C: It is background information irrelevant to the conclusion.
choices.D: It is a premise that supports the argument's conclusion.
choices.E: It is a view the argument rejects.

questions.explanation:
It's the reason given for storing tomatoes at room temperature.
A — The conclusion is about room temperature.
B — The misconception is refrigerating tomatoes.
C — It directly supports the conclusion.
E — The argument accepts it.

questions.stimulus: Historian: It is widely believed that the Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye. Astronauts, however, have consistently reported that they cannot see it without aid. The wall is long but very narrow, roughly the width of a highway. So the popular belief is false.
questions.stem: The statement that the wall is roughly the width of a highway functions in the historian's argument as

choices.A: a claim the historian argues against
choices.B: a concession to those who hold the popular belief
choices.C: an explanation that supports the astronauts' reports and thus the conclusion
choices.D: the main conclusion
choices.E: evidence that the wall is visible from space

questions.explanation:
It explains why the wall wouldn't be visible, backing up the astronauts and the conclusion.
A — The historian accepts it.
B — It isn't a concession.
D — The conclusion is that the belief is false.
E — It supports the opposite.

questions.stimulus:
Lee: Our town should ban fireworks because they frighten pets.
Maya: Thunderstorms frighten pets too, but we can't ban those. The fact that something frightens pets isn't enough reason to ban it.
questions.stem: Maya responds to Lee by

choices.A: proposing that thunderstorms be regulated
choices.B: questioning Lee's motives
choices.C: offering evidence that fireworks are safe
choices.D: denying that fireworks frighten pets
choices.E: arguing that the reason Lee gives is not sufficient to justify the conclusion

questions.explanation:
Maya says frightening pets isn't enough to warrant a ban.
A — She says they can't be banned.
B — Not done.
C — Not offered.
D — Maya accepts it.

questions.stimulus:
Andre: The company's decision to allow employees to work from home two days a week has improved productivity. Output per employee has risen since the change.
Bianca: Output did rise, but the company also hired a new production manager at the same time who reorganized workflows. The remote-work policy may have had nothing to do with it.
questions.stem: Andre and Bianca disagree over whether

choices.A: the remote-work policy is responsible for the rise in productivity
choices.B: workflows were reorganized
choices.C: the company hired a new production manager
choices.D: output per employee has risen
choices.E: remote work should be expanded

questions.explanation:
Andre credits the policy; Bianca suggests the new manager might be responsible.
B — Andre doesn't address this.
C — Andre doesn't address this.
D — Bianca concedes it did.
E — Neither discusses expansion.

questions.stimulus: If the museum receives the grant, it will build a new wing. The museum will receive the grant only if it submits its application on time. So if the museum does not submit its application on time, it will not build a new wing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above, including any flaw it may contain?

choices.A: Leah will study abroad only if she wins the scholarship. She will win only if she maintains a high GPA. So if she doesn't maintain a high GPA, she won't study abroad.
choices.B: If Leah wins the scholarship, she will study abroad. Leah will win the scholarship only if she maintains a high GPA. So if Leah does not maintain a high GPA, she will not study abroad.
choices.C: If Leah maintains a high GPA, she will win the scholarship. She won it. So she maintained a high GPA.
choices.D: Leah wants to study abroad, so she will maintain a high GPA.
choices.E: If Leah wins the scholarship, she will study abroad. She did not win. So she will not study abroad.

questions.explanation:
Both: A → B; A → C (A only if C); so not C → not B. That ignores other routes to B, such as building with other funds or studying abroad without the scholarship. Same flaw.
A — Valid: study abroad → scholarship → GPA. The original is flawed.
C — Affirms the consequent, a different flaw.
D — A different structure.
E — Denies the antecedent directly, a related but simpler flaw without the second conditional.

questions.stimulus: The best basketball players are all tall. Therefore, if I grow taller, I will become one of the best basketball players.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: Successful novelists earn a lot. So novelists are wealthy.
choices.B: All successful novelists read a great deal. I don't read much. So I am not a successful novelist.
choices.C: All successful novelists read a great deal. So if I read a great deal, I will become a successful novelist.
choices.D: I read a great deal, so I enjoy reading.
choices.E: Some successful novelists write daily. So writing daily guarantees success.

questions.explanation:
Both treat a trait shared by the best (necessary) as enough to make one of the best (sufficient).
A — A generalization, a different form.
B — Valid.
D — Unrelated.
E — Starts from "some," a different structure.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A museum should allow photography in a gallery unless flash photography would damage the artworks or photographs would violate an artist's copyright.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle?

choices.A: The museum should allow photography in its sculpture garden, since flash cannot damage the stone sculptures and none of them is under copyright.
choices.B: The museum should ban photography of watercolors because flash fades them, but allow flash photography of oil paintings that flash also damages.
choices.C: The museum should charge a fee for photography.
choices.D: The museum should allow photography of a copyrighted painting because visitors enjoy it.
choices.E: The museum should ban photography in all galleries to reduce crowding.

questions.explanation:
Neither exception applies, so the principle says allow photography.
B — The second part violates the exception.
C — Fees aren't addressed.
D — Copyright is an exception.
E — Crowding isn't an exception.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The film's director should not have used real footage of the disaster victims without their families' consent. Even though the footage was publicly available and the film was a serious documentary, the victims' families had a right not to have their loved ones' final moments shown to a paying audience without permission.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the critic's position?

choices.A: Publicly available footage may be used in any film.
choices.B: Documentaries should never depict disasters.
choices.C: Filmmakers should seek to educate audiences about disasters.
choices.D: Depicting identifiable victims of a tragedy in a commercial work requires the consent of their families, regardless of whether the material is publicly available.
choices.E: Footage should be used only if it is of high quality.

questions.explanation:
Facts: identifiable victims, a paying audience, public availability, no consent. The principle says consent is required regardless of public availability.
A — Would permit the use.
B — Far broader than the critic's point.
C — Doesn't address consent.
E — Quality is irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A city lowered its speed limits on residential streets from 30 to 20 miles per hour. Afterward, the number of collisions on those streets stayed the same, but the number of serious injuries from collisions fell sharply.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain these results?

choices.A: The city added more traffic signs.
choices.B: Most collisions occur on major roads.
choices.C: The number of cars on residential streets increased.
choices.D: Drivers often exceed the new speed limits.
choices.E: Collisions at lower speeds are much less likely to cause serious injury than collisions at higher speeds.

questions.explanation:
Same number of crashes, but at lower speeds they're less severe. That explains fewer serious injuries.
A — Doesn't explain the pattern.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Doesn't explain fewer injuries.
D — Would suggest speeds didn't fall.

questions.stimulus: This brand of sneakers is the best-selling brand in the country. Therefore, it must be the most comfortable brand.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: relies on a small sample
choices.B: confuses cause and effect
choices.C: assumes that because a product sells well, it has a particular quality
choices.D: fails to define "best-selling"
choices.E: attacks competing brands

questions.explanation:
Sales can reflect price, marketing, or style, not comfort.
A — National sales aren't a small sample.
B — Not a causal reversal.
D — Not the core flaw.
E — No attack.

questions.stimulus: Either we cut the after-school arts program or we raise student fees. Parents strongly oppose higher fees. So we must cut the arts program.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: ignores other possible ways of addressing the problem
choices.B: relies on an appeal to emotion
choices.C: fails to explain why the arts program is valuable
choices.D: assumes parents' opposition is justified
choices.E: treats a sufficient condition as necessary

questions.explanation:
Other options, such as fundraising, grants, or cuts elsewhere, are ignored.
B — No emotional appeal.
C — Not the flaw.
D — The argument doesn't depend on that.
E — No conditional is misused.

questions.stimulus: Several studies have found that people who meditate daily report lower stress. Therefore, anyone who begins meditating daily will experience lower stress.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

choices.A: assumes stress is harmful
choices.B: draws a conclusion about every individual from evidence about a group tendency
choices.C: attacks critics of meditation
choices.D: fails to define meditation
choices.E: relies on self-reports, which may be unreliable

questions.explanation:
The studies show a tendency, perhaps even causal, but not that every individual will benefit.
A — Not assumed.
C — No critics are mentioned.
D — Not the core flaw.
E — A possible weakness, but the overgeneralization to "anyone" is the main flaw.

questions.stimulus: The park district wants to reduce the number of geese in the park by installing decoy coyotes, which geese tend to avoid.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Coyotes are native to the area.
choices.B: Every goose in the park will leave.
choices.C: Decoys are inexpensive.
choices.D: Geese damage the park's grass.
choices.E: The geese will not quickly realize the decoys pose no real threat.

questions.explanation:
If the geese get used to the decoys, they'll stop avoiding them.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
C — Not required.
D — A motive, not something the plan depends on.

questions.stimulus: Since the Delmar bookstore moved its bestsellers to a display table at the entrance, sales of bestsellers have increased by 25 percent. The manager concludes that the new display caused the increase.
questions.stem: The manager's conclusion depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Sales of other books decreased.
choices.B: Every customer noticed the display.
choices.C: Most customers enter through the front entrance.
choices.D: The increase in bestseller sales was not mainly caused by a particularly popular new book released during the same period.
choices.E: Bestsellers are the store's most profitable books.

questions.explanation:
If one blockbuster explains the jump, the display didn't cause it.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
C — Helpful, but not strictly required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Anyone who reads the entire assigned novel will be able to write the essay. Hector was able to write the essay. So Hector must have read a summary of the novel.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Anyone who reads a summary of the novel can write the essay.
choices.B: Hector usually reads summaries instead of novels.
choices.C: Anyone who was able to write the essay but did not read the entire novel read a summary of it, and Hector did not read the entire novel.
choices.D: Hector did not read the entire assigned novel.
choices.E: Most students who wrote the essay read a summary.

questions.explanation:
Only this combination guarantees the conclusion: Hector didn't read it all, and anyone who wrote the essay without reading it all read a summary.
A — Gives summary → essay, not essay → summary.
B — "Usually" doesn't guarantee he did this time.
D — Doesn't establish he read a summary.
E — "Most" doesn't guarantee Hector did.

questions.stimulus: Gardener: My tomato plants produced more fruit this year than last year. I started using a new fertilizer this year, so the fertilizer must have increased the yield.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the gardener's argument?

choices.A: The gardener planted more tomato plants this year.
choices.B: The weather this year was very similar to last year's.
choices.C: Some neighbors also had large tomato harvests.
choices.D: The fertilizer is organic.
choices.E: This year was unusually sunny.

questions.explanation:
Ruling out weather differences makes the fertilizer a more likely cause.
A — An alternative cause.
C — Suggests a common factor such as weather.
D — Irrelevant.
E — An alternative cause.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: People who spend more time in nature report higher well-being. This suggests that exposure to natural environments improves psychological well-being.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the psychologist's argument?
