choices.A: Natural environments often have cleaner air than cities.
choices.B: People who live near parks tend to have higher incomes.
choices.C: Many people enjoy hiking.
choices.D: People with higher well-being are more likely to seek out natural environments.
choices.E: People randomly assigned to walk in a park reported greater well-being afterward than people randomly assigned to walk on a busy city street for the same length of time.

questions.explanation:
Random assignment with the same activity (walking) isolates the natural setting as the cause.
A — Suggests a possible mechanism but also an alternative (air, not nature per se). Weaker.
B — Income is a confound.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Reverse causation weakens.

questions.stimulus: A fitness app company claims that its users lose more weight than people who don't use the app. Therefore, the app helps people lose weight.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the company's argument?

choices.A: Some users stop using the app after a month.
choices.B: The app tracks calories and exercise.
choices.C: The app is free to download.
choices.D: People who download fitness apps are typically already more committed to losing weight than people who don't.
choices.E: The app has positive reviews.

questions.explanation:
Self-selection: committed people both use the app and lose weight.
A — Doesn't explain the difference.
B — A plausible mechanism, which supports the claim.
C — Irrelevant.
E — Not evidence of effect.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The decline of the ancient city of Varo coincided with a sharp drop in the number of trade goods from Varo found at distant sites. Thus the city's decline was caused by the collapse of its trade networks.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the historian's argument?

choices.A: Excavations show that Varo's population had already fallen sharply because of a plague several decades before its trade goods disappeared from distant sites.
choices.B: Trade goods are often found far from where they were made.
choices.C: Some of Varo's trade goods have been found at sites dated after the city's decline.
choices.D: Other cities in the region also traded with distant sites.
choices.E: Varo traded primarily in pottery.

questions.explanation:
If population collapse came first, the trade decline is likely a result of the city's decline, not its cause.
B — Background.
C — A few late finds don't explain the causal ordering.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: All the cookies in the jar are chocolate chip. Liam took a cookie from the jar.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Liam took a chocolate chip cookie.
choices.B: All chocolate chip cookies are in the jar.
choices.C: The jar is now empty.
choices.D: Liam likes chocolate chip cookies.
choices.E: Liam took more than one cookie.

questions.explanation:
Every cookie in the jar is chocolate chip.
B — Reverses the statement.
C — Not stated.
D — Not stated.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: Every applicant who was offered a job at Halcyon Labs has a doctorate. Some applicants with doctorates were not offered interviews. No applicant was offered a job without first being offered an interview.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Most applicants with doctorates were offered jobs.
choices.B: Every applicant with a doctorate was offered an interview.
choices.C: Some applicants with doctorates were not offered jobs.
choices.D: Every applicant who was offered an interview has a doctorate.
choices.E: Some applicants who were offered jobs do not have doctorates.

questions.explanation:
Some doctorate holders got no interview, and a job requires an interview. So those applicants got no job offer.
A — Not established.
B — Contradicts the second statement.
D — Not established.
E — Contradicts the first statement.

questions.stimulus: When a coastal town banned plastic bags, the volume of plastic litter found on its beaches fell by 30 percent over the following year. Plastic litter on beaches in nearby towns without bans stayed about the same.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The nearby towns will soon ban plastic bags.
choices.B: Plastic bags are the main source of beach litter everywhere.
choices.C: Plastic litter on the town's beaches will continue to fall.
choices.D: Residents of the town support the ban.
choices.E: The plastic bag ban likely contributed to the reduction in beach litter in the town.

questions.explanation:
Litter fell only where the ban took effect, which points to the ban as a likely contributor.
A — Not supported.
B — Overgeneralizes.
C — A prediction beyond the data.
D — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: Although many people throw away bread once it becomes stale, stale bread has many uses. It can be made into breadcrumbs, croutons, or bread pudding. Stale bread should therefore not be thrown away.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: many people throw away stale bread
choices.B: stale bread should not be thrown away
choices.C: stale bread can be made into breadcrumbs
choices.D: stale bread has many uses
choices.E: fresh bread is healthier than stale bread

questions.explanation:
"Therefore" marks the conclusion.
A — Background.
C — Support.
D — An intermediate premise.
E — Not discussed.

questions.stimulus: Some people claim that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis. But a study of thousands of people found no difference in arthritis rates between knuckle-crackers and non-crackers. The claim, therefore, appears to be false.
questions.stem: The study described plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is a claim the argument rejects.
choices.B: It is a concession to the opposing view.
choices.C: It is the main conclusion.
choices.D: It is evidence offered against a claim.
choices.E: It is an example of a popular belief.

questions.explanation:
The study is the support for rejecting the knuckle-cracking claim.
A — The argument relies on the study.
B — It opposes that view.
C — The conclusion is that the claim appears false.
E — The belief is the claim, not the study.

questions.stimulus: Commentator: Proponents of the new curriculum point out that test scores rose in the schools that adopted it. But they neglect to mention that these schools were selected for the pilot program precisely because they already had strong administrative leadership and rising scores. The rise in scores, therefore, cannot be credited to the curriculum.
questions.stem: The commentator's argument proceeds by

choices.A: arguing that the new curriculum is harmful
choices.B: attacking the proponents' motives
choices.C: showing that the proponents' conclusion contradicts their premises
choices.D: identifying a feature of the selection of cases that offers an alternative explanation for the evidence cited
choices.E: disputing the accuracy of the test score data

questions.explanation:
The commentator shows the pilot schools were chosen for traits (strong leadership, rising scores) that could explain the gains.
A — The commentator only denies credit for the gains.
B — The proponents' omission is noted, but motives aren't attacked.
C — No contradiction.
E — The data is accepted.

questions.stimulus:
Nora: Students should be allowed to use calculators on math tests. In the real world, people use calculators all the time.
Owen: Calculators are useful, but math tests should measure whether students understand the underlying concepts, which calculators can hide.
questions.stem: Nora and Owen disagree over whether

choices.A: people use calculators in the real world
choices.B: calculators are useful
choices.C: students should be allowed to use calculators on math tests
choices.D: math tests should measure conceptual understanding
choices.E: calculators should be banned from classrooms

questions.explanation:
Nora says yes. Owen's reasoning implies no.
A — Owen doesn't dispute this.
B — Both agree.
D — Nora doesn't address this.
E — Neither says so.

questions.stimulus:
Teodor: The new bridge design is beautiful, but it is far over budget. The city should choose a simpler design.
Uma: It is over budget, and that's a concern. But a landmark bridge will attract tourists whose spending will repay the extra cost within a decade.
questions.stem: Teodor and Uma are committed to agreeing that

choices.A: the new bridge design exceeds the budget
choices.B: the city should choose a simpler design
choices.C: tourists will repay the extra cost
choices.D: the new design is beautiful
choices.E: the budget should be increased

questions.explanation:
Teodor: "far over budget." Uma: "It is over budget."
B — Uma disagrees.
C — Only Uma says so.
D — Only Teodor says so.
E — Neither says so.

questions.stimulus: No reptiles are warm-blooded. Snakes are reptiles. So snakes are not warm-blooded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: All metals conduct electricity. Copper conducts electricity. So copper is a metal.
choices.B: No metals are transparent. Copper is not transparent. So copper is a metal.
choices.C: No metals are transparent. Glass is transparent. So glass is a metal.
choices.D: Some metals are magnetic. Iron is a metal. So iron is magnetic.
choices.E: No metals are transparent. Copper is a metal. So copper is not transparent.

questions.explanation:
No A are B; C is A; so C is not B.
A — Affirms the consequent.
B — Invalid.
C — A different, invalid conclusion.
D — "Some" breaks the form.

questions.stimulus: Dr. Patel argues that the new drug is unsafe. But Dr. Patel works for a company that makes a competing drug. So we can dismiss her argument.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: Many shop owners oppose the mall, so it must be harmful.
choices.B: Councilor Reyes argues that the new mall will hurt local shops. But Reyes owns a shop downtown. So we can ignore her argument.
choices.C: Councilor Reyes argues that the mall will hurt shops, and her evidence is weak. So we should doubt her conclusion.
choices.D: Councilor Reyes owns a shop downtown, so she should vote on the mall proposal.
choices.E: Reyes has been wrong before, so she is wrong now.

questions.explanation:
Both dismiss an argument because of the arguer's interests rather than its merits.
A — An appeal to popularity.
C — Evaluating evidence is reasonable.
D — A different structure.
E — A related but different flaw (past record).

questions.stimulus: Principle: Library books may be renewed online unless another patron has placed a hold on them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following conforms to the principle?

choices.A: Mia could not renew her book online because she had renewed it before.
choices.B: Jae renewed his book online, since no one had placed a hold on it.
choices.C: Kim renewed her book online even though another patron had placed a hold on it.
choices.D: Lou renewed his book online because it was overdue.
choices.E: Ola renewed her book online after being told another patron had placed a hold on it.

questions.explanation:
No hold, so online renewal is allowed.
A — Prior renewals aren't the criterion.
C — A hold blocks online renewal.
D — Overdue status isn't the criterion.
E — A hold blocks online renewal.

questions.stimulus: Parent: My son should not be required to take the advanced swimming class. He already passed the swimming test that the class prepares students for.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the parent's position?

choices.A: Classes should be taught by certified instructors.
choices.B: Students should choose their own classes.
choices.C: A student who has already met the goal of a required class should not have to take that class.
choices.D: Swimming is an important life skill.
choices.E: All swimming classes should be optional.

questions.explanation:
Facts: he met the class's goal. The principle says no requirement.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Too broad.
D — Might favor taking the class.
E — Too broad.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: When the hospital mistakenly overbilled Mr. Grant, it was obligated to refund the overpayment. But when the hospital mistakenly underbilled Ms. Lee, it was not entitled to demand the difference, because Ms. Lee had already arranged her finances on the basis of the bill she received and would suffer significant hardship if forced to pay more.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.A: Patients should always pay exactly what they owe.
choices.B: A billing error should be corrected only if the party that made the error asks for the correction.
choices.C: Hospitals should never make billing errors.
choices.D: A party that makes a billing error must correct it when the error harms the other party, but need not be compensated for it when collecting would cause significant hardship to someone who reasonably relied on the bill.
choices.E: A party that makes a billing error should always bear the full cost of correcting it.

questions.explanation:
This principle covers both cases: refund the overcharge (it harmed Grant), and don't collect the undercharge (reasonable reliance plus hardship for Lee).
A — Would require Lee to pay.
B — Would let the hospital skip refunding Grant, and it ignores reliance and hardship.
C — Doesn't justify either judgment.
E — Covers the refund but doesn't mention reliance or hardship.

questions.stimulus: A movie theater lowered its ticket prices, but its total revenue from ticket sales decreased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: The lower prices attracted only a few additional customers, not enough to make up for the lower price per ticket.
choices.B: Many customers buy snacks at the theater.
choices.C: The theater began showing more films.
choices.D: The theater renovated its seating.
choices.E: A nearby theater raised its prices.

questions.explanation:
Revenue fell because the drop in price per ticket outweighed the small rise in attendance.
B — Irrelevant to ticket revenue.
C — Doesn't explain the revenue decrease.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Would tend to send customers here.

questions.stimulus: A school district found that students who took a new online math course scored higher on the state math exam than students who took the traditional course. The district concludes that the online course is more effective.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the district's conclusion?

choices.A: whether the online course includes videos
choices.B: whether teachers prefer the online course
choices.C: how much the online course costs
choices.D: whether the state exam is difficult
choices.E: whether students chose which course to take or were assigned to one

questions.explanation:
If students chose, stronger or more motivated students may have picked the online course. Either answer bears on whether the course caused the higher scores.
A — Course features don't test the causal claim.
B — Preference isn't effectiveness.
C — Cost is irrelevant.
D — Applies to both groups.

questions.stimulus: The first two episodes of the new television series were boring. So the entire series will be boring.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: generalizes about a whole from too small a portion of it
choices.B: confuses popularity with quality
choices.C: reverses cause and effect
choices.D: assumes the series is long
choices.E: relies on the opinion of critics

questions.explanation:
Two episodes may not represent a whole series.
B — Popularity isn't mentioned.
C — No causal reversal.
D — Not assumed.
E — No critics.

questions.stimulus: Security consultant: Our tests showed that a skilled hacker could break into the company's database within an hour. Since the database contains valuable customer data, it is virtually certain that it will be breached within the year.
questions.stem: The consultant's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that customer data is valuable to hackers
choices.B: relies on tests that may have been poorly designed
choices.C: confuses a necessary condition for a breach with a sufficient condition
choices.D: moves from the claim that something could happen to the claim that it is almost certain to happen
choices.E: fails to consider that the company could improve its security

questions.explanation:
The tests show a breach is possible for a skilled hacker. That doesn't establish one is virtually certain, since that depends on attackers actually targeting the company.
A — The premise states the data is valuable.
B — A generic worry, not the logical flaw.
C — Close, but the core problem is the leap from "could" to "virtually certain."
E — A possible gap, but even unchanged, possibility isn't near-certainty.

questions.stimulus: The coffee shop plans to attract more customers in the afternoon by offering half-price pastries between 2 and 4 p.m.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Every afternoon customer will buy a pastry.
choices.B: Some people who don't currently visit in the afternoon would be drawn by discounted pastries.
choices.C: Most customers visit in the morning.
choices.D: The discount will not reduce profits.
choices.E: Pastries are the shop's most popular item.

questions.explanation:
The discount helps only if it draws new afternoon visitors.
A — Not required.
C — Not required.
D — The goal is more customers.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: The city's decision to replace grass in public parks with drought-resistant native plants will save water. Native plants require far less irrigation than grass once they are established.
questions.stem: The columnist's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Residents support the change.
choices.B: Grass in the parks is currently watered every day.
choices.C: The water needed to establish the native plants will not exceed the water saved once they are established.
choices.D: All parks in the city will be converted.
choices.E: Native plants are more attractive than grass.

questions.explanation:
If getting the plants established takes enormous amounts of water, the savings might never materialize.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
D — Not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Only certified electricians may install the new wiring. So Tomas will not install the new wiring.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Tomas is a plumber.
choices.B: Some certified electricians do not install wiring.
choices.C: Tomas has never installed wiring before.
choices.D: All certified electricians will install the wiring.
choices.E: Tomas is not a certified electrician.

questions.explanation:
Install → certified. If Tomas isn't certified, he won't install.
A — He might also be a certified electrician.
B — Irrelevant to Tomas.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Doesn't address Tomas.

questions.stimulus: Anyone who can speak Mandarin fluently can apply for the Shanghai position. Anyone who can apply for the Shanghai position and has at least five years of experience will be interviewed. Wen has at least five years of experience. So Wen will be interviewed.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Wen would like to work in Shanghai.
choices.B: Everyone who will be interviewed can speak Mandarin fluently.
choices.C: Wen has more experience than any other applicant.
choices.D: Most applicants for the Shanghai position speak Mandarin.
choices.E: Wen can speak Mandarin fluently.

questions.explanation:
Fluent → can apply. Can apply and five-plus years → interviewed. If Wen is fluent, she can apply, and with her experience she'll be interviewed.
A — Wanting the job doesn't establish that she can apply.
B — Reverses direction.
C — Not needed.
D — Doesn't establish that Wen does.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: In a study, people who slept at least eight hours a night caught fewer colds than people who slept less. So getting more sleep helps prevent colds.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?

choices.A: When participants were exposed to the same cold virus, those who had slept longer were less likely to become infected.
choices.B: Many people sleep less than eight hours a night.
choices.C: People who sleep less tend to work in crowded offices.
choices.D: Colds are caused by viruses.
choices.E: Some people who sleep a lot still catch colds.

questions.explanation:
Equal exposure rules out the possibility that short sleepers simply encountered more germs.
B — Irrelevant.
C — An alternative explanation.
D — Background.
E — Exceptions don't undercut the trend.

questions.stimulus: Store owner: Since I moved the candy display away from the checkout counter, sales of fresh fruit, which is now displayed there, have doubled. Clearly, placing products near the checkout increases their sales.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the store owner's conclusion?

choices.A: Fresh fruit is healthier than candy.
choices.B: Sales of candy dropped after it was moved away from the checkout counter.
choices.C: Many customers buy fruit on impulse.
choices.D: The store also lowered fruit prices at the same time.
choices.E: The store sells more candy than fruit overall.

questions.explanation:
Candy sales falling when moved away mirrors fruit sales rising when moved there, which supports the effect of placement.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Plausible mechanism, but less direct than the mirror evidence.
D — An alternative cause.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Since the town opened a new library branch, the number of library cards issued has increased. Officials say the new branch has made reading more popular.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the officials' conclusion?

choices.A: The new branch is in a busy neighborhood.
choices.B: Library cards are free.
choices.C: The town also began requiring a library card to use its public computers, which many residents need for job applications.
choices.D: The new branch is open on weekends.
choices.E: The new branch has many new books.

questions.explanation:
People may be getting cards for computer access, not reading.
A — Doesn't separate reading from other uses.
B — Irrelevant.
D — Supports greater use.
E — Supports the officials.

questions.stimulus: Sociologist: Cities that have more public parks per resident have lower crime rates. So building more parks would reduce crime.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the sociologist's argument?

choices.A: Some parks have high crime rates.
choices.B: Many cities plan to build more parks.
choices.C: Parks are popular with families.
choices.D: Cities with more parks per resident tend to have higher median incomes, and higher incomes are strongly associated with lower crime.
choices.E: Building parks is expensive.

questions.explanation:
Income could explain both more parks and less crime.
A — A few exceptions don't undercut the overall correlation.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Every student in Ms. Rivera's class passed the quiz. Jordan is a student in Ms. Rivera's class.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Jordan studied for the quiz.
choices.B: Jordan passed the quiz.
choices.C: Everyone who passed is in Ms. Rivera's class.
choices.D: Jordan got the highest score.
choices.E: The quiz was easy.

questions.explanation:
Every student in the class passed.
A — Not stated.
C — Reverses the statement.
D — Not stated.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: Each employee at Brennan Co. who works in the marketing department attended the training session. Some employees who attended the training session work in the finance department. No employee works in more than one department.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Some marketing employees did not attend the training.
choices.B: Some employees in the finance department did not attend the training session.
choices.C: Every employee who attended the training works in marketing.
choices.D: Every finance employee attended the training.
choices.E: Some employees who attended the training session do not work in the marketing department.

questions.explanation:
Some attendees work in finance, and since no one works in two departments, those attendees aren't in marketing.
A — All marketing employees attended.
B — Possible, but nothing requires it.
C — Some attendees work in finance.
D — Only some did.

questions.stimulus: A study found that regions where people drink more green tea have lower rates of a certain cancer. However, within those regions, individuals who drink the most green tea have the same cancer rates as those who drink the least.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: People in those regions drink green tea every day.
choices.B: The study was poorly designed.
choices.C: Something other than individual green tea consumption may account for the regional differences in cancer rates.
choices.D: Green tea causes cancer.
choices.E: Green tea prevents cancer.

questions.explanation:
If heavy and light drinkers within a region have the same rates, individual tea drinking doesn't explain the regional pattern. Some other regional factor may.
A — Not stated.
B — Not supported.
D — Not supported.
E — The within-region data cuts against this.

questions.stimulus: Many people avoid eggs because they worry about cholesterol. But for most people, eating eggs has little effect on blood cholesterol levels. Eggs are also an inexpensive source of protein. Most people need not avoid eggs.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: everyone should eat eggs daily
choices.B: eggs are an inexpensive source of protein
choices.C: eating eggs has little effect on cholesterol for most people
choices.D: most people need not avoid eggs
choices.E: many people worry about cholesterol

questions.explanation:
The final sentence is the conclusion.
A — Not claimed.
B — A premise.
C — A premise.
E — Background.

questions.stimulus: Literary critic: Some readers dismiss the novel because its narrator is unlikable. But an unlikable narrator is not a flaw if the author intends readers to see the narrator's faults, and this novel's structure makes clear that the author does. Readers who dismiss the novel for this reason have therefore misjudged it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the critic's argument?

choices.A: Readers who dismiss the novel because of its unlikable narrator have misjudged it.
choices.B: The novel's narrator is unlikable.
choices.C: The novel's structure makes clear the author's intentions.
choices.D: An unlikable narrator is not a flaw if the author intends readers to see the narrator's faults.
choices.E: The novel is the author's best work.

questions.explanation:
"Therefore" leads to the conclusion; the principle and the evidence about the author's intent support it.
B — Accepted background.
C — A premise.
D — A principle used as a premise.
E — Not claimed.

questions.stimulus: Some people believe that goldfish have a memory span of only three seconds. However, experiments have shown that goldfish can be trained to respond to sounds and remember them for months. So the belief is mistaken.
questions.stem: The statement that goldfish can be trained to remember sounds for months plays which role?

choices.A: It is irrelevant background.
choices.B: It is the popular belief.
choices.C: It is evidence offered against a popular belief.
choices.D: It is a concession.
choices.E: It is the conclusion.

questions.explanation:
It's the support for rejecting the three-second-memory belief.
A — It's central.
B — The popular belief is the three-second memory.
D — It isn't conceded; it's offered as support.
E — The conclusion is that the belief is mistaken.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Some argue that automation will cause permanent mass unemployment. Yet historically, technological advances have eliminated specific jobs while creating new kinds of work. Admittedly, the transition can be painful for displaced workers, and this time the pace of change may be faster. But nothing in the current wave of automation suggests it will break the historical pattern entirely. Hence, fears of permanent mass unemployment are probably overstated.
questions.stem: The claim that the pace of change may be faster this time plays which one of the following roles in the economist's argument?

choices.A: It is evidence that automation creates new kinds of work.
choices.B: It is a premise directly supporting the conclusion.
choices.C: It is the main conclusion.
choices.D: It acknowledges a consideration that could seem to support the view the economist argues against.
choices.E: It is a claim the economist argues is false.

questions.explanation:
It's part of the "Admittedly" concession: a point opponents could use. The economist grants it without accepting their conclusion.
A — Unrelated.
B — It cuts the other way.
C — The conclusion is that fears are overstated.
E — The economist concedes it might be true and argues it isn't decisive.

questions.stimulus:
Ivy: Sharks are dangerous to swimmers because they have sharp teeth.
Jon: Many animals with sharp teeth, like house cats, pose little danger to swimmers. Having sharp teeth doesn't by itself make an animal dangerous to swimmers.
questions.stem: Jon responds to Ivy by

choices.A: arguing that the feature Ivy cites is not sufficient for her conclusion
choices.B: attacking Ivy's credibility
choices.C: denying that sharks have sharp teeth
choices.D: agreeing with Ivy's conclusion
choices.E: offering evidence that sharks are safe

questions.explanation:
Jon notes that sharp teeth alone don't make an animal dangerous.
B — Not done.
C — Jon doesn't deny it.
D — He challenges her reasoning.
E — Not offered.

questions.stimulus:
Paula: Our town should build a skate park. Young people need a safe place to skateboard.
Quinn: A skate park would be too expensive for our small town's budget.
questions.stem: Paula and Quinn disagree over whether

choices.A: skateboarding is dangerous
choices.B: the town should build a skate park
choices.C: the town's budget is small
choices.D: young people enjoy skateboarding
choices.E: young people need a place to skateboard

questions.explanation:
Paula says build it; Quinn says it's too expensive.
A — Not discussed.
C — Paula doesn't address it.
D — Not discussed.
E — Quinn doesn't dispute it.

questions.stimulus: Not every member of the committee voted for the proposal. Everyone who voted for the proposal attended the meeting. Therefore, if everyone who attended the meeting voted for the proposal, then not every member of the committee attended the meeting.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?

choices.A: Not every guest brought a gift. Everyone who signed the card brought a gift. Therefore, not every guest signed the card.
choices.B: Everyone who signed the card brought a gift. Some guests signed the card. Therefore, some guests brought a gift.
choices.C: Not every guest brought a gift. Therefore, some guests did not sign the card.
choices.D: Every guest brought a gift. Everyone who brought a gift signed the card. Therefore, every guest signed the card.
choices.E: Not every guest at the party brought a gift. Everyone who brought a gift signed the card. Therefore, if everyone who signed the card brought a gift, then not every guest signed the card.

questions.explanation:
Same structure: not all M are V; all V are A; so if all A are V, then not all M are A. Each term maps directly.
A — Valid, but a different structure (no conditional conclusion).
B — Valid, but a different form.
C — Missing the conditional structure.
D — A simple valid chain, different form.

questions.stimulus: If it is raining, the streets are wet. The streets are wet. So it must be raining.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: If the oven is on, the kitchen is warm. The kitchen is warm. So the oven must be on.
choices.B: If the oven is on, the kitchen is warm. The oven is on. So the kitchen is warm.
choices.C: The oven is usually on in the evening. So it is evening.
choices.D: The kitchen is warm because the oven is on.
choices.E: If the oven is on, the kitchen is warm. The kitchen is not warm. So the oven is off.

questions.explanation:
Both affirm the consequent.
B — Valid.
C — A different, probabilistic flaw.
D — Not an argument of the same form.
E — Valid.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A journalist may withhold the identity of a source only if revealing it would put the source at risk of serious harm and the information the source provided is of significant public importance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: Reporter Jensen may withhold her source's identity because the information concerns government corruption.
choices.B: Reporter Haines should not withhold her source's identity, since although revealing it would endanger the source, the information concerned only a minor celebrity rumor.
choices.C: Reporter Ito may withhold his source's identity because the source asked him to.
choices.D: Reporter Lee may withhold his source's identity if his editor approves.
choices.E: Reporter Kaur must withhold her source's identity whenever the source is at risk.

questions.explanation:
The information isn't of significant public importance, so withholding isn't allowed.
A — Importance alone isn't enough; risk of harm is also required.
C — A request isn't a condition.
D — Approval isn't a condition.
E — The principle permits withholding under conditions; it doesn't require it.

questions.stimulus: Manager: We should not fire Darnell for being late to work last week. He was late because he stopped to help an injured person at the scene of a car accident, and he called to let us know.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the manager's position?

choices.A: Managers should fire employees who are late more than once.
choices.B: Lateness should always be excused.
choices.C: Employees should never be fired.
choices.D: Employees who help others should be rewarded.
choices.E: Employees should not be punished for lateness caused by responding to an emergency, provided they notify their employer.

questions.explanation:
Both conditions hold: an emergency and notification. So no punishment.
A — Doesn't apply.
B — Too broad.
C — Too broad.
D — Doesn't address punishment for lateness.

questions.stimulus: A city's library extended its hours on weekday evenings. Over the next year, the total number of library visits increased, but the number of books checked out declined.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: The library charged late fees.
choices.B: The library added many new books.
choices.C: The library's staff increased.
choices.D: Many of the new evening visitors came to use the library's computers and study rooms rather than to borrow books.
choices.E: Evening hours are popular with students.

questions.explanation:
More visits but fewer checkouts makes sense if the new visitors came for other services.
A — Doesn't explain the change.
B — Would predict more checkouts.
C — Irrelevant.
E — Doesn't explain fewer checkouts.

questions.stimulus: In the country of Ostrava, the proportion of adults with college degrees has risen steadily for thirty years. Yet the proportion of jobs that require a college degree has stayed nearly constant over the same period, and unemployment among college graduates has not increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how all of these facts can be true?

choices.A: Many college graduates in Ostrava move abroad.
choices.B: College tuition in Ostrava has risen.
choices.C: A growing share of college graduates in Ostrava now hold jobs that do not require a college degree.
choices.D: Jobs requiring degrees pay more than other jobs.
choices.E: The total number of jobs in Ostrava has decreased.

questions.explanation:
More graduates, a constant share of degree-requiring jobs, and no rise in graduate unemployment: graduates are filling jobs that don't require degrees.
A — Emigration could help, but the passage concerns adults in Ostrava. A partial explanation at best.
B — Irrelevant.
D — Doesn't explain the pattern.
E — Would tend to increase unemployment.

questions.stimulus: The store will offer free delivery only if the order is over $50. Grace's order qualifies for free delivery.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Grace's order contains more than one item.
choices.B: Grace's order is over $50.
choices.C: Grace's order is exactly $50.
choices.D: Grace pays for delivery.
choices.E: Every order over $50 gets free delivery.

questions.explanation:
Free delivery → over $50. Grace qualifies, so her order is over $50.
A — Not stated.
C — It must be over $50.
D — She qualifies for free delivery.
E — Reverses the condition.

questions.stimulus: A famous chef says that this brand of running shoes is the best for marathon training. So marathon runners should buy these shoes.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: generalizes from a single runner
choices.B: confuses cause and effect
choices.C: relies on someone whose expertise lies in an unrelated field
choices.D: fails to mention the shoes' price
choices.E: assumes all runners train for marathons

questions.explanation:
A chef's expertise is cooking, not running shoes.
A — No runner is cited.
B — No causal claim.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Not assumed.

questions.stimulus: Mayor Grant criticizes the city council for overspending. But Grant herself exceeded her office's budget last year. So the council has not overspent.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: relies on an unrepresentative sample
choices.B: confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one
choices.C: fails to define "overspending"
choices.D: concludes that a criticism is false because the critic has done the same thing
choices.E: assumes the mayor's budget is larger than the council's

questions.explanation:
Grant's own overspending doesn't show the council didn't overspend.
A — No sample.
B — No conditional.
C — Not the core flaw.
E — Not assumed.

questions.stimulus: Health official: The percentage of hospital patients who contract infections during their stay has fallen from 6 percent to 4 percent over the past five years. Therefore, fewer patients contracted hospital infections this year than five years ago.
questions.stem: The official's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: ignores the possibility that the total number of hospital patients has grown substantially
choices.B: relies on data from too few hospitals
choices.C: fails to consider that some patients may be infected before admission
choices.D: assumes that all infections are equally serious
choices.E: confuses cause and effect

questions.explanation:
A lower rate applied to a much larger patient population could mean more infections in absolute terms.
B — No data issue is indicated.
C — A definitional quibble, not the main flaw.
D — Severity is irrelevant.
E — No causal claim.

questions.stimulus: The museum plans to boost attendance by offering free admission on the first Sunday of each month.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Most visitors come on weekends.
choices.B: The museum has recently added new exhibits.
choices.C: The museum is crowded on weekdays.
choices.D: Free admission will not reduce donations.
choices.E: The cost of admission currently keeps some people from visiting the museum.

questions.explanation:
Free admission helps only if cost is a barrier for some people.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
C — Not required.
D — Not part of the attendance goal.

questions.stimulus: Paleontologist: Fossilized dinosaur eggs found at the Hollow Creek site are arranged in tight circular clusters, with the narrow end of each egg pointing toward the center. Modern birds that arrange eggs this way do so to allow a parent to sit on the clutch. Thus the dinosaurs that laid these eggs probably sat on their nests.
questions.stem: The paleontologist's argument requires assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Dinosaurs are the ancestors of modern birds.
choices.B: All dinosaurs sat on their nests.
choices.C: The eggs at Hollow Creek all hatched successfully.
choices.D: The circular arrangement of the eggs did not result primarily from natural processes, such as water flow, that occurred after the eggs were laid.
choices.E: Modern birds that do not sit on their eggs arrange them randomly.

questions.explanation:
The inference treats the arrangement as deliberate nesting behavior. If currents or settling arranged the eggs afterward, the comparison to birds fails.
A — Helpful background for the analogy, but the argument works by analogy of behavior, not necessarily descent.
B — Far too strong.
C — Not required.
E — Strengthens, but isn't required.

questions.stimulus: Any employee who completes the leadership program is eligible for a management position. So Dana is eligible for a management position.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Every manager completed the leadership program.
choices.B: Some employees in the leadership program are eligible.
choices.C: Dana completed the leadership program.
choices.D: Dana has worked at the company for many years.
choices.E: Dana wants a management position.

questions.explanation:
Completed program → eligible.
A — Reverses direction.
B — Doesn't place Dana in the program.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Wanting isn't eligibility.

questions.stimulus: Nutritionist: People who eat breakfast regularly tend to maintain healthier weights. So eating breakfast helps people maintain a healthy weight.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the nutritionist's argument?

choices.A: Many people skip breakfast.
choices.B: In a study where participants were randomly assigned to eat or skip breakfast, those who ate breakfast ate fewer total calories during the day.
choices.C: Breakfast cereals are often high in sugar.
choices.D: People who eat breakfast also exercise more.
choices.E: Some breakfast eaters are overweight.

questions.explanation:
Random assignment plus a mechanism (fewer daily calories) supports causation.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Suggests breakfast could hurt.
D — A confound.
E — Exceptions don't undercut the trend.

questions.stimulus: Transit official: Raising bus fares by 25 cents will increase the transit system's total fare revenue, because most riders depend on the bus and will continue riding despite the increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the official's argument?

choices.A: Many riders have complained about fare increases in the past.
choices.B: Gas prices have recently fallen.
choices.C: Other cities have raised bus fares.
choices.D: The transit system needs more revenue.
choices.E: When fares were raised by a similar amount five years ago, ridership fell by less than 2 percent.

questions.explanation:
Past evidence that riders kept riding after a comparable increase supports the prediction.
A — Complaints don't show behavior.
B — Cheaper driving might pull riders away.
C — Without outcomes, this doesn't help.
D — A motive, not support.

questions.stimulus: A company introduced flexible work hours, and over the next year employee turnover fell by 15 percent. Management concludes that flexible hours improved employee retention.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens management's conclusion?

choices.A: During the same year, the job market tightened sharply, with few openings at other companies.
choices.B: Employees reported liking flexible hours.
choices.C: Flexible hours are common in the industry.
choices.D: Some employees didn't use flexible hours.
choices.E: The company also hired many new employees.

questions.explanation:
With few jobs elsewhere, employees would stay regardless of flexible hours.
B — Supports management.
C — Doesn't explain the drop.
D — Doesn't explain the overall drop.
E — Irrelevant to turnover rate.

questions.stimulus: Political scientist: In countries that adopted mandatory voting, the gap in turnout between wealthy and poor citizens nearly disappeared. Therefore, mandatory voting would make our country's election outcomes better reflect the preferences of all citizens.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the political scientist's argument?

choices.A: Our country already has high turnout among wealthy citizens.
choices.B: In countries with mandatory voting, many citizens who would not otherwise vote cast blank or randomly marked ballots to avoid penalties.
choices.C: Mandatory voting is unpopular with some citizens.
choices.D: Some countries without mandatory voting have small turnout gaps.
choices.E: Mandatory voting requires administrative resources.

questions.explanation:
If new voters cast blank or random ballots, equal turnout doesn't mean outcomes reflect everyone's preferences.
A — Consistent with the argument.
C — Popularity is irrelevant.
D — Doesn't undercut the claim about mandatory voting's effect.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Only members of the Hiking Club can join Saturday's trip. Rosa is going on Saturday's trip.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: The trip is on a mountain.
choices.B: Rosa organized the trip.
choices.C: Every Hiking Club member is going on the trip.
choices.D: Rosa enjoys hiking.
choices.E: Rosa is a member of the Hiking Club.

questions.explanation:
Joining the trip → member.
A — Not stated.
B — Not stated.
C — Not stated.
D — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: All of the paintings in Gallery 3 are by Impressionists. Some of the paintings by Impressionists in the museum were donated. None of the donated paintings in the museum are insured.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Some paintings by Impressionists in the museum are not insured.
choices.B: None of the paintings in Gallery 3 are insured.
choices.C: All donated paintings are by Impressionists.
choices.D: Some paintings in Gallery 3 are not insured.
choices.E: Some paintings in Gallery 3 were donated.

questions.explanation:
Some Impressionist paintings were donated, and no donated painting is insured.
B — Not established.
C — Not established.
D — The donated Impressionist works might not be in Gallery 3.
E — Not established.

questions.stimulus: When a popular radio station switched to an all-news format, its overall audience shrank, but the average age of its listeners rose and the number of listeners during the morning commute increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: The station's advertising revenue fell.
choices.B: Most listeners tune in during the morning commute.
choices.C: The format change attracted some new listeners even as it lost others.
choices.D: The station will switch back to its old format.
choices.E: Older people prefer news to music.

questions.explanation:
More morning commuters and an older average age point to new listeners arriving while overall numbers fell.
A — Not stated.
B — Not stated.
D — Not supported.
E — A possible explanation, not shown.

questions.stimulus: Although electric cars produce no tailpipe emissions, they are not emission-free. The electricity that charges them often comes from power plants that burn fossil fuels. Manufacturing their batteries also produces significant emissions. Claims that electric cars have zero environmental impact are therefore misleading.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: electric cars are worse for the environment than gas cars
choices.B: electricity often comes from fossil fuels
choices.C: battery manufacturing produces emissions
choices.D: claims that electric cars have zero environmental impact are misleading
choices.E: electric cars produce no tailpipe emissions

questions.explanation:
"Therefore" marks the conclusion.
A — Not claimed.
B — A premise.
C — A premise.
E — A concession.

questions.stimulus: Some believe that reading in dim light damages the eyes. But eye doctors say dim light causes only temporary eye strain, not lasting damage. Reading in dim light, then, is not harmful to the eyes in the long run.
questions.stem: The statement attributed to eye doctors plays which role in the argument?

choices.A: It is the popular belief the argument rejects.
choices.B: It provides support for the argument's conclusion.
choices.C: It is a concession to the opposing view.
choices.D: It is the conclusion.
choices.E: It is an example of a misconception.

questions.explanation:
The doctors' statement is the basis for concluding there's no long-term harm.
A — That's the dim-light belief.
C — It opposes that view.
D — The conclusion is the last sentence.
E — It's accepted as accurate.

questions.stimulus:
Tess: Our town's new recycling program has failed. The amount of trash sent to the landfill hasn't decreased.
Uri: Actually, it has decreased per person. The total stayed the same only because the town's population grew by 20 percent.
questions.stem: Uri responds to Tess by

choices.A: arguing that landfills are harmless
choices.B: questioning Tess's motives
choices.C: denying that the recycling program exists
choices.D: showing that the data she cites can be interpreted differently once another factor is considered
choices.E: agreeing that the program failed

questions.explanation:
Uri brings in population growth, which recasts flat totals as a per-person decline.
A — Not argued.
B — Not done.
C — He accepts it exists.
E — He disagrees.

questions.stimulus:
Simone: The new zoning law, which allows apartment buildings in single-family neighborhoods, will make housing more affordable by increasing the supply of homes.
Theo: Increasing supply generally lowers prices, I agree. But developers will build luxury apartments that sell at high prices, so the law won't help people who need affordable housing.
questions.stem: Simone and Theo disagree over whether

choices.A: the new zoning law will make housing more affordable for those who need it
choices.B: the law allows apartment buildings in single-family neighborhoods
choices.C: developers prefer luxury apartments
choices.D: increasing supply generally lowers prices
choices.E: single-family neighborhoods should be preserved

questions.explanation:
Simone says it will; Theo says the new units will be luxury and won't help those in need.
B — Both accept this.
C — Only Theo says this.
D — Theo agrees.
E — Neither says so.

questions.stimulus:
Wren: The concert was too loud. The music was good, but I couldn't enjoy it with the volume so high.
Xavier: The music was excellent. I didn't mind the volume.
questions.stem: Wren and Xavier are committed to agreeing that

choices.A: the concert was too long
choices.B: they both enjoyed the concert
choices.C: the music at the concert was good
choices.D: the volume should have been lower
choices.E: the concert was too loud

questions.explanation:
Wren: "The music was good." Xavier: "The music was excellent."
A — Not discussed.
B — Wren didn't.
D — Only Wren implies this.
E — Xavier didn't mind the volume.

questions.stimulus: Every student who scored above 90 received an award. Dani did not receive an award. So Dani did not score above 90.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: Every car that passed inspection received a sticker. This car received a sticker. So it passed inspection.
choices.B: Most cars pass inspection. This car is new. So it will pass.
choices.C: Every car that passed inspection received a sticker. This car did not pass. So it did not receive a sticker.
choices.D: Some cars that received stickers passed inspection. This car received a sticker. So it passed.
choices.E: Every car that passed inspection received a sticker. This car did not receive a sticker. So it did not pass inspection.

questions.explanation:
All A are B; not B; so not A.
A — Affirms the consequent.
B — A different, probabilistic form.
C — Denies the antecedent.
D — Invalid "some" reasoning.

questions.stimulus: This textbook is reliable because it was written by experts. We know the authors are experts because they wrote this reliable textbook.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: This website was created by a university, so it is probably trustworthy.
choices.B: This website is trustworthy because many people use it.
choices.C: This website cites sources, so it must be accurate.
choices.D: This website has been wrong before, so it is untrustworthy now.
choices.E: This website is trustworthy because it cites reputable sources. We know the sources are reputable because this trustworthy website cites them.

questions.explanation:
Both are circular: each claim is supported by the other.
A — An appeal to authority, not circular.
B — An appeal to popularity, not circular.
C — An unsupported leap, not circular.
D — A different flaw.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A restaurant should honor a customer's reservation unless the customer arrives more than fifteen minutes late without calling ahead.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: The restaurant should honor reservations only for regular customers.
choices.B: The restaurant should honor Mo's reservation even though he arrived thirty minutes late without calling.
choices.C: The restaurant should honor Kim's reservation, since although she arrived twenty minutes late, she had called ahead to say she would be delayed.
choices.D: The restaurant may give away Nia's table because the restaurant was busy.
choices.E: The restaurant may give away Lee's table, since he arrived ten minutes late.

questions.explanation:
She called ahead, so the exception doesn't apply. Honor the reservation.
A — Not a condition.
B — The exception applies; the principle doesn't require honoring it.
D — Not a condition.
E — Ten minutes is within the allowed window.

questions.stimulus: Teacher: Hira should be allowed to retake the exam. She missed it because she was in the hospital, and she has a doctor's note.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the teacher's position?

choices.A: A student who misses an exam because of a documented medical emergency should be allowed to retake it.
choices.B: Students should be allowed to retake any exam they fail.
choices.C: Doctors' notes should be required for all absences.
choices.D: Students who study hard should get extra credit.
choices.E: Exams should always be optional.

questions.explanation:
Facts: medical emergency, documented. The principle says allow a retake.
B — Hira missed the exam; she didn't fail it.
C — Doesn't address retakes.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Too broad.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: It was wrong for the journalist to publish the leaked memo, even though the memo was authentic and of public interest. The journalist knew that publishing it would reveal the identity of the employee who leaked it, exposing that employee to retaliation, and the memo's key information could have been reported without the document itself.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.A: Journalists should publish any authentic material of public interest.
choices.B: Journalists should never publish leaked documents.
choices.C: Employees who leak documents should be protected by law.
choices.D: A journalist should not publish material that will expose a source to serious harm if the material's important content can be conveyed in a way that does not expose the source.
choices.E: Journalists should always verify leaked documents before publishing.

questions.explanation:
Facts: publishing exposed the source to retaliation, and the content could have been reported without the document. The principle covers exactly this.
A — Would favor publishing.
B — The ethicist's reasoning depends on the specifics.
C — About law, not the journalist's duty.
E — The memo was authentic.

questions.stimulus: In the town of Eastbrook, the number of reported bicycle thefts rose sharply after the police department launched an online form that lets residents report thefts quickly. Yet police patrols found fewer stolen bicycles abandoned around town than in previous years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain these findings?

choices.A: Many stolen bicycles are sold online.
choices.B: Before the online form existed, most bicycle thefts went unreported because reporting required a visit to the police station.
choices.C: Eastbrook installed more bike racks.
choices.D: Bicycle use in Eastbrook has declined.
choices.E: The police department hired more officers.

questions.explanation:
The rise in reports reflects easier reporting, not more thefts. Fewer abandoned bikes is consistent with flat or falling actual thefts.
A — Might explain fewer abandoned bikes, but not the rise in reports.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Could explain fewer thefts, but not the rise in reports.
E — Doesn't explain both findings.

questions.stimulus: Since a city began offering free public Wi-Fi in its downtown area, foot traffic downtown has increased by 15 percent. City officials conclude that the Wi-Fi has drawn people downtown.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the officials' conclusion?

choices.A: how fast the Wi-Fi connection is
choices.B: whether residents have home internet
choices.C: how much the Wi-Fi cost to install
choices.D: whether new shops, restaurants, or events opened downtown during the same period
choices.E: whether other cities offer free Wi-Fi

questions.explanation:
Other attractions could explain the increase. Knowing whether they appeared tests the Wi-Fi explanation.
A — Speed matters a little, but it doesn't test causation directly.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Cost doesn't test causation.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: If we allow students to use phones during lunch, soon they'll be using them in class, then during tests, and eventually no one will learn anything. So phones must be banned at lunch.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: confuses correlation with causation
choices.B: attacks the character of students
choices.C: assumes without justification that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of increasingly bad outcomes
choices.D: fails to define "phone"
choices.E: relies on an appeal to authority

questions.explanation:
Nothing shows lunchtime phone use leads to cheating on tests and the end of learning.
A — No data is given.
B — No attack.
D — Not the flaw.
E — No authority.

questions.stimulus: A survey of visitors to an organic food festival found that 85 percent believe organic food is healthier than conventional food. So most people in the country believe organic food is healthier.
questions.stem: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to define "healthier"
choices.B: relies on a sample that is too large
choices.C: assumes organic food is more expensive
choices.D: confuses belief with knowledge
choices.E: draws a conclusion about a population from a sample likely to differ from that population in relevant ways

questions.explanation:
Organic food festival-goers are likely more pro-organic than the general public.
A — Not the main flaw.
B — Size isn't the problem.
C — Not assumed.
D — The conclusion is about belief, so no confusion.

questions.stimulus: Business analyst: In nearly every successful startup I've studied, the founders worked more than eighty hours a week during the company's first year. So for a startup to succeed, its founders must work more than eighty hours a week in the first year.
questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes long hours cause burnout
choices.B: concludes that a feature common among successes is required for success, without considering whether failures shared the same feature or whether some successes lacked it
choices.C: relies on too small a sample of startups
choices.D: confuses a sufficient condition with a necessary one
choices.E: fails to define "successful"

questions.explanation:
"Nearly every" success had long hours, which doesn't make long hours necessary. Some successes didn't, and many failures may have had long hours too.
A — Not assumed.
C — Possibly, but even a large sample wouldn't establish necessity.
D — Related, but the argument treats a common trait as necessary rather than reversing a stated conditional.
E — Not the main flaw.

questions.stimulus: The city plans to reduce noise complaints from residents near the airport by planting a row of tall trees between the runway and the neighborhood.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Tall trees can reduce the amount of airport noise that reaches the neighborhood.
choices.B: Residents want more trees in their neighborhood.
choices.C: The airport will not expand.
choices.D: Trees are inexpensive to plant.
choices.E: Every resident has complained about noise.

questions.explanation:
If trees don't block noise, the plan can't reduce complaints.
B — Not required.
C — Not required.
D — Not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The new translation of the ancient poem is superior to earlier translations because it captures the poem's original rhythm, which earlier translations ignored.
questions.stem: The critic's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: The new translator is a poet.
choices.B: Earlier translations were inaccurate in every respect.
choices.C: Most readers prefer rhythmic translations.
choices.D: Capturing the poem's original rhythm is an important factor in the quality of a translation.
choices.E: The poem's original rhythm is known with certainty.

questions.explanation:
Rhythm makes this translation superior only if rhythm matters to translation quality.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
C — Helpful, but not required.
E — Overly strong.

questions.stimulus: Every book on this shelf is a mystery novel. So the book Carlos is reading is a mystery novel.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The book Carlos is reading came from this shelf.
choices.B: Some books on this shelf are long.
choices.C: Carlos reads quickly.
choices.D: All mystery novels are on this shelf.
choices.E: Carlos enjoys mystery novels.

questions.explanation:
Shelf → mystery.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Reverses the statement.
E — Doesn't establish the book's genre.

questions.stimulus: Commentator: The city's new parking fees disproportionately burden low-income residents. Therefore, the city should repeal them.
questions.stem: The commentator's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The parking fees raise substantial revenue.
choices.B: Low-income residents use parking less than other residents.
choices.C: Low-income residents oppose the parking fees.
choices.D: Some cities have repealed parking fees.
choices.E: A city should repeal any fee that disproportionately burdens low-income residents.

questions.explanation:
Disproportionate burden → repeal. The fees disproportionately burden, so repeal.
A — A reason to keep them.
B — Undercuts the burden claim.
C — Opposition doesn't establish that repeal is required.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: After a school installed water fountains in every hallway, students' visits to the nurse for headaches decreased. The nurse believes better hydration reduced headaches.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the nurse's belief?

choices.A: The nurse's office moved to another floor.
choices.B: Some students bring water bottles.
choices.C: Students drank significantly more water after the fountains were installed.
choices.D: The school also shortened the school day.
choices.E: Headaches can have many causes.

questions.explanation:
This confirms the mechanism: more hydration.
A — Could reduce visits for other reasons.
B — Doesn't show change.
D — An alternative cause.
E — Doesn't support hydration specifically.

questions.stimulus: Anthropologist: The Kel people's tradition of sharing meat from a hunt with all families in the village, rather than only the hunter's family, likely developed as insurance against the high variability of hunting success, since any given hunter might go many days without a kill.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the anthropologist's explanation?

choices.A: The Kel people also share tools.
choices.B: Among neighboring groups, those that rely heavily on hunting share meat widely, while those that rely mainly on reliable farm crops share far less.
choices.C: Meat spoils quickly without refrigeration.
choices.D: Kel hunters sometimes hunt in groups.
choices.E: The Kel people value generosity highly.

questions.explanation:
Sharing tracks food variability across groups, as the insurance hypothesis predicts.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Offers a competing explanation (spoilage), not support for insurance.
D — Irrelevant.
E — An alternative cultural explanation that doesn't support the insurance hypothesis.

questions.stimulus: A study found that children who attend preschool score higher on kindergarten readiness tests. So preschool attendance prepares children for kindergarten.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.A: Some children who didn't attend preschool scored high.
choices.B: Families who send children to preschool tend to spend more time reading with their children at home.
choices.C: Preschool is expensive in many areas.
choices.D: Preschool teachers are often certified.
choices.E: Kindergarten readiness tests are widely used.

questions.explanation:
Home reading is an alternative explanation for higher readiness.
A — Exceptions don't undercut the trend.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Supports effectiveness.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A city plans to reduce traffic downtown by charging drivers a fee to enter the downtown area during peak hours. The city expects the fee to persuade many drivers to use public transit instead.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most casts doubt on the plan's likely success?

choices.A: Some drivers already use public transit.
choices.B: Many residents support reducing traffic.
choices.C: Other cities have used similar fees successfully.
choices.D: The fee will generate revenue.
choices.E: Downtown has very limited public transit service, with few routes and infrequent buses.

questions.explanation:
If transit is poor, drivers have no practical alternative and may pay the fee anyway.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Supports the plan.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: None of the restaurants in the food court serves breakfast. Café Luna serves breakfast.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: All restaurants outside the food court serve breakfast.
choices.B: Café Luna serves only breakfast.
choices.C: Café Luna is not in the food court.
choices.D: The food court is closed in the morning.
choices.E: Café Luna is near the food court.

questions.explanation:
Food court → no breakfast. Café Luna serves breakfast, so it isn't in the food court.
A — Not stated.
B — Not stated.
D — Not stated.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: A clothing store found that when it played upbeat music, customers spent less time in the store but bought about the same amount as when it played slow music.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Slow music increases sales.
choices.B: The store should play upbeat music.
choices.C: Customers prefer upbeat music.
choices.D: The type of music played did not substantially affect how much customers bought.
choices.E: Customers dislike slow music.

questions.explanation:
Purchases were about the same under both types of music.
A — Purchases were about the same.
B — A recommendation beyond the data.
C — Not shown.
E — Not shown.

questions.stimulus: Wildlife biologists found that in forests where wolves had been reintroduced, beavers built more dams than in comparable forests without wolves. Wolves rarely prey on beavers. However, wolves do prey heavily on elk, which feed on the willow trees that beavers use to build dams.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Wolves may increase beaver dam building indirectly, by reducing the number of elk that eat willows.
choices.B: Elk populations are lower in every forest with wolves.
choices.C: Beaver dams cause elk populations to decline.
choices.D: Wolves protect beavers from other predators.
choices.E: Beavers prefer forests with wolves.

questions.explanation:
Wolves eat elk, elk eat willows, beavers use willows. An indirect pathway fits the data. "May" keeps it modest.
B — "Every" overreaches.
C — Reverses the direction.
D — Not stated.
E — Preference isn't shown.

questions.stimulus: Some say that writing by hand is obsolete now that most people type. But studies show that students who take notes by hand remember material better than those who type their notes. Handwriting therefore still has important value.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: handwriting still has important value
choices.B: students who take notes by hand remember material better
choices.C: typing should be banned in schools
choices.D: most people type
choices.E: writing by hand is obsolete

questions.explanation:
"Therefore" marks the conclusion.
B — A premise.
C — Not claimed.
D — Background.
E — The opposing view.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Although the new museum building has been praised for its bold design, it fails as a museum. Its curved walls make it nearly impossible to hang paintings, and its skylights let in sunlight that damages artwork. A museum building's primary purpose is to display and protect art.
questions.stem: The claim that a museum building's primary purpose is to display and protect art plays which role in the critic's argument?

choices.A: It is a concession to those who praise the design.
choices.B: It is the main conclusion.
choices.C: It is evidence that the design is bold.
choices.D: It is a claim the critic argues against.
choices.E: It is a principle that links the building's specific problems to the conclusion that it fails as a museum.

questions.explanation:
The problems (can't hang art, sun damage) count as failure because of this principle.
A — The concession is the praise for the design.
B — The conclusion is that the building fails as a museum.
C — Unrelated.
D — The critic relies on it.

questions.stimulus: Xia: Opponents of the new tax say it will drive businesses out of the city. But when the neighboring city adopted an identical tax three years ago, the number of businesses there actually grew. So the opponents' prediction is unfounded.
questions.stem: Xia's argument proceeds by

choices.A: arguing that the tax is fair
choices.B: questioning the opponents' motives
choices.C: citing a comparable case in which the predicted outcome did not occur
choices.D: conceding the opponents' point
choices.E: showing that the opponents' argument is circular

questions.explanation:
Xia uses the neighboring city's experience to undercut the prediction.
A — Fairness isn't discussed.
B — Not done.
D — Xia disputes it.
E — No circularity.

questions.stimulus:
Amir: Self-driving cars will make roads safer because they don't get distracted or tired.
Bea: They don't get distracted, but their software can fail in unexpected situations, so they won't necessarily make roads safer.
questions.stem: Amir and Bea disagree over whether

choices.A: self-driving cars get distracted
choices.B: self-driving cars will make roads safer
choices.C: software can fail
choices.D: self-driving cars should be banned
choices.E: human drivers get tired

questions.explanation:
Amir says they will; Bea says not necessarily.
A — Both agree they don't.
C — Only Bea addresses this.
D — Neither says so.
E — Bea doesn't dispute it.

questions.stimulus: Only residents can park on Elm Street overnight. Jackie parked on Elm Street overnight. So Jackie is a resident.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: Most ticket holders enter the stadium. Malik is a ticket holder. So he entered.
choices.B: Only ticket holders can enter. Malik is not a ticket holder. So he will try to enter.
choices.C: Only ticket holders can enter the stadium. Malik is a ticket holder. So Malik entered the stadium.
choices.D: Only ticket holders can enter the stadium. Malik entered the stadium. So Malik is a ticket holder.
choices.E: Malik entered the stadium. So all ticket holders entered.

questions.explanation:
Only A can do B; X did B; so X is A.
A — A probabilistic, different form.
B — A non sequitur.
C — Treats a necessary condition as sufficient.
E — Overgeneralizes.

questions.stimulus: Every successful novelist I know writes every day. I write every day. So I will become a successful novelist.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: I practice daily and am a top player. So everyone who practices daily is a top player.
choices.B: Some top tennis players practice six hours a day. So I should practice six hours a day.
choices.C: Top tennis players earn a lot. So I should become a tennis player.
choices.D: Every top tennis player I know practices six hours a day. I practice six hours a day. So I will become a top tennis player.
choices.E: Every top tennis player practices daily. I don't practice daily. So I won't become a top player.

questions.explanation:
Both: a trait shared by successful people I know, I have it, so I'll succeed. That treats a shared trait as sufficient, generalized from an acquaintance sample.
A — A different overgeneralization.
B — A recommendation, not a prediction.
C — A different structure.
E — Valid, given the premise.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A store should accept a returned item for a full refund if the item is returned within 30 days with a receipt.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: The store should refund Eli because he is a loyal customer.
choices.B: The store should give Ava a full refund, since she returned the blender within 30 days and had the receipt.
choices.C: The store should refund Cal even though he has no receipt.
choices.D: The store should give Dee store credit instead of a refund.
choices.E: The store should refuse Ben's return, since he returned the item after 35 days.

questions.explanation:
Both conditions are met.
A — Loyalty isn't a condition.
C — The receipt condition isn't met.
D — Not addressed.
E — The principle states when to accept, not when to refuse.

questions.stimulus: Librarian: The library should not remove the controversial book from its shelves. Although some patrons find it offensive, many others want to read it, and the library's purpose is to provide access to a wide range of ideas.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the librarian's position?

choices.A: Libraries should only stock popular books.
choices.B: Patrons should be allowed to vote on which books to remove.
choices.C: A library should not remove a book that serves its purpose of providing access to diverse ideas merely because some patrons find it offensive.
choices.D: Libraries should remove books that offend anyone.
choices.E: Libraries should buy more copies of popular books.

questions.explanation:
The book serves the library's purpose; offense alone isn't enough to remove it.
A — Not the reasoning.
B — Not the reasoning.
D — Would favor removal.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A restaurant added a calorie count next to each item on its menu. Afterward, sales of its high-calorie desserts increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: Some customers ignore calorie counts.
choices.B: Calorie counts are required by law in many cities.
choices.C: The restaurant also raised dessert prices.
choices.D: The restaurant added new salads.
choices.E: Many customers had assumed the desserts were even higher in calories than the listed counts showed.

questions.explanation:
The posted counts reassured customers who had overestimated, so they ordered more desserts.
A — Explains no change, not an increase.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Higher prices would lower sales.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: If the committee approves the budget, then either the library will expand or the park will be renovated, but not both. The park will be renovated only if the city receives a state grant. The city will not receive a state grant.
questions.stem: If the committee approves the budget, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: The library will expand.
choices.B: Neither the library nor the park project will happen.
choices.C: Both the library and the park projects will happen.
choices.D: The park will be renovated.
choices.E: The city will apply for a different grant.

questions.explanation:
No grant → no park renovation. With approval, exactly one of library or park happens. The park can't, so the library expands.
B — Approval guarantees one.
C — "Not both."
D — Impossible without the grant.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: A bakery's sales increased after it put a sign on the sidewalk. The owner believes the sign attracted new customers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the owner's belief?

choices.A: whether anything else changed at the bakery around the time the sign was put up
choices.B: what color the sign is
choices.C: whether other bakeries use signs
choices.D: how much the sign cost
choices.E: whether the owner likes the sign

questions.explanation:
Other changes could explain the sales increase.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Irrelevant.
