questions.stimulus: Shakespeare is the greatest playwright because his plays are better than anyone else's.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.A: relies on an outdated source
choices.B: confuses popularity with quality
choices.C: generalizes from one play
choices.D: ignores other art forms
choices.E: uses its conclusion, restated, as its only support

questions.explanation:
"Greatest playwright" and "plays better than anyone else's" say the same thing.
A — No source is cited.
B — Popularity isn't mentioned.
C — No play is cited.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Students who participate in school sports have higher grade-point averages than students who don't. So participating in sports improves academic performance.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: ignores the cost of school sports
choices.B: fails to consider that students with higher grades may be more likely to be allowed or choose to play sports
choices.C: confuses academic performance with intelligence
choices.D: assumes all students play sports
choices.E: relies on too small a sample

questions.explanation:
Many schools require minimum grades to play, so grades may drive participation rather than the reverse.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Not discussed.
D — Not assumed.
E — No sample size is given.

questions.stimulus: Despite decades of searching, no one has proven that life exists on other planets. Therefore, Earth is the only planet with life.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes all planets are similar
choices.B: relies on an unqualified authority
choices.C: treats the lack of proof that something exists as proof that it does not exist
choices.D: attacks scientists who search for life
choices.E: confuses a cause with an effect

questions.explanation:
Not finding life elsewhere doesn't prove there is none.
A — Not assumed.
B — No authority.
D — No attack.
E — No causal claim.

questions.stimulus: The town plans to reduce speeding on Maple Street by installing a sign that displays each car's speed as it passes.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Speeding causes most accidents.
choices.B: Every driver will notice the sign.
choices.C: Maple Street has a lot of traffic.
choices.D: Some drivers who speed will slow down when they see their speed displayed.
choices.E: The sign will be inexpensive.

questions.explanation:
The sign works only if seeing their speed changes some drivers' behavior.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
C — Not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Economist: A country that relies heavily on a single export is vulnerable to price swings in that commodity. Delavia earns most of its export revenue from copper. Therefore, Delavia should invest in developing other export industries to reduce its vulnerability.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.A: Developing other export industries would reduce the share of Delavia's export revenue that depends on copper.
choices.B: Delavia has abundant resources other than copper.
choices.C: Delavia's copper mines will soon be exhausted.
choices.D: Copper prices will fall in the near future.
choices.E: Other countries have diversified successfully.

questions.explanation:
Investing in other industries reduces vulnerability only if it actually shrinks copper's share of export revenue.
B — Helpful, but other industries needn't be resource-based.
C — Not required.
D — Not required. Vulnerability exists regardless of direction.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Only people who have read the book can join the discussion. So Kenji cannot join the discussion.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Kenji dislikes discussions.
choices.B: Some readers didn't enjoy the book.
choices.C: Kenji has not read the book.
choices.D: Everyone who read the book will join.
choices.E: Kenji has read a different book.

questions.explanation:
Join → read. Kenji hasn't read, so he can't join.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Irrelevant.
D — Not relevant to Kenji.
E — He might also have read this one.

questions.stimulus: Any vehicle that weighs more than three tons is prohibited from crossing the old bridge. Therefore, the delivery truck is prohibited from crossing the old bridge.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The old bridge is in poor condition.
choices.B: Every prohibited vehicle weighs more than three tons.
choices.C: Most delivery trucks weigh more than three tons.
choices.D: The delivery truck carries heavy cargo.
choices.E: The delivery truck weighs more than three tons.

questions.explanation:
Over three tons → prohibited.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Reverses the statement.
C — Doesn't establish that this truck does.
D — Heavy cargo doesn't guarantee a total over three tons.

questions.stimulus: Dentist: Children who drink fluoridated water have fewer cavities than children who don't. So fluoride helps prevent cavities.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the dentist's argument?

choices.A: Some children with fluoridated water still get cavities.
choices.B: Fluoridated water tastes the same as regular water.
choices.C: Children who drink fluoridated water also brush more often.
choices.D: In towns that began fluoridating water, children's cavity rates fell, while rates in similar towns that didn't fluoridate stayed the same.
choices.E: Fluoride is found in many toothpastes.

questions.explanation:
A before-and-after change with a comparison group supports a causal effect.
A — Exceptions don't undercut the trend.
B — Irrelevant.
C — A confound.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: The recent increase in the bird population on Farrow Island is due to the removal of invasive rats, which had been eating the birds' eggs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologist's claim?

choices.A: The birds on Farrow Island nest on the ground.
choices.B: Bird populations on nearby islands where rats were not removed did not increase during the same period.
choices.C: The island's climate was favorable this year.
choices.D: Rats were removed using traps.
choices.E: Many tourists visit Farrow Island.

questions.explanation:
The comparison islands without rat removal show no increase, isolating rat removal as the likely cause.
A — Makes egg predation plausible but doesn't show removal caused the rise.
C — An alternative cause.
D — Method is irrelevant.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Since the town painted bike lanes on Main Street, the number of cyclists has doubled. The town council credits the bike lanes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the council's conclusion?

choices.A: The bike lanes are brightly painted.
choices.B: Some cyclists don't use the lanes.
choices.C: Main Street is the town's busiest road.
choices.D: A bike-sharing station opened on Main Street at the same time the lanes were painted.
choices.E: Cyclists say they feel safer in the lanes.

questions.explanation:
Bike sharing could explain the increase on its own.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Doesn't explain the increase.
C — Irrelevant.
E — Supports the council.

questions.stimulus: Researchers found that people who own pets visit the doctor less often than people who don't. They conclude that pet ownership improves health.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Pets can reduce loneliness.
choices.B: Many pet owners have more than one pet.
choices.C: Pet owners spend money on veterinary care.
choices.D: Dogs require daily walks.
choices.E: People with chronic health conditions are often advised not to own pets because of the care pets require.

questions.explanation:
If sicker people are steered away from pets, pet owners would be healthier on average regardless of any effect of pets.
A — A possible mechanism.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
D — A possible mechanism for better health.

questions.stimulus: Every player on the team has a uniform. Some players on the team are goalies.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Some players don't have uniforms.
choices.B: Some goalies have a uniform.
choices.C: All players are goalies.
choices.D: Every goalie is on the team.
choices.E: Goalies have different uniforms.

questions.explanation:
Some players are goalies, and all players have uniforms.
A — Every player has one.
C — Only some are.
D — Not stated.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: In the Westwood school district, every school that offers Latin also offers Greek. Every school that offers Greek has a classics teacher. No school with fewer than 300 students has a classics teacher. Ridgeview School has fewer than 300 students.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Ridgeview School offers Greek but not Latin.
choices.B: Every school with more than 300 students offers Latin.
choices.C: Ridgeview School does not offer Latin.
choices.D: Some schools that offer Greek do not offer Latin.
choices.E: Ridgeview School has a classics teacher.

questions.explanation:
Latin → Greek → classics teacher → at least 300 students. Ridgeview has under 300, so no classics teacher, no Greek, no Latin.
A — It can't offer Greek either.
B — Reverses the chain.
D — Possible, but not required.
E — It can't.

questions.stimulus: Shops on Elm Street that stayed open until 9 p.m. saw a 20 percent increase in sales, while shops that closed at 6 p.m. saw no change.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Staying open later was associated with higher sales among the shops on Elm Street.
choices.B: Every shop should stay open until 9 p.m.
choices.C: Shops that close early will go out of business.
choices.D: Staying open later causes higher sales.
choices.E: Customers prefer shopping at night.

questions.explanation:
That's the observed pattern.
B — A recommendation.
C — Not supported.
D — Causation isn't established.
E — Not shown.

questions.stimulus: Some people believe that you should never wake a sleepwalker. However, doctors say it is generally safe to wake one gently, and doing so can prevent the sleepwalker from being injured. You should feel free to gently wake a sleepwalker.
questions.stem: The main conclusion of the argument is that

choices.A: doctors are experts on sleep
choices.B: sleepwalking is dangerous
choices.C: you should never wake a sleepwalker
choices.D: waking a sleepwalker can prevent injury
choices.E: it is acceptable to gently wake a sleepwalker

questions.explanation:
The last sentence is the conclusion.
A — Not claimed.
B — Implied, but not the conclusion.
C — The opposing belief.
D — A premise.

questions.stimulus: Many people think that bulls are enraged by the color red. In fact, bulls are colorblind to red. What provokes them in a bullfight is the movement of the cape. So the cape's color is irrelevant to the bull's behavior.
questions.stem: The claim that bulls are colorblind to red plays which role?

choices.A: It is irrelevant to the argument.
choices.B: It is a concession.
choices.C: It supports the argument's conclusion.
choices.D: It is the belief the argument rejects.
choices.E: It is the conclusion.

questions.explanation:
It's a reason the cape's color doesn't matter.
A — It's central.
B — It isn't conceded.
D — The rejected belief is that red enrages bulls.
E — The conclusion is that color is irrelevant.

questions.stimulus:
Rina: Sugar makes children hyperactive. I see it at every birthday party.
Sol: Studies show that children given sugar and children given a sugar-free placebo behave the same. Birthday parties are exciting for other reasons.
questions.stem: Sol responds to Rina by

choices.A: attacking Rina's parenting
choices.B: offering controlled evidence and an alternative explanation for what Rina observes
choices.C: denying that children attend birthday parties
choices.D: arguing that sugar is healthy
choices.E: agreeing that sugar causes hyperactivity

questions.explanation:
Sol cites placebo-controlled studies and explains the parties' effect another way.
A — Not done.
C — Not denied.
D — Not argued.
E — He disagrees.

questions.stimulus:
Gwen: Museums should return artifacts to their countries of origin. These objects were often taken without consent, and they belong to the cultures that created them.
Hector: Some artifacts were indeed taken without consent, and those should be returned. But many were acquired legally, through purchase or exchange, and museums have no obligation to return those.
questions.stem: Gwen and Hector disagree over whether

choices.A: museums should return artifacts that were legally acquired
choices.B: artifacts taken without consent should be returned
choices.C: artifacts were sometimes purchased
choices.D: some artifacts were taken without consent
choices.E: museums should display artifacts

questions.explanation:
Gwen's position covers artifacts generally ("artifacts... belong to the cultures that created them"). Hector exempts legally acquired ones.
B — Both agree.
C — Gwen doesn't address this.
D — Both agree.
E — Not discussed.

questions.stimulus:
Lara: The new phone's camera is impressive, but its battery life is disappointing.
Milo: I agree the battery life is disappointing. The camera is just average, though.
questions.stem: Lara and Milo agree that

choices.A: the camera is average
choices.B: the camera is impressive
choices.C: the phone is overpriced
choices.D: the new phone's battery life is disappointing
choices.E: they would not buy the phone

questions.explanation:
Both say so.
A — Lara calls it impressive.
B — Milo says it's average.
C — Not discussed.
E — Not discussed.

questions.stimulus: If the meeting is canceled, Jada will work from home. The meeting was canceled. So Jada will work from home.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: Leo usually buys books. So he will buy this one.
choices.B: If the store has the book, Leo will buy it. Leo bought it. So the store had it.
choices.C: If the store has the book, Leo will buy it. The store doesn't have it. So Leo won't buy it.
choices.D: The store has many books. So Leo will buy one.
choices.E: If the store has the book, Leo will buy it. The store has the book. So Leo will buy it.

questions.explanation:
If A then B; A; so B.
A — Probabilistic.
B — Affirms the consequent.
C — Denies the antecedent.
D — A non sequitur.

questions.stimulus: All dogs have four legs. My cat has four legs. So my cat is a dog.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: Some roses are red. This rose is red. So all roses are red.
choices.B: All roses have thorns. This plant has thorns. So this plant is a rose.
choices.C: No roses are blue. This flower is blue. So it isn't a rose.
choices.D: All roses have thorns. This plant is a rose. So it has thorns.
choices.E: Roses are popular. So everyone likes roses.

questions.explanation:
Both affirm the consequent: all A are B; X is B; so X is A.
A — A different flaw.
C — Valid.
D — Valid.
E — A different flaw.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A company should disclose a product defect to customers if the defect could cause injury, even if disclosure would hurt sales.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: ToyCo need not disclose a cosmetic scratch on some toys.
choices.B: ToyCo should hide a choking hazard to protect sales.
choices.C: ToyCo should disclose defects only if customers complain.
choices.D: ToyCo should tell customers that a toy's small parts could come loose and pose a choking hazard, even though sales may drop.
choices.E: ToyCo should disclose all defects, no matter how minor.

questions.explanation:
The defect could cause injury, so disclose regardless of sales.
A — The principle doesn't address non-injury defects.
B — Violates the principle.
C — The principle requires disclosure regardless.
E — Broader than the principle.

questions.stimulus: Coach: Although Riley is our best scorer, she should sit out tonight's game. She skipped practice twice this week without explanation, and every player is expected to attend practice.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the coach's position?

choices.A: Players who fail to meet team expectations should face consequences, regardless of their skill.
choices.B: The best scorer should always play.
choices.C: Players should explain their absences.
choices.D: Coaches should treat star players differently.
choices.E: Practice is more important than games.

questions.explanation:
Riley broke an expectation; the principle says consequences apply regardless of skill.
B — Would favor her playing.
C — Doesn't establish consequences.
D — Opposes the coach's reasoning.
E — Close, but doesn't establish benching.

questions.stimulus: A city added more lanes to a busy highway, yet traffic congestion on the highway became worse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: Public transit fares fell.
choices.B: The highway is the city's main route.
choices.C: The added lanes encouraged many more people to drive on the highway.
choices.D: The new lanes were well built.
choices.E: Some drivers prefer side streets.

questions.explanation:
Induced demand filled the new capacity.
A — Would reduce driving.
B — Background.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Doesn't explain worse congestion.

questions.stimulus: Unless it snows, the school will be open tomorrow. The school will not be open tomorrow.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: It will not snow tomorrow.
choices.B: The school will be open the next day.
choices.C: If it snows, the school will close.
choices.D: It will snow tomorrow.
choices.E: Teachers will work from home.

questions.explanation:
Not snowing → open. Not open → it snowed (contrapositive).
A — The opposite.
B — Not stated.
C — Not stated; snow is only necessary for closing.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: Professor Lin argues that the university should increase financial aid. But Professor Lin went to an expensive private college herself, so her argument should be ignored.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: dismisses an argument based on a fact about the person making it rather than on its merits
choices.B: fails to define "financial aid"
choices.C: confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one
choices.D: relies on an unrepresentative sample
choices.E: assumes financial aid is unnecessary

questions.explanation:
Where Lin went to college has no bearing on whether her argument is sound.
B — Not the flaw.
C — No conditional.
D — No sample.
E — Not assumed.

questions.stimulus: Most people who exercise regularly sleep well. Most people who sleep well are productive at work. So most people who exercise regularly are productive at work.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

choices.A: relies on self-reports of sleep quality
choices.B: treats a sufficient condition as a necessary one
choices.C: assumes that sleep causes productivity
choices.D: fails to define "productive"
choices.E: fails to recognize that the regular exercisers who sleep well might largely be among the minority of good sleepers who are not productive

questions.explanation:
Two "most" statements can't be chained. The overlap might be small.
A — No data source is mentioned.
B — No conditional is reversed.
C — A causal reading isn't the flaw; the quantifier chaining is.
D — Not the core flaw.

questions.stimulus: A bakery plans to sell more bread by offering free samples near the entrance.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: The bakery's bread is the best in town.
choices.B: The samples will be inexpensive.
choices.C: Some customers who taste a sample will decide to buy bread they otherwise would not have bought.
choices.D: Every customer will take a sample.
choices.E: Most customers like bread.

questions.explanation:
Samples increase sales only if they prompt extra purchases.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
D — Not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Since the hospital began requiring doctors to use a surgical checklist, complications from surgery have fallen by 30 percent. The hospital's board concludes that the checklist reduced complications.
questions.stem: The board's conclusion depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Other hospitals use similar checklists.
choices.B: The hospital did not begin performing a much larger share of low-risk surgeries during the same period.
choices.C: Every doctor follows the checklist perfectly.
choices.D: The checklist is short.
choices.E: Doctors like using the checklist.

questions.explanation:
If the surgical mix shifted toward easier cases, complications might fall regardless of the checklist.
A — Not required.
C — Not required.
D — Not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: All the employees at the bakery are trained in food safety. So Sam is trained in food safety.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Everyone trained in food safety works at the bakery.
choices.B: Sam likes baking.
choices.C: Sam is an employee at the bakery.
choices.D: The bakery is popular.
choices.E: Sam has worked in restaurants.

questions.explanation:
Bakery employee → trained.
A — Reverses the statement.
B — Irrelevant.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Doesn't establish his training.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: An action is morally right only if it treats every person as an end. Lying to someone in order to profit from their mistaken belief treats that person merely as a means. Therefore, lying for profit is not morally right.
questions.stem: The philosopher's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Profit is never a legitimate motive.
choices.B: Some lies do not treat people merely as means.
choices.C: Every action that treats people as ends is morally right.
choices.D: Most people believe lying is wrong.
choices.E: No action that treats someone merely as a means also treats every person as an end.

questions.explanation:
Right → treats every person as an end. Lying for profit treats someone merely as a means. The missing link: treating someone merely as a means → not treating every person as an end. Then lying for profit isn't right.
A — Not needed.
B — Irrelevant to lies told for profit.
C — Makes the condition sufficient, the wrong direction.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: After a city planted trees along its main street, shops on that street reported higher sales. The city believes the trees made the street more attractive to shoppers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the city's belief?

choices.A: Some shops closed during the period.
choices.B: Surveys show that shoppers spend more time on the street since the trees were planted.
choices.C: Trees require maintenance.
choices.D: The city also lowered parking fees at the same time.
choices.E: Trees provide shade.

questions.explanation:
More time spent there supports the idea that the trees drew shoppers.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
D — An alternative cause.
E — A possible reason, but weaker than evidence of behavior change.

questions.stimulus: Nutrition researcher: Diets high in fiber reduce the risk of heart disease. In a ten-year study, participants who ate the most fiber had the lowest rates of heart disease.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's conclusion?

choices.A: Most participants ate too little fiber.
choices.B: Fiber is found in fruits and vegetables.
choices.C: Many high-fiber foods are also low in fat.
choices.D: The relationship between fiber intake and heart disease held even after accounting for participants' exercise habits, smoking, and income.
choices.E: The study lasted ten years.

questions.explanation:
Ruling out major confounds makes fiber a more plausible cause.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Background.
C — An alternative explanation (low fat).
E — Already stated.

questions.stimulus: Since the park began charging an entrance fee, the number of visitors has dropped. Officials conclude that the fee is discouraging visitors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the officials' conclusion?

choices.A: The park's main trail was closed for repairs during the same period.
choices.B: The fee is small.
choices.C: Other parks charge fees.
choices.D: Many visitors complained about the fee.
choices.E: The fee revenue is used for maintenance.

questions.explanation:
A closed main trail could explain fewer visitors.
B — Doesn't rule out deterrence.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Supports the officials.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Medical researcher: Among patients who took Drug X, 70 percent recovered within two weeks. Since this recovery rate is higher than the 50 percent rate for the illness generally, Drug X is effective.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researcher's argument?

choices.A: Drug X has side effects.
choices.B: Drug X is expensive.
choices.C: The illness is common.
choices.D: Drug X is prescribed mainly to patients diagnosed early, and patients diagnosed early recover within two weeks about 70 percent of the time even without treatment.
choices.E: Some patients who took Drug X did not recover.

questions.explanation:
The 70 percent matches what early-diagnosed patients achieve anyway, so the drug adds nothing beyond who gets it.
A — Irrelevant to effectiveness.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
E — Expected; it doesn't undercut the comparison.

questions.stimulus: No one under 18 may enter the club. Ana entered the club.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Ana is not under 18.
choices.B: Ana is exactly 18.
choices.C: Ana is a club member.
choices.D: Ana's friends are over 18.
choices.E: Everyone 18 or older entered the club.

questions.explanation:
Under 18 → can't enter. Ana entered.
B — She could be older.
C — Not stated.
D — Not stated.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: Every chef at Bistro Nova trained in France. Some chefs who trained in France also trained in Italy. No chef who trained in Italy works the night shift at Bistro Nova.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Some chefs at Bistro Nova trained in Italy.
choices.B: Every chef who trained in France works at Bistro Nova.
choices.C: No chef at Bistro Nova works the night shift.
choices.D: Some chefs at Bistro Nova did not train in France.
choices.E: Some chefs who trained in France do not work the night shift at Bistro Nova.

questions.explanation:
Some France-trained chefs also trained in Italy, and no Italy-trained chef works the night shift at Bistro Nova. So those France-trained chefs don't.
A — The France-and-Italy chefs might not work at Bistro Nova.
B — Reverses the first statement.
C — Chefs without Italian training might.
D — Contradicts the first statement.

questions.stimulus: A survey found that 80 percent of people who use a fitness tracker say it motivates them to exercise more. However, people with trackers exercised about the same number of hours per week as people without them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Fitness trackers reduce exercise.
choices.B: Tracker users' reports of increased motivation did not correspond to more exercise time compared with non-users.
choices.C: Most people own fitness trackers.
choices.D: People without trackers are more motivated.
choices.E: Fitness trackers are useless.

questions.explanation:
Users report motivation, but their exercise hours match non-users'.
A — Exercise was about the same.
C — Not stated.
D — Not shown.
E — Too strong.

questions.stimulus: Drinking enough water is important for health. It helps regulate body temperature, keeps joints lubricated, and aids digestion.
questions.stem: The main conclusion is that

choices.A: people drink too little water
choices.B: water is better than other drinks
choices.C: drinking enough water is important for health
choices.D: water aids digestion
choices.E: water regulates body temperature

questions.explanation:
The first sentence is supported by the list that follows.
A — Not stated.
B — Not stated.
D — Support.
E — Support.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Opponents argue that raising the gas tax would hurt low-income drivers. But the revenue could fund public transit, which low-income residents use disproportionately, and rebates could offset the cost for those who must drive. Properly designed, a gas tax increase need not burden low-income residents.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the columnist's argument?

choices.A: Rebates could offset the cost for drivers.
choices.B: Raising the gas tax would hurt low-income drivers.
choices.C: Low-income residents use public transit disproportionately.
choices.D: The gas tax should be eliminated.
choices.E: A well-designed gas tax increase does not have to place a burden on low-income residents.

questions.explanation:
The last sentence is the conclusion; the transit and rebate points support it.
A — A premise.
B — The opponents' claim.
C — A premise.
D — Not claimed.

questions.stimulus: Some say that cats are aloof and don't form attachments to their owners. However, a recent study found that cats show signs of distress when separated from their owners, similar to dogs and infants. Cats, therefore, do form attachments.
questions.stem: The study described plays which role in the argument?

choices.A: It is the conclusion.
choices.B: It is the view the argument rejects.
choices.C: It is evidence for the argument's conclusion.
choices.D: It is a concession.
choices.E: It undermines the conclusion.

questions.explanation:
It supports the claim that cats form attachments.
A — The conclusion is that cats form attachments.
B — The rejected view is that cats are aloof.
D — It isn't conceded.
E — It supports it.

questions.stimulus: Advocate: Opponents claim that the proposed wind farm would harm bird populations. But studies show that far more birds are killed each year by buildings and house cats than by wind turbines. If we accepted the opponents' reasoning, we would have to ban buildings and pet cats.
questions.stem: The advocate's argument proceeds by

choices.A: suggesting that the opponents' reasoning, if applied consistently, would lead to unacceptable conclusions
choices.B: arguing that wind energy is cheaper
choices.C: questioning the opponents' motives
choices.D: providing evidence that birds are not endangered
choices.E: denying that wind turbines kill any birds

questions.explanation:
The advocate extends the opponents' logic to buildings and cats.
B — Not argued.
C — Not done.
D — Not provided.
E — The advocate doesn't deny it.

questions.stimulus:
Kara: Our office should switch to a four-day workweek. Employees would be happier and just as productive.
Leon: Employees might be happier, but clients expect us to be available five days a week. A four-day week would hurt our business.
questions.stem: Kara and Leon disagree over whether

choices.A: productivity matters
choices.B: the office should switch to a four-day workweek
choices.C: clients expect five-day availability
choices.D: the office should hire more staff
choices.E: employees would be happier

questions.explanation:
Kara favors it; Leon argues it would hurt the business.
A — Not in dispute.
C — Kara doesn't address this.
D — Not discussed.
E — Leon allows they might be.

questions.stimulus:
Nadia: The proposed highway will reduce commute times, but it will destroy wetlands that protect the region from flooding. The costs outweigh the benefits.
Omar: The highway will destroy some wetlands, yes. But the engineers plan to create new wetlands nearby, and shorter commutes will benefit thousands.
questions.stem: Nadia and Omar are committed to agreeing that

choices.A: the wetlands protect the region from flooding
choices.B: new wetlands will be created
choices.C: the highway should be built
choices.D: the proposed highway would destroy some wetlands
choices.E: the costs of the highway outweigh its benefits

questions.explanation:
Nadia says it will destroy wetlands; Omar concedes "yes."
A — Only Nadia says this.
B — Only Omar says this.
C — They disagree.
E — Omar disagrees.

questions.stimulus: Some of the paintings in the exhibit are by Monet. All of Monet's paintings are valuable. So some of the paintings in the exhibit are valuable.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: Some of the books on the shelf are by Austen. All of Austen's books are classics. So some of the books on the shelf are classics.
choices.B: Some of the books on the shelf are classics. All classics are old. So all books on the shelf are old.
choices.C: All of the books on the shelf are by Austen. Some of Austen's books are classics. So some books on the shelf are classics.
choices.D: All of Austen's books are classics. This book is a classic. So it is by Austen.
choices.E: No books on the shelf are by Austen. So none are classics.

questions.explanation:
Some A are B; all B are C; so some A are C.
B — Overgeneralizes.
C — All A are B; some B are C; so some A are C. Invalid.
D — Affirms the consequent.
E — Denies the antecedent.

questions.stimulus: The new policy will either increase sales or reduce costs. It did not increase sales. So it must have reduced costs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: If the plant gets sun, it will grow. It got sun. So it grew.
choices.B: The plant produced flowers. So it got enough water.
choices.C: The plant grew taller and produced flowers. So it is healthy.
choices.D: Most plants grow taller in summer. So this one will.
choices.E: The plant will either grow taller or produce flowers. It did not grow taller. So it must have produced flowers.

questions.explanation:
Both assume the two options are the only possible outcomes (a false dichotomy), then eliminate one.
A — Valid.
B — A different leap.
C — A different structure.
D — Probabilistic.

questions.stimulus: Principle: Employees may work from home on Fridays if they have completed all their assigned tasks for the week.
questions.stem: Which one of the following conforms to the principle?

choices.A: Uma worked from home on Friday even though she had unfinished tasks.
choices.B: Tia worked from home on Friday because she had completed all her assigned tasks for the week.
choices.C: Wes worked from home on Friday because his manager was away.
choices.D: Vic worked from home on Monday because he finished his tasks early.
choices.E: Xia stayed in the office on Friday because she enjoys it.

questions.explanation:
The condition was met, so working from home is allowed.
A — The condition isn't met.
C — Not the condition.
D — The principle covers Fridays.
E — Not addressed.

questions.stimulus: Neighbor: The Smiths should trim their tree. Its branches hang over our yard and drop leaves into our pool.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the neighbor's position?

choices.A: Pools should be covered.
choices.B: Trees should never be cut.
choices.C: Neighbors should share yard work.
choices.D: Property owners should prevent their trees from causing problems on neighboring properties.
choices.E: Leaves are good for gardens.

questions.explanation:
The tree causes problems next door, so the Smiths should trim it.
A — Not the reasoning.
B — Opposes the neighbor.
C — Not the reasoning.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: After a company introduced a policy allowing unlimited paid vacation, employees took fewer vacation days on average than under the old policy of fifteen days per year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: The company's revenue increased.
choices.B: Some employees took more vacation than before.
choices.C: Without a fixed allowance, many employees were unsure how much vacation was acceptable and took less to avoid seeming uncommitted.
choices.D: Vacation improves productivity.
choices.E: The old policy allowed unused days to roll over.

questions.explanation:
Uncertainty about norms made people cautious, so they took fewer days.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Doesn't explain the lower average.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Might explain something, but not directly why people took fewer days.

questions.stimulus: A city found that neighborhoods with more streetlights have fewer burglaries. Officials propose adding streetlights to high-burglary areas to reduce crime.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the proposal?

choices.A: what type of bulbs the streetlights use
choices.B: whether residents like streetlights
choices.C: whether burglaries happen mostly at night
choices.D: whether neighborhoods with more streetlights also differ in other ways, such as income or police presence, that could affect burglary rates
choices.E: how much streetlights cost to install

questions.explanation:
If other differences explain the burglary gap, adding lights may not help.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Somewhat relevant to mechanism, but the confound question is more fundamental.
E — Cost isn't effectiveness.

questions.stimulus: My grandmother ate bacon every day and lived to be 100. So bacon isn't bad for your health.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: relies on an unqualified expert
choices.B: confuses cause and effect
choices.C: draws a general conclusion from one person's experience
choices.D: assumes all foods are healthy
choices.E: ignores the cost of bacon

questions.explanation:
One long-lived grandmother doesn't show bacon is harmless for people in general.
A — No expert.
B — No causal reversal.
D — Not assumed.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The film's special effects are not as impressive as those in last year's blockbuster. Therefore, the film is a failure.
questions.stem: The critic's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: relies on box office data
choices.B: judges the film's overall success on a single aspect compared with a single other film
choices.C: attacks the film's director
choices.D: assumes special effects are unimportant
choices.E: confuses popularity with quality

questions.explanation:
Weaker effects than one blockbuster don't make the whole film a failure.
A — No data.
C — No attack.
D — The critic treats them as decisive.
E — Not discussed.

questions.stimulus: Military analyst: Returning bombers in the war showed bullet holes concentrated on the wings and tail, with few on the engines. Therefore, armor should be added to the wings and tail, where the planes are most often hit.
questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on too small a sample of bombers
choices.B: confuses a correlation with a cause
choices.C: fails to consider the cost of armor
choices.D: assumes that bullet holes are evenly distributed
choices.E: fails to consider that planes hit in the engines may not have returned at all, so the sample excludes the most damaging hits

questions.explanation:
Only surviving planes were examined. Few engine hits among survivors suggests engine hits were fatal, so the engines may need armor most.
A — Size isn't the main problem; selection is.
B — Not the issue.
C — A practical concern, not the logical flaw.
D — The argument notes they are concentrated.

questions.stimulus: To reduce food waste, a school cafeteria plans to let students choose their own portion sizes instead of serving fixed portions.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Students will tend to choose portions closer to what they will actually eat than the fixed portions were.
choices.B: Fixed portions were too small.
choices.C: Students prefer pizza to vegetables.
choices.D: Every student will finish their food.
choices.E: The cafeteria will save money.

questions.explanation:
Choice reduces waste only if students pick amounts that better match what they eat.
B — If too small, choice could increase waste.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The sudden appearance of iron tools in the Kalen region around 800 BCE shows that the Kalen people learned ironworking from their neighbors to the east, who had used iron for centuries.
questions.stem: The historian's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Every Kalen village used iron tools.
choices.B: The eastern neighbors traded with many regions.
choices.C: The eastern neighbors conquered the Kalen.
choices.D: The Kalen people did not independently develop ironworking techniques around that time.
choices.E: Iron tools are superior to bronze tools.

questions.explanation:
If they invented it themselves, the tools wouldn't show learning from neighbors.
A — Not required.
B — Helpful, but not required.
C — Not required.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Every student in the honors program must complete a thesis. So Mila must complete a thesis.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Every student who completes a thesis is in the honors program.
choices.B: Mila is a student in the honors program.
choices.C: Mila has a high GPA.
choices.D: Mila enjoys writing.
choices.E: Some honors students write long theses.

questions.explanation:
Honors student → thesis.
A — Reverses the statement.
C — Doesn't establish she's in the program.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A gym found that members who attended group fitness classes renewed their memberships at higher rates. The gym concludes that classes increase renewals.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the gym's conclusion?

choices.A: Members who started attending classes became more likely to renew than they had been before attending.
choices.B: Class attendees tend to live closer to the gym.
choices.C: Many members prefer working out alone.
choices.D: Classes are included in the membership fee.
choices.E: Some class attendees did not renew.

questions.explanation:
A change in the same members after they started classes supports causation.
B — A confound.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Exceptions don't undercut the trend.

questions.stimulus: Climatologist: The unusually warm winter in the region was caused by a shift in ocean currents, which brought warmer water closer to the coast.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the climatologist's explanation?

choices.A: Snowfall in the region was below average.
choices.B: Ocean currents shift every few decades.
choices.C: Coastal areas warmed much more than inland areas of the region during the winter.
choices.D: Winters have been getting warmer globally.
choices.E: The region's summer was also warm.

questions.explanation:
If warm water drove the change, coastal areas should warm most. That pattern fits.
A — Consistent with warmth but not with the cause.
B — Background, not support for this case.
D — An alternative, broader explanation.
E — Doesn't link specifically to currents.

questions.stimulus: A city reports that since it installed red-light cameras, the number of drivers running red lights has fallen by half. Officials conclude the cameras have made intersections safer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the officials' conclusion?

choices.A: The cameras were expensive.
choices.B: Some drivers still run red lights.
choices.C: The cameras generate revenue.
choices.D: Other cities use red-light cameras.
choices.E: Since the cameras were installed, rear-end collisions at those intersections have tripled as drivers brake suddenly.

questions.explanation:
Safety depends on accidents. A sharp rise in rear-end crashes cuts against the claim of safer intersections.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Doesn't undercut the overall improvement.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Sociologist: Over the past decade, neighborhoods where new coffee shops opened experienced rising property values. Therefore, coffee shops drive up property values in the neighborhoods where they open.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the sociologist's argument?

choices.A: Coffee prices have increased.
choices.B: Some coffee shops closed within a year.
choices.C: Property values rose in most neighborhoods during the decade.
choices.D: Coffee shops are popular with young professionals.
choices.E: Coffee shop chains use market research to open new locations in neighborhoods where property values are already beginning to rise.

questions.explanation:
If chains choose neighborhoods that are already appreciating, the coffee shops follow rising values rather than causing them.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Irrelevant.
C — A general rise matters, but the specific selection explanation is stronger.
D — Could suggest a mechanism either way.

questions.stimulus: Every car in the parking garage has a permit. Some cars in the parking garage are electric.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: All electric cars are in the garage.
choices.B: Some electric cars have a permit.
choices.C: No electric cars are outside the garage.
choices.D: All cars with permits are electric.
choices.E: Some cars in the garage don't have permits.

questions.explanation:
Some garage cars are electric, and all garage cars have permits.
A — Not stated.
C — Not stated.
D — Not stated.
E — All do.

questions.stimulus: A library found that when it lengthened its loan period from two weeks to three, the number of overdue books dropped, but the number of books checked out stayed the same.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: The library's collection grew.
choices.B: The library should eliminate due dates.
choices.C: Patrons read faster now.
choices.D: The longer loan period did not reduce the number of checkouts.
choices.E: Most books are returned late.

questions.explanation:
Checkouts stayed the same.
A — Not stated.
B — A recommendation.
C — Not shown.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: An ecologist observed that in ponds with many frogs, mosquito larvae were scarce. In ponds without frogs, mosquito larvae were abundant. Frogs are known to eat mosquito larvae, but so do several species of fish found in most of the ponds without frogs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The fish that eat mosquito larvae do not by themselves keep larvae as scarce as they are in ponds with many frogs.
choices.B: Ponds with frogs have no fish.
choices.C: Mosquito larvae avoid ponds with frogs.
choices.D: Fish eat frogs.
choices.E: Frogs eat more mosquito larvae than fish do in every pond.

questions.explanation:
Most frog-free ponds had larva-eating fish, yet larvae were abundant there. So fish alone don't produce the scarcity seen with frogs.
B — Not stated.
C — A possible explanation, not supported.
D — Not stated.
E — Too strong.

questions.stimulus: Some people avoid flu shots because they think the shot can give them the flu. But flu shots contain inactivated virus that cannot cause infection. Mild symptoms some people experience afterward are the immune system's normal response. Fear of getting the flu from the shot is unfounded.
questions.stem: The main conclusion is that

choices.A: flu shots contain inactivated virus
choices.B: some people experience mild symptoms
choices.C: fear of getting the flu from a flu shot is unfounded
choices.D: some people avoid flu shots
choices.E: everyone should get a flu shot

questions.explanation:
The last sentence is the conclusion.
A — A premise.
B — A premise.
D — Background.
E — Not claimed.

questions.stimulus: Some believe that the Great Pyramids were built by slaves. However, archaeologists have found evidence that the builders were paid laborers who lived in nearby villages. So the belief is likely mistaken.
questions.stem: The evidence found by archaeologists plays which role in the argument?

choices.A: It supports the conclusion that the belief is likely mistaken.
choices.B: It is irrelevant.
choices.C: It is the belief the argument rejects.
choices.D: It is the conclusion.
choices.E: It is a concession.

questions.explanation:
It's the reason for doubting the slave-labor belief.
B — It's central.
C — The rejected belief is slave labor.
D — The conclusion is that the belief is mistaken.
E — It isn't conceded.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Some argue that raising tariffs will protect domestic jobs. In the short run, that may be true for protected industries. But tariffs raise prices for consumers and for businesses that use imported materials, reducing employment in those sectors. Over time, tariffs typically cost more jobs than they save.
questions.stem: The claim that tariffs may protect jobs in the short run for protected industries plays which role in the argument?

choices.A: It is evidence that tariffs raise prices.
choices.B: It is the main conclusion.
choices.C: It is a limited concession that the economist outweighs with other considerations.
choices.D: It is a claim the economist argues is false.
choices.E: It is a premise directly supporting the conclusion.

questions.explanation:
"That may be true" concedes a short-run benefit, which the economist then argues is outweighed.
A — Unrelated.
B — The conclusion is that tariffs cost more jobs than they save.
D — The economist grants it might be true in the short run.
E — It cuts the other way.

questions.stimulus:
Alma: Coffee is bad for you because it has caffeine.
Ben: Tea and chocolate also have caffeine, and you don't call those bad. So caffeine alone can't make coffee bad.
questions.stem: Ben responds to Alma by

choices.A: attacking Alma's character
choices.B: providing evidence that coffee is healthy
choices.C: agreeing with Alma
choices.D: pointing out that her reason would apply to things she doesn't consider bad
choices.E: denying that coffee has caffeine

questions.explanation:
Ben shows "has caffeine → bad" would condemn tea and chocolate, which Alma doesn't.
A — Not done.
B — Not provided.
C — He disagrees.
E — Not denied.

questions.stimulus:
Rosa: The new law requiring helmets for all cyclists will reduce head injuries.
Sam: Helmets do reduce head injuries for those who wear them. But the law will discourage many people from cycling, and cyclists in cities with fewer riders face more danger from cars. Overall, the law may not reduce head injuries.
questions.stem: Rosa and Sam disagree over whether

choices.A: cycling is healthy
choices.B: cars are dangerous to cyclists
choices.C: the law will discourage cycling
choices.D: helmets reduce head injuries for those who wear them
choices.E: the helmet law will reduce head injuries overall

questions.explanation:
Rosa says it will; Sam says it may not, overall.
A — Not discussed.
B — Rosa doesn't address this.
C — Rosa doesn't address this.
D — Sam agrees.

questions.stimulus: Whenever it rains, the outdoor market closes. The outdoor market is open today. So it is not raining today.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: The power went out yesterday. So it will go out today.
choices.B: Whenever the power goes out, the elevator stops. The elevator is running. So the power is not out.
choices.C: Whenever the power goes out, the elevator stops. The elevator stopped. So the power went out.
choices.D: Whenever the power goes out, the elevator stops. The power is on. So the elevator is running.
choices.E: The elevator usually runs. So the power is on.

questions.explanation:
If A then B; not B; so not A.
A — A non sequitur.
C — Affirms the consequent.
D — Denies the antecedent.
E — Probabilistic.

questions.stimulus: Most people who buy luxury cars are wealthy. Ines bought a luxury car. So Ines must be wealthy.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: All people who run marathons are fit. Jo ran a marathon. So Jo is fit.
choices.B: Jo is fit. So all marathon runners are fit.
choices.C: Most people who run marathons are fit. Jo is fit. So Jo ran a marathon.
choices.D: Most people who run marathons are fit. Jo ran a marathon. So Jo is probably fit.
choices.E: Most people who run marathons are fit. Jo ran a marathon. So Jo must be fit.

questions.explanation:
Both move from "most" to a certain claim about one individual.
A — Valid with "all."
B — A different flaw.
C — A different flaw (reversal).
D — Hedged and reasonable.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A teacher should allow a student to submit an assignment late only if the student requested an extension before the due date.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: Ms. Lee should accept Pia's late assignment because Pia is a strong student.
choices.B: Ms. Lee must accept Quinn's late assignment because he asked for an extension before the due date.
choices.C: Ms. Lee should not accept Omar's late assignment, since he did not ask for an extension until after the due date.
choices.D: Ms. Lee should accept all late assignments.
choices.E: Ms. Lee should not accept any assignment early.

questions.explanation:
He didn't request in time, so late submission isn't allowed.
A — Not a condition.
B — The principle states a necessary condition, not a guarantee.
D — Contradicts the principle.
E — Not addressed.

questions.stimulus: Resident: The city should not cut down the old oak tree to widen the road. The tree is over 200 years old, and the road could be widened on the other side instead.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the resident's position?

choices.A: Roads should never be widened.
choices.B: Old trees are dangerous.
choices.C: Residents should vote on road projects.
choices.D: A historic natural feature should not be destroyed if the goal can be achieved another way.
choices.E: The city should plant more trees.

questions.explanation:
The tree is historic, and the road can be widened elsewhere.
A — Too broad.
B — Would favor cutting.
C — Not the reasoning.
E — Not the reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: It was wrong for the company to fire Lena for posting criticism of its environmental practices on her personal social media account. Her posts were accurate, did not reveal confidential information, and addressed a matter of public concern.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's judgment?

choices.A: An employer should not punish an employee for accurate public statements about matters of public concern that disclose no confidential information.
choices.B: Companies should improve their environmental practices.
choices.C: Social media should be regulated.
choices.D: An employee's personal social media account should never be monitored.
choices.E: Employees should never criticize their employers publicly.

questions.explanation:
All three facts (accurate, no confidential info, public concern) match the principle's conditions.
B — Not about firing.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Doesn't address punishing the employee for the content.
E — Would favor the company.

questions.stimulus: After a store began offering free gift wrapping, its sales during the holiday season fell compared with the previous year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: Gift wrapping is popular.
choices.B: A large competitor opened nearby just before the holiday season and drew away many customers.
choices.C: The store hired more staff.
choices.D: Some customers didn't use the gift wrapping.
choices.E: The store's prices stayed the same.

questions.explanation:
A new competitor explains the drop despite the added service.
A — Would predict higher sales.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Doesn't explain falling sales.
E — Doesn't explain the drop.

questions.stimulus: In the town of Kelso, the number of people diagnosed with seasonal allergies has risen sharply over the past decade. Yet pollen counts in Kelso have not increased, and air quality has improved.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how all of these facts can be true?

choices.A: Air pollution can worsen allergy symptoms.
choices.B: Pollen counts in neighboring towns have increased.
choices.C: Kelso's population has declined.
choices.D: Allergies can be treated with medication.
choices.E: A new clinic in Kelso began routinely screening patients for allergies, identifying many mild cases that previously went undiagnosed.

questions.explanation:
More screening finds more cases. Diagnoses can rise without any change in pollen or air.
A — Air improved, which deepens the puzzle.
B — Kelso's own counts didn't rise.
C — Would tend to reduce diagnoses.
D — Irrelevant to diagnosis rates.

questions.stimulus: If the store is open, the lights are on. The lights are off.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: If the lights are on, the store is open.
choices.B: The store is not open.
choices.C: The lights are broken.
choices.D: The store will open soon.
choices.E: The store is open.

questions.explanation:
Open → lights on. Lights off → not open.
A — Reverses the conditional.
C — Not stated.
D — Not stated.
E — Contradicts the conditional.

questions.stimulus: The proposed factory would create 500 jobs. Anyone who opposes it must not care about the struggling families in our town. So the factory should be approved.
questions.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: characterizes opponents unfavorably instead of addressing possible reasons to oppose the factory
choices.B: confuses a cause with an effect
choices.C: relies on an expert's opinion
choices.D: assumes 500 jobs is a small number
choices.E: fails to define "struggling families"

questions.explanation:
Opponents might care about families and still have good reasons, like pollution. The argument smears them instead of engaging.
B — No causal reversal.
C — No expert.
D — Not assumed.
E — Not the flaw.

questions.stimulus: Statistician: The average family in Brookdale has 2.3 children. Since no family can have 0.3 of a child, the statistic must be wrong.
questions.stem: The statistician's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: confuses a cause with an effect
choices.B: assumes all families are the same size
choices.C: fails to consider families without children
choices.D: treats a property of a group average as if it had to describe an actual individual family
choices.E: relies on outdated census data

questions.explanation:
An average can be a fraction even though every family has a whole number of children.
A — No causal claim.
B — Close, but the real error is expecting the average to be a possible family size.
C — Families with no children are included in the average; that isn't the flaw.
E — No data issue.

questions.stimulus: A movie theater plans to attract more customers by installing reclining seats, even though it will reduce the number of seats in each auditorium.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Most customers watch action films.
choices.B: Every customer prefers reclining seats.
choices.C: The increase in customers drawn by reclining seats will not be prevented by the reduced number of seats.
choices.D: Other theaters don't have reclining seats.
choices.E: Reclining seats are expensive.

questions.explanation:
If shows sell out with fewer seats, the theater can't serve more customers no matter how attractive the seats are.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
D — Helpful but not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Neuroscientist: Patients with damage to a particular brain region cannot recognize faces, though they can recognize other objects normally. Thus this brain region is specialized for face recognition.
questions.stem: The neuroscientist's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Face recognition is the most important visual skill.
choices.B: Every patient with damage to this region was tested.
choices.C: The patients' difficulty with faces does not result simply from faces being harder to distinguish than the other objects tested.
choices.D: The patients' vision is otherwise perfect.
choices.E: The brain region has no other functions.

questions.explanation:
If faces are just harder, damage might impair only the most difficult task, not show specialization for faces.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Not required.
D — Too strong; they need only see well enough to recognize objects.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Anyone who arrives after the doors close will not be admitted. So Leo will not be admitted.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Leo will arrive after the doors close.
choices.B: The doors close at 8 p.m.
choices.C: Leo is often late.
choices.D: Leo has a ticket.
choices.E: Everyone admitted arrived before the doors closed.

questions.explanation:
Arrive after close → not admitted.
B — Doesn't say when Leo arrives.
C — "Often" doesn't guarantee he'll be late this time.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Restates the premise.

questions.stimulus: A proposal can be voted on at the meeting only if it was submitted a week in advance. The parking proposal was not voted on at the meeting. So the parking proposal was not submitted a week in advance.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The meeting ran out of time.
choices.B: Every proposal submitted a week in advance was voted on at the meeting.
choices.C: Some proposals submitted in advance were not voted on.
choices.D: The parking proposal was controversial.
choices.E: Every proposal voted on at the meeting was submitted a week in advance.

questions.explanation:
Premise: voted → submitted. Conclusion needs: not voted → not submitted, that is, submitted → voted. That's the assumption.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Would undermine the conclusion.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Restates the premise (voted → submitted); doesn't give the needed direction.

questions.stimulus: Researchers found that students who listen to classical music while studying score higher on tests. They conclude that classical music improves learning.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Students like classical music.
choices.B: Some students find music distracting.
choices.C: Students who listen to classical music tend to come from families that value education.
choices.D: Classical music is popular among older adults.
choices.E: Students randomly assigned to study with classical music scored higher than those randomly assigned to study in silence.

questions.explanation:
Random assignment supports causation.
A — Liking isn't effect.
B — Suggests music may not help.
C — A confound.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The decline in literacy in the region after 600 CE was caused by the collapse of the urban schools that had trained scribes, which followed the abandonment of the region's cities.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's explanation?

choices.A: The urban schools taught mathematics as well.
choices.B: Literacy declined in other regions too.
choices.C: Writing materials became scarce after 600 CE.
choices.D: In the few cities of the region that remained occupied and kept their schools, literacy did not decline.
choices.E: Scribes were highly paid.

questions.explanation:
Where schools survived, literacy held. That isolates the schools as the key factor.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Suggests broader causes.
C — An alternative cause.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A study found that people who drink red wine moderately have lower rates of heart disease. So drinking red wine reduces the risk of heart disease.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.A: Some wine drinkers have heart disease.
choices.B: Heavy drinking increases heart disease.
choices.C: Red wine is more expensive than beer.
choices.D: Moderate red wine drinkers tend to have higher incomes and better access to health care.
choices.E: Red wine contains antioxidants.

questions.explanation:
Income and health care offer an alternative explanation.
A — Exceptions don't undercut the trend.
B — Doesn't bear on moderate drinking.
C — Irrelevant.
E — A possible mechanism.

questions.stimulus: Since the company introduced an employee wellness program, the number of sick days taken has decreased by 20 percent. The company concludes that the wellness program has improved employee health.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the company's conclusion?

choices.A: At the same time, the company began requiring a doctor's note for any sick day, discouraging employees from taking them.
choices.B: The wellness program includes exercise classes.
choices.C: The program costs the company money.
choices.D: Some employees didn't join the program.
choices.E: Employees enjoy the wellness program.

questions.explanation:
Fewer sick days may reflect the new hassle, not better health.
B — A possible mechanism.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Doesn't explain the overall drop.
E — Enjoyment isn't health.

questions.stimulus: Every student who passed the final exam passed the course. Maya passed the final exam.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Maya studied hard.
choices.B: Maya passed the course.
choices.C: Everyone who passed the course passed the final.
choices.D: The final was difficult.
choices.E: Maya got an A.

questions.explanation:
Passed the final → passed the course.
A — Not stated.
C — Reverses the statement.
D — Not stated.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: At Corbin College, every student who majors in physics takes calculus. No student who takes calculus is exempt from the math placement test. Some students who are exempt from the math placement test major in chemistry.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Every chemistry major is exempt from the placement test.
choices.B: Some physics majors are exempt from the placement test.
choices.C: Some chemistry majors at Corbin College do not take calculus.
choices.D: No physics major is a chemistry major.
choices.E: Every student who takes calculus majors in physics.

questions.explanation:
Some exempt students major in chemistry. Exempt students don't take calculus (contrapositive of the second statement). So those chemistry majors don't take calculus.
A — Only some are.
B — Physics majors take calculus, so they aren't exempt.
D — Possible, but not established. A physics major could also major in chemistry and simply not be exempt.
E — Reverses the first statement.

questions.stimulus: When a cafeteria moved its salad bar to the front of the line and placed desserts at the end, salad sales rose by 40 percent and dessert sales fell by 15 percent.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Desserts are unhealthy.
choices.B: All cafeterias should move salads to the front.
choices.C: Salad prices fell.
choices.D: People prefer salad to dessert.
choices.E: The placement of food items in the cafeteria line influenced what people chose.

questions.explanation:
Moving items changed sales of both items.
A — Not stated.
B — A recommendation.
C — Not stated.
D — Not shown.

questions.stimulus: Although many consider texting to be ruining young people's writing skills, research suggests otherwise. Students who text frequently perform as well on formal writing assessments as those who text rarely, and some studies find that texting builds awareness of how language works.
questions.stem: The main conclusion is that

choices.A: texting builds awareness of language
choices.B: texting does not appear to harm young people's writing skills
choices.C: formal writing assessments are unreliable
choices.D: young people should text more
choices.E: many consider texting harmful

questions.explanation:
"Research suggests otherwise" is the conclusion, supported by the studies.
A — Support.
C — Not claimed.
D — Not claimed.
E — Background.

questions.stimulus: Some argue that zoos are cruel because animals are confined. However, modern zoos fund conservation programs that have saved several species from extinction. So zoos can serve an important purpose.
questions.stem: The claim that zoos fund conservation programs plays which role?

choices.A: It is the conclusion.
choices.B: It is a concession.
choices.C: It undermines the conclusion.
choices.D: It supports the conclusion that zoos can serve an important purpose.
choices.E: It is the view the argument rejects.

questions.explanation:
It's the evidence for zoos' value.
A — The conclusion is the last sentence.
B — It isn't conceded.
C — It supports it.
E — The rejected view is that zoos are cruel.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: Some argue that because we cannot be certain that other people have minds, we have no reason to believe they do. But we cannot be certain of anything beyond our own immediate experience, including that the sun will rise tomorrow. Yet we clearly have reason to believe the sun will rise. So the lack of certainty does not show we lack reason for belief.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument proceeds by

choices.A: providing evidence that other people have minds
choices.B: appealing to the authority of science
choices.C: questioning whether certainty is possible
choices.D: arguing that the sun's rising is certain
choices.E: showing that a principle implicit in the opposing argument would lead to an absurd conclusion in another case

questions.explanation:
The opposing principle: no certainty → no reason. The philosopher shows it would deny reason to believe the sun will rise, which is absurd.
A — No such evidence is offered.
B — No authority is invoked.
C — The philosopher accepts limits on certainty; the move is about what follows.
D — The philosopher says it isn't certain.

questions.stimulus:
Tom: The new library should be built downtown, where most people work.
Uma: Most people work downtown, but families with children live in the suburbs and need easy library access. The library should be built in the suburbs.
questions.stem: Tom and Uma disagree over whether

choices.A: families need library access
choices.B: suburbs are growing
choices.C: the new library should be built downtown
choices.D: the library should be large
choices.E: most people work downtown

questions.explanation:
Tom says downtown; Uma says the suburbs.
A — Tom doesn't address this.
B — Not discussed.
D — Not discussed.
E — Uma agrees.

questions.stimulus:
Vera: The new phone is too expensive for what it offers, though its design is beautiful.
Will: The design is beautiful, and the price is fair given the features.
questions.stem: Vera and Will agree that

choices.A: the new phone's design is beautiful
choices.B: the price is fair
choices.C: the features are excellent
choices.D: they would buy the phone
choices.E: the phone is too expensive

questions.explanation:
Both say so.
B — Vera disagrees.
C — Only Will implies this.
D — Not discussed.
E — Will thinks the price is fair.

questions.stimulus: All squares are rectangles. All rectangles have four sides. So all squares have four sides.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: All poodles are dogs. Some dogs are small. So some poodles are small.
choices.B: All poodles are mammals. All dogs are mammals. So all poodles are dogs.
choices.C: All poodles are dogs. All dogs are mammals. So all poodles are mammals.
choices.D: Some poodles are white. So all dogs are white.
choices.E: All dogs are mammals. All cats are mammals. So all dogs are cats.

questions.explanation:
All A are B; all B are C; so all A are C.
A — Invalid.
B — Invalid: sharing a category doesn't make one group part of the other.
D — Invalid.
E — Invalid.

questions.stimulus: If you study hard, you'll pass the exam. You didn't study hard. So you won't pass.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: If it's sunny, we'll go to the beach. We went. So it was sunny.
choices.B: It's often sunny in July. So we'll go to the beach.
choices.C: If it's sunny, we'll go to the beach. It's sunny. So we'll go.
choices.D: If it's sunny, we'll go to the beach. We didn't go. So it wasn't sunny.
choices.E: If it's sunny, we'll go to the beach. It's not sunny. So we won't go to the beach.

questions.explanation:
Both deny the antecedent.
A — Affirms the consequent, a different flaw.
B — A different form.
C — Valid.
D — Valid.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A city should fund a public art project only if the project is accessible to the public free of charge and was selected through an open competition.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: The city should not fund the mural, since although it is free to view, the artist was chosen privately by the mayor without a competition.
choices.B: The city should fund art only in parks.
choices.C: The city should fund the museum exhibit, which charges admission, because it was chosen by competition.
choices.D: The city must fund every project chosen by open competition.
choices.E: The city should fund the sculpture because it is free to view.

questions.explanation:
No open competition, so no funding.
B — Location isn't a condition.
C — It isn't free.
D — The conditions are necessary, not sufficient.
E — The competition condition is unknown or unmet.

questions.stimulus: Doctor: I should not prescribe antibiotics to Mr. Hale for his cold. Although he insists on them, colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not affect, and unnecessary antibiotic use contributes to drug-resistant bacteria.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the doctor's position?

choices.A: Antibiotics should never be prescribed.
choices.B: A doctor should not prescribe a treatment that will not help the patient and could contribute to broader harm, even if the patient requests it.
choices.C: Doctors should always follow patients' wishes.
choices.D: Doctors should prescribe whatever is cheapest.
choices.E: Patients should research their illnesses.

questions.explanation:
Ineffective treatment, broader harm, patient request. The principle covers all three.
A — Too broad.
C — Would favor prescribing.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A town's swimming pool lowered its admission price, but the number of swimmers decreased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: Swimming is good exercise.
choices.B: Other pools raised prices.
choices.C: The pool advertised the price cut.
choices.D: The summer was unusually cool and rainy.
choices.E: The pool added new lifeguards.

questions.explanation:
Bad weather would keep swimmers away despite lower prices.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Would push swimmers here.
C — Would predict more swimmers.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the number of physicians per capita in the country of Arvel has increased by 25 percent. Yet the average wait time for a doctor's appointment has also increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: Patients prefer specialists.
choices.B: Medical schools in Arvel have expanded.
choices.C: Some physicians work part time.
choices.D: The aging of Arvel's population has greatly increased the number of appointments needed per person.
choices.E: Physicians in Arvel are well paid.

questions.explanation:
Demand grew faster than supply.
A — Could matter, but doesn't explain the overall increase.
B — Consistent with more doctors, but doesn't explain longer waits.
C — A partial factor, not a clear explanation of the trend.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Since a city began offering free bus service, ridership has increased by 50 percent. The mayor claims the program has reduced car traffic.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the mayor's claim?

choices.A: how many bus routes exist
choices.B: how much the program costs
choices.C: whether other cities offer free buses
choices.D: whether buses are clean
choices.E: whether most new bus riders previously drove or previously walked or biked

questions.explanation:
If new riders came from walking or biking, car traffic wouldn't fall.
A — Doesn't test the claim.
B — Irrelevant to traffic.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Advertisement: Our herbal supplement is completely natural, made only from plants. Since natural products are good for you, our supplement is good for your health.
questions.stem: The advertisement's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that because something comes from nature, it must be beneficial
choices.B: confuses correlation with causation
choices.C: fails to list the plants used
choices.D: relies on an endorsement from a celebrity
choices.E: attacks competing products

questions.explanation:
Many natural substances, such as poisonous plants, are harmful. "Natural" doesn't mean healthy.
B — No data.
C — Not the core flaw.
D — No endorsement.
E — No attack.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Every film that won Best Picture in the past decade had a budget over $20 million. Therefore, a film with a budget under $20 million cannot win Best Picture.
questions.stem: The critic's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one
choices.B: treats a pattern observed in a limited period as a rule that holds without exception
choices.C: relies on the opinions of film critics
choices.D: fails to define "Best Picture"
choices.E: assumes that budget determines quality

questions.explanation:
Ten years of winners don't establish that low-budget films can't win. Earlier or future winners could differ.
A — The argument doesn't claim a high budget guarantees winning.
C — No opinions are cited.
D — Not relevant.
E — Related, but the argument's core move is overgeneralizing a pattern.
tags: inferring from part of a range

questions.stimulus: A city plans to reduce littering in its parks by doubling the fine for littering.
questions.stem: The plan depends on which one of the following assumptions?
