choices.A: The fines will fund park cleanup.
choices.B: Every litterer will be caught.
choices.C: People who litter are aware of, or will become aware of, the higher fine.
choices.D: The parks are clean now.
choices.E: Most litter is plastic.

questions.explanation:
A fine deters only if people know about it.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
D — The plan aims to reduce littering, so they aren't.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Linguist: The Tala language has no word for "blue," using the same word for blue and green. Yet Tala speakers distinguish blue from green objects as accurately as English speakers in sorting tasks. Therefore, lacking a word for a color does not prevent people from perceiving it as distinct.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.A: The sorting tasks were difficult.
choices.B: Every language has a word for green.
choices.C: Tala speakers learned English.
choices.D: English speakers perceive more colors than Tala speakers.
choices.E: Accurate sorting of blue and green objects in the tasks reflects perceiving the colors as distinct.

questions.explanation:
The evidence is about sorting; the conclusion is about perception. The argument needs sorting accuracy to indicate distinct perception.
A — Not required.
B — Not required.
C — Not required.
D — Not required.

questions.stimulus: No one who works the night shift can attend the morning training. Therefore, no one in the new-hire group works the night shift.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Everyone in the new-hire group will attend the morning training.
choices.B: Everyone who attends the morning training is a new hire.
choices.C: Some new hires work the day shift.
choices.D: The morning training is required for all employees.
choices.E: Night-shift workers are paid more than day-shift workers.

questions.explanation:
Night shift → can't attend. If every new hire attends, none of them can be on the night shift (contrapositive).
B — Gives attend → new hire, the wrong direction; new hires might not attend.
C — "Some" leaves room for others on the night shift.
D — A requirement isn't attendance; night-shift workers can't attend regardless.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Agronomist: The new irrigation system increased crop yields on the farms that adopted it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the agronomist's claim?

choices.A: Some farms that adopted the system had poor harvests.
choices.B: The irrigation system uses less water.
choices.C: Farms that adopted the system had yields similar to non-adopting farms before adoption, and only adopting farms saw yields rise afterward.
choices.D: Farms that adopted the system were larger.
choices.E: The weather was favorable last year.

questions.explanation:
Similar starting points plus divergence after adoption supports a causal effect.
A — Exceptions don't undercut the trend.
B — Not about yields.
D — A confound.
E — An alternative cause.

questions.stimulus: Economist: The sharp rise in housing prices in Kellport over the past five years was caused primarily by restrictive zoning laws that limited new construction.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's claim?

choices.A: Interest rates were low during the period.
choices.B: Many residents oppose new construction.
choices.C: Housing prices rose nationwide.
choices.D: In nearby cities with similar population growth but less restrictive zoning, housing prices rose far more slowly.
choices.E: Kellport's population grew rapidly.

questions.explanation:
Comparable growth with different zoning and different price outcomes points to zoning as the key factor.
A — An alternative cause.
B — Background on zoning, not evidence of its effect.
C — Suggests broader causes.
E — Demand could explain prices.

questions.stimulus: A study found that employees who work in offices with plants report higher job satisfaction. So adding plants to offices will increase employee satisfaction.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.A: Some employees are allergic to plants.
choices.B: Offices with plants tend to belong to companies that also offer higher salaries and better benefits.
choices.C: Many offices have plants.
choices.D: Plants improve air quality.
choices.E: Plants require watering.

questions.explanation:
Better pay and benefits could explain higher satisfaction.
A — Doesn't undercut the overall finding much.
C — Irrelevant.
D — A possible mechanism.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Songbird populations in Hollis County declined 30 percent after the county began spraying a new insecticide. Since the insecticide kills the insects these birds eat, the spraying caused the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the ornithologist's argument?

choices.A: Some songbird species increased in the county.
choices.B: Songbird populations declined by a similar amount over the same period in neighboring counties that did not use the insecticide.
choices.C: The insecticide is expensive.
choices.D: Songbirds eat seeds as well as insects.
choices.E: The insecticide is also used in other states.

questions.explanation:
If unsprayed counties saw the same decline, something other than the spraying is likely responsible.
A — Doesn't explain the overall decline.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Weakens a little, but doesn't explain the decline.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Every member of the orchestra plays a string instrument. No one who plays a string instrument plays the trumpet.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Every string player is in the orchestra.
choices.B: No trumpet player plays any instrument.
choices.C: No member of the orchestra plays the trumpet.
choices.D: Trumpet players are in a different orchestra.
choices.E: Some orchestra members play piano.

questions.explanation:
Member → string → not trumpet.
A — Reverses the statement.
B — Trumpet is an instrument.
D — Not stated.
E — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: When a city switched its streetlights from yellow sodium lamps to bright white LEDs, residents reported feeling safer at night, but the number of reported nighttime crimes did not change.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Residents' sense of safety changed without a corresponding change in reported nighttime crime.
choices.B: Crime was low before the switch.
choices.C: LEDs are cheaper to operate.
choices.D: White light prevents crime.
choices.E: Residents prefer yellow light.

questions.explanation:
That's what the data shows.
B — Not stated.
C — Not stated.
D — Reported crime didn't change.
E — They felt safer with white.

questions.stimulus: In a study, participants who were told a wine was expensive rated it as tasting better than participants who were told the same wine was cheap. Brain scans showed greater activity in pleasure-related regions among those told the wine was expensive.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Expensive wines taste better than cheap wines.
choices.B: Brain scans are unreliable.
choices.C: Most people cannot tell wines apart.
choices.D: People lie about wine preferences.
choices.E: Beliefs about a product's price can affect the pleasure people experience from it, not just what they report.

questions.explanation:
Ratings differed, and so did pleasure-related brain activity, for the same wine. Price beliefs affected experienced pleasure, not merely self-reports.
A — The wine was the same.
B — Not supported.
C — Not shown.
D — The brain scans suggest real experience.

questions.stimulus: Some people claim that video calls are just as good as meeting in person. But video calls miss subtle body language, are prone to technical problems, and make casual conversation awkward. Video calls, then, are not a full substitute for meeting in person.
questions.stem: The main conclusion is that

choices.A: video calls are prone to technical problems
choices.B: some people claim video calls are as good
choices.C: video calls miss body language
choices.D: video calls are not a full substitute for in-person meetings
choices.E: video calls should be banned

questions.explanation:
"Then" marks the conclusion.
A — A premise.
B — The opposing view.
C — A premise.
E — Not claimed.

questions.stimulus: Historian: It is often said that the printing press democratized knowledge. Yet for its first century, printed books were expensive, most people could not read, and printers focused on religious and legal texts for elite buyers. The press did eventually transform access to knowledge, but the popular account compresses a slow, uneven process into a sudden revolution.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the historian's argument?

choices.A: The printing press did not democratize knowledge.
choices.B: Most people could not read in the early printing era.
choices.C: The popular account misrepresents the printing press's effect on access to knowledge as faster and more uniform than it was.
choices.D: Printed books were expensive for a century.
choices.E: Printers focused on religious texts.

questions.explanation:
The final clause states the conclusion: the popular story compresses a slow process into a sudden revolution.
A — The historian says it eventually transformed access.
B — A premise.
D — A premise.
E — A premise.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The museum's decision to charge admission has been defended on the grounds that it raised revenue. That is undeniable. But the museum's mission is to make art accessible to everyone, and attendance among low-income visitors has dropped sharply. The decision therefore conflicts with the museum's mission.
questions.stem: The claim that the museum's mission is to make art accessible to everyone plays which role in the critic's argument?

choices.A: It is the conclusion.
choices.B: It is a concession.
choices.C: It is evidence that revenue increased.
choices.D: It is a claim the critic rejects.
choices.E: It is a premise that, combined with the attendance data, supports the conclusion.

questions.explanation:
Mission plus the attendance drop yields the conflict.
A — The conclusion is that the decision conflicts with the mission.
B — The concession is about revenue.
C — Unrelated.
D — The critic relies on it.

questions.stimulus:
Lena: Our team lost because the referee made bad calls.
Mark: The referee made a few bad calls, but they went against both teams equally. We lost because we missed eight free throws.
questions.stem: Mark responds to Lena by

choices.A: offering an alternative explanation for the outcome
choices.B: denying the referee made bad calls
choices.C: questioning the score
choices.D: attacking the referee
choices.E: agreeing with Lena

questions.explanation:
Mark credits missed free throws, not the referee.
B — He concedes some.
C — Not done.
D — Not done.
E — He disagrees.

questions.stimulus:
Paolo: The school should require uniforms because they reduce bullying over clothing.
Quin: Uniforms might reduce that kind of bullying, but they limit students' self-expression, which is more important.
questions.stem: Paolo and Quin disagree over whether

choices.A: bullying is a problem
choices.B: the school should require uniforms
choices.C: uniforms reduce clothing-based bullying
choices.D: uniforms are expensive
choices.E: self-expression is valuable

questions.explanation:
Paolo says require; Quin says self-expression is more important, implying don't.
A — Not in dispute.
C — Quin concedes they might.
D — Not discussed.
E — Paolo doesn't address it.

questions.stimulus: Every candidate who won the debate gained in the polls. No candidate who gained in the polls dropped out of the race. Therefore, no candidate who won the debate dropped out of the race.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: Every student who completed the project earned extra credit. No student who failed completed the project. So no student who failed earned extra credit.
choices.B: No student who failed earned extra credit. Some students completed the project. So some who completed the project did not fail.
choices.C: Every student who completed the project earned extra credit. Some students who earned extra credit failed. So some who completed the project failed.
choices.D: Every student who completed the project earned extra credit. No student who earned extra credit failed the course. Therefore, no student who completed the project failed the course.
choices.E: Most students who completed the project earned extra credit. So most passed.

questions.explanation:
All A are B; no B are C; so no A are C. An exact match.
A — Invalid: a student who failed could have earned extra credit some other way.
B — Invalid.
C — Invalid.
E — "Most" breaks the form.

questions.stimulus: Ever since I started carrying an umbrella, it hasn't rained. So carrying an umbrella prevents rain.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: My team wins when it practices. So practice helps.
choices.B: All my socks are lucky. So my team will always win.
choices.C: I wore lucky socks and my team won. So socks are comfortable.
choices.D: Ever since I started wearing my lucky socks, my team has won every game. So my socks cause my team to win.
choices.E: My team has won every game this season. So it will win the championship.

questions.explanation:
Both infer causation from a coincidence in time.
A — A plausible causal inference.
B — A different structure.
C — A non sequitur.
E — A prediction, a different flaw.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A dog park should ban a dog if the dog has bitten another dog or a person in the park.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: The park should ban Coco because she bit someone outside the park.
choices.B: The park should ban Max because he barks loudly.
choices.C: The park should ban all large dogs.
choices.D: The park should not ban Bella, who bit a person in the park, because she is usually friendly.
choices.E: The park should ban Rex, who bit another dog in the park last week.

questions.explanation:
He bit a dog in the park, so ban him.
A — The principle concerns bites in the park.
B — Barking isn't a condition.
C — Size isn't a condition.
D — Violates the principle.

questions.stimulus: Parent: My daughter shouldn't be penalized for missing the school play rehearsal. She was at her grandmother's funeral, and we informed the director in advance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the parent's position?

choices.A: Students should not be penalized for absences due to family emergencies when they notify the responsible person in advance.
choices.B: Parents should attend school plays.
choices.C: Directors should cancel rehearsals during holidays.
choices.D: Students should attend all rehearsals.
choices.E: Rehearsals should be optional.

questions.explanation:
Family emergency plus advance notice: no penalty.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Would favor a penalty.
E — Too broad.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: The scientist acted wrongly in publishing her findings on a dangerous virus in full detail. Although the research advanced understanding, the published methods could enable others to create a more dangerous version, and the scientific value could have been preserved by withholding the specific methods.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's judgment?

choices.A: Scientists should publish all findings in full.
choices.B: Dangerous research should never be conducted.
choices.C: Researchers should withhold details whose publication could enable serious harm when the research's scientific value can be preserved without them.
choices.D: Governments should fund virus research.
choices.E: Research is valuable only if published.

questions.explanation:
Facts: details enable harm, and value could be preserved without them. The principle covers both.
A — Would favor publishing.
B — Too broad.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Would favor publishing.

questions.stimulus: A city's public schools raised teacher salaries by 15 percent to attract more qualified teachers. Yet the number of applicants for teaching positions fell the following year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this?

choices.A: Teachers value job security.
choices.B: At the same time, neighboring districts raised salaries by 25 percent, making them more attractive by comparison.
choices.C: The salary increase was publicized.
choices.D: Some teachers retired.
choices.E: The city's schools are large.

questions.explanation:
Relative pay matters. Rivals offered even more.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Would predict more applicants.
D — Affects openings, not applicants.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: If the merger is approved, the company will relocate its headquarters. If the company relocates its headquarters, some employees will be laid off. No employees will be laid off.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: The company will relocate anyway.
choices.B: If there are layoffs, the merger was approved.
choices.C: Some employees will quit.
choices.D: The merger will be approved next year.
choices.E: The merger will not be approved.

questions.explanation:
Merger → relocate → layoffs. No layoffs, so no relocation, so no merger.
A — Relocation would mean layoffs.
B — Reverses the chain.
C — Not stated.
D — Not stated.

questions.stimulus: A company emailed a satisfaction survey to all its customers. Of the 300 customers who responded, 90 percent said they were very satisfied. The company concludes that about 90 percent of its customers are very satisfied.
questions.stem: The company's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to define "satisfied"
choices.B: overlooks the possibility that customers who chose to respond differ in satisfaction from those who did not
choices.C: relies on too small a sample
choices.D: assumes all customers received the email
choices.E: confuses satisfaction with loyalty

questions.explanation:
Respondents self-selected. Very satisfied or very unhappy customers may be more likely to reply.
A — Not the core flaw.
C — 300 may be adequate; the issue is who responded.
D — Possibly, but self-selection is the main problem.
E — Loyalty isn't discussed.

questions.stimulus: Safety analyst: More accidents involve drivers aged 30 to 50 than drivers over 70. Therefore, drivers aged 30 to 50 are more dangerous than drivers over 70.
questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes all accidents are equally serious
choices.B: fails to define "accident"
choices.C: ignores that there may be far more drivers aged 30 to 50 on the road, driving far more miles, than drivers over 70
choices.D: attacks older drivers
choices.E: relies on outdated accident data

questions.explanation:
Raw accident counts don't reflect risk per driver or per mile. A bigger group driving more will have more accidents even if each driver is safer.
A — Severity isn't the main gap.
B — Not the core flaw.
D — No attack.
E — No data issue.
tags: conflating rate and count across groups

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: Our new automatic refill program will improve patients' health, because patients who use it will no longer forget to refill their prescriptions.
questions.stem: The pharmacist's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: All medications improve health.
choices.B: Most patients currently forget to refill prescriptions.
choices.C: Other pharmacies do not offer automatic refills.
choices.D: Patients who receive their refills will take their medications as prescribed.
choices.E: The program is free.

questions.explanation:
Getting refills improves health only if patients actually take the medicine.
A — Too strong.
B — Not required. Some is enough.
C — Not required.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Traces of wine residue found in 7,000-year-old pottery jars at the Hajji site indicate that people there were making wine at that time.
questions.stem: The archaeologist's conclusion depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: The residue was not left by wine introduced into the jars at a much later date.
choices.B: Wine was the only beverage made at the site.
choices.C: Grapes grew wild near the site.
choices.D: The jars were made at the Hajji site.
choices.E: The people at the site traded wine.

questions.explanation:
If later occupants put wine in old jars, the residue wouldn't date wine-making to 7,000 years ago.
B — Not required.
C — Helpful but not required.
D — Helpful but not strictly required; the wine still had to be made by someone at the time.
E — Not required.

questions.stimulus: Every committee member who supports the proposal will vote for it. A majority of the committee supports the proposal. So the proposal will pass.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The proposal will pass only if a majority of the committee votes for it.
choices.B: The proposal will pass if a majority of the committee votes for it.
choices.C: Most members who vote for the proposal support it.
choices.D: No committee member who opposes the proposal will vote for it.
choices.E: Every committee member will vote.

questions.explanation:
Majority supports → majority votes for it. The missing link is majority votes → passes.
A — Makes a majority necessary for passage, not sufficient.
C — Doesn't connect votes to passage.
D — Doesn't connect votes to passage.
E — Doesn't connect votes to passage.

questions.stimulus: Epidemiologist: The rise in childhood asthma in Port Ellis over the past decade is due to increased air pollution from the new highway that runs through the city.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the epidemiologist's claim?

choices.A: The highway carries mostly trucks.
choices.B: Many children with asthma have allergies.
choices.C: Asthma rates rose most sharply among children living closest to the highway.
choices.D: Diagnosis of asthma has improved.
choices.E: Asthma rates rose nationally during the decade.

questions.explanation:
A gradient by distance from the source supports pollution as the cause.
A — Suggests heavier pollution but doesn't link it to asthma.
B — Irrelevant.
D — An alternative explanation for the rise.
E — Suggests broader causes.

questions.stimulus: A town found that after it added speed bumps to residential streets, the number of pedestrian accidents on those streets fell. Officials conclude the speed bumps improved safety.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the officials' conclusion?

choices.A: The town also added crosswalks.
choices.B: Speed bumps are inexpensive.
choices.C: Fewer people walked on those streets.
choices.D: Average driving speeds on those streets fell after the speed bumps were added.
choices.E: Residents complained about the speed bumps.

questions.explanation:
This confirms the mechanism: slower driving.
A — An alternative cause.
B — Irrelevant.
C — An alternative explanation.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A survey found that people who use standing desks report less back pain than people who use regular desks. The survey's authors conclude that standing desks reduce back pain.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the authors' conclusion?

choices.A: Standing burns more calories than sitting.
choices.B: Standing desks are becoming popular.
choices.C: Some standing-desk users have back pain.
choices.D: Standing desks are more expensive.
choices.E: Many people with severe back pain avoid standing desks because standing for long periods aggravates their condition.

questions.explanation:
If people with bad backs avoid standing desks, standing-desk users would report less pain regardless.
A — Irrelevant.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Exceptions don't undercut the trend.
D — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Since the restaurant added a children's menu, more families have been dining there. The owner concludes the children's menu attracted families.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the owner's conclusion?

choices.A: A new elementary school opened nearby at the same time.
choices.B: The restaurant is popular.
choices.C: The children's menu is inexpensive.
choices.D: Children like the menu.
choices.E: Some families don't order from the children's menu.

questions.explanation:
More families in the area could explain the increase.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Supports the owner.
D — Supports the owner.
E — Doesn't explain the increase.

questions.stimulus: All of the novels on the reading list were written before 1950. Some of the novels on the reading list were written by women. None of the novels written before 1950 that are on the reading list is available as an e-book.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Every novel written before 1950 is on the reading list.
choices.B: No novel written by a woman is available as an e-book.
choices.C: Most novels on the list were written by women.
choices.D: Some novels on the list were written after 1950.
choices.E: Some novels written by women are not available as e-books.

questions.explanation:
Some list novels are by women. All list novels are pre-1950, and no pre-1950 list novel is an e-book. So those novels by women aren't e-books.
A — Reverses the first statement.
B — Only list novels are covered.
C — Only some are.
D — Contradicts the first statement.

questions.stimulus: When a city replaced its traditional traffic signals at a busy intersection with a roundabout, the total number of collisions there stayed about the same, but collisions causing injury fell by 75 percent.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported?

choices.A: Drivers prefer roundabouts.
choices.B: Traffic volume at the intersection decreased.
choices.C: Collisions at the roundabout tended to be less severe than those at the former signalized intersection.
choices.D: Roundabouts reduce the total number of collisions.
choices.E: All intersections should be converted to roundabouts.

questions.explanation:
Same number of collisions, far fewer injuries. The collisions are less severe.
A — Not shown.
B — Not stated.
D — The total stayed the same.
E — A recommendation.

questions.stimulus: Some believe that bats are blind. But many bat species have good eyesight, and some fruit bats rely mainly on vision. The belief is therefore inaccurate.
questions.stem: The claim that some fruit bats rely mainly on vision plays which role?

choices.A: It is a concession.
choices.B: It supports the conclusion that the belief is inaccurate.
choices.C: It is the belief being rejected.
choices.D: It undermines the conclusion.
choices.E: It is the conclusion.

questions.explanation:
It's evidence against the blindness belief.
A — It isn't conceded.
C — That's the blindness belief.
D — It supports it.
E — The conclusion is that the belief is inaccurate.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Removing dams from the Kell River would restore salmon runs, since salmon could once again reach their upstream spawning grounds. Restored salmon runs would in turn provide food for bears and eagles and return ocean nutrients to the forest. So dam removal would benefit the entire river ecosystem, not just salmon.
questions.stem: The claim that removing dams would restore salmon runs plays which role in the ecologist's argument?

choices.A: It is a conclusion supported by one claim that in turn supports the argument's main conclusion.
choices.B: It is the main conclusion.
choices.C: It is a claim the ecologist argues against.
choices.D: It is offered without any support.
choices.E: It is a concession.

questions.explanation:
It's supported by "salmon could reach spawning grounds" and then feeds the benefits to bears, eagles, and the forest, which support the main conclusion.
B — The main conclusion is about the whole ecosystem.
C — The ecologist relies on it.
D — It's supported by the spawning-grounds point.
E — It isn't conceded.

questions.stimulus: Councilor: My opponent says the new park will cost too much. But she supported building the stadium, which cost five times as much. Her objection to the park's cost is therefore not credible.
questions.stem: The councilor's argument proceeds by

choices.A: arguing that parks are more valuable than stadiums
choices.B: showing that the stadium was a mistake
choices.C: providing evidence that the park is inexpensive
choices.D: challenging an opponent's position by pointing to an apparent inconsistency in her past positions
choices.E: appealing to public opinion

questions.explanation:
The councilor cites the opponent's stadium support to suggest inconsistency, which is a tu quoque move.
A — Not argued.
B — Not argued.
C — The park's cost isn't addressed.
E — Not done.

questions.stimulus:
Rhea: Standardized tests are the fairest way to evaluate applicants because every student takes the same test.
Seth: Every student takes the same test, but students from wealthier families can afford expensive test prep. So the tests aren't a fair measure.
questions.stem: Rhea and Seth disagree over whether

choices.A: test prep is expensive
choices.B: standardized tests are a fair way to evaluate applicants
choices.C: wealthier students score higher
choices.D: colleges should use tests
choices.E: every student takes the same test

questions.explanation:
Rhea says they're fairest; Seth says they aren't fair.
A — Rhea doesn't address this.
C — Seth implies this; Rhea doesn't address it.
D — Not exactly their dispute.
E — Seth agrees.

questions.stimulus:
Dara: The novel's plot is predictable, but its characters are so vivid that it's worth reading.
Emil: The characters are vivid, I agree. But a predictable plot ruins a novel for me, so I wouldn't recommend it.
questions.stem: Dara and Emil are committed to agreeing that

choices.A: the novel is worth reading
choices.B: the plot is original
choices.C: the plot ruins the novel
choices.D: the novel should be recommended
choices.E: the novel's characters are vivid

questions.explanation:
Dara says so, and Emil agrees.
A — Emil disagrees.
B — Dara calls it predictable, and Emil implies the same.
C — Only Emil says this.
D — Emil wouldn't.

questions.stimulus: Only applicants with a degree in engineering are considered for the position. Carmen is being considered for the position. So Carmen has a degree in engineering.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

choices.A: Only members may use the pool. Ravi is a member. So Ravi is using the pool.
choices.B: Ravi uses the pool every day. So he enjoys swimming.
choices.C: Members may use the pool. Ravi is not a member. So Ravi may not use the pool.
choices.D: Only members may use the pool. Ravi is using the pool. So Ravi is a member.
choices.E: Most members use the pool. Ravi is a member. So he uses it.

questions.explanation:
Only A can B; X does B; so X is A.
A — Treats a necessary condition as sufficient.
B — A non sequitur.
C — Denies the antecedent.
E — Probabilistic.

questions.stimulus: Every player on the All-Star team is among the best in the league. Therefore, the All-Star team would beat any team in the league.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.A: Every song on this album was a hit single. Therefore, this album is the best-selling album of the year.
choices.B: Every player on the team is tall. So the team's average height is high.
choices.C: The team won last year. So it will win this year.
choices.D: Some players on the team are fast. So the team will win.
choices.E: The choir won the regional contest. So every member of the choir is an excellent singer.

questions.explanation:
Both infer a property of the whole (team wins, album sells best) from strong parts. Teamwork or sales dynamics may differ.
B — Valid; an average of tall players is high.
C — A different flaw.
D — Starts from "some," a different flaw.
E — Reasons from the whole to each part, the reverse direction.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A company should offer a refund for a canceled event if the cancellation was the company's decision, but not if the cancellation resulted from severe weather.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.A: EventCo should refund tickets for the concert canceled because of a blizzard.
choices.B: EventCo should refund half the ticket price for all cancellations.
choices.C: EventCo should not refund tickets for the concert canceled because of a blizzard.
choices.D: EventCo should not refund tickets for a concert it canceled because of low sales.
choices.E: EventCo should refund tickets only for outdoor events.

questions.explanation:
Severe weather: no refund.
A — Violates the principle.
B — Not addressed.
D — The company's decision means a refund.
E — Not addressed.

questions.stimulus: Professor: Although Tomas's paper is excellent, I must give it a failing grade. Large portions were copied from a published source without attribution, and the course syllabus states that plagiarism results in failure.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the professor's position?

choices.A: Professors should not read published sources.
choices.B: Clearly stated course policies should be applied consistently, regardless of the quality of the work involved.
choices.C: Excellent papers should always receive high grades.
choices.D: Students should cite all sources.
choices.E: Plagiarism is common.

questions.explanation:
The syllabus policy applies despite the paper's excellence.
A — Irrelevant.
C — Would favor a high grade.
D — True, but doesn't justify applying the policy despite quality.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: In the country of Marovia, the proportion of adults who smoke has declined steadily for twenty years. Yet the number of new lung cancer diagnoses each year has increased over the same period.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how both trends can be true?

choices.A: Lung cancer treatments have improved.
choices.B: Some nonsmokers develop lung cancer.
choices.C: Lung cancer often develops decades after exposure, and Marovia's population of older adults, many of whom smoked heavily when they were younger, has grown substantially.
choices.D: Cigarette prices have risen.
choices.E: Smoking rates have declined in other countries.

questions.explanation:
Today's diagnoses reflect past smoking, and the aging population includes many former heavy smokers.
A — Treatment doesn't affect diagnoses.
B — True, but doesn't explain the increase.
D — Consistent with less smoking; doesn't explain more diagnoses.
E — Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: A tech company reports that employees who use its new productivity software complete 20 percent more tasks per week than employees who don't. The company concludes that the software increases productivity.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the company's conclusion?

choices.A: whether the employees who adopted the software were already completing more tasks before they began using it
choices.B: how many features the software has
choices.C: whether other companies sell similar software
choices.D: how much the software costs
choices.E: whether the software is easy to use

questions.explanation:
If adopters were already more productive, the gap reflects who chose the software, not its effect.
B — Irrelevant.
C — Irrelevant.
D — Irrelevant.
E — Ease matters only indirectly.

questions.stimulus: The festival will be held outdoors unless it rains. If the festival is held outdoors, food trucks will attend. If food trucks attend, the city will close Main Street. The city did not close Main Street.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: The festival was held outdoors.
choices.B: The festival was canceled.
choices.C: If it rains, the festival is held indoors.
choices.D: Food trucks attended.
choices.E: It rained.

questions.explanation:
No Main Street closure → no food trucks → not outdoors → (unless it rains, it's outdoors) it rained.
A — That would have brought food trucks.
B — It could have been held indoors.
C — Not stated; rain is only necessary for not being outdoors.
D — That would have closed Main Street.

questions.stimulus: Urban planner: Critics say that the new high-rise apartments will strain the neighborhood's schools and transit. Some strain is likely in the short term. But the buildings' developer is required to fund a new school annex and two additional bus lines, and the added residents will support local businesses that have struggled for years. On balance, the high-rises will benefit the neighborhood.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the urban planner's argument?

choices.A: The high-rises will strain schools and transit in the short term.
choices.B: The developer must fund a school annex and bus lines.
choices.C: The critics of the high-rises are mistaken about every point.
choices.D: Overall, the new high-rise apartments will be good for the neighborhood.
choices.E: Local businesses have struggled for years.

questions.explanation:
"On balance" introduces the conclusion; the funding requirements and business support outweigh the conceded short-term strain.
A — A concession.
B — A premise.
C — The planner concedes some strain.
E — Background for a premise.
